HOW I USE CLAUDE: MY METHOD, UPDATED SEPTEMBER 2026 (CLAUDE.MD, OKF BRAIN, CHAT/COWORK/CODE, SKILLS)
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/how-to/
Published: 2026-05-30
================================================================

Hugo Lahutte's complete method for working with Claude, updated in September 2026: versioned CLAUDE.md files, a private Brain in the OKF format, the Chat / Cowork / Code split, two agents, skills and MCP connectors, Compound Engineering and session capture, guardrails. A step-by-step guide with a prompt to copy.

Method · The most requested guide · v2, September 2026
How I use Claude
In fifteen months, the way I work with Claude has changed in nature. At first, a file of instructions pasted into a chat. Today, a system: versioned files, a private brain, three ways of using Claude, two agents, packaged procedures and guardrails. Here's the setup as it actually runs — and where to start if you're just getting going.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · First version: May 30, 2026 · ~12 min read In 30 seconds
- Context is everything, not the prompt. What makes Claude good in my setup is what it knows about me before I type the first line.
- Two layers of context: the CLAUDE.md files (how to work with me) and the Brain (what we know: entities, projects, decisions, method), a private wiki in the open OKF format that all my Claude instances read.
- Three doors: Chat writes and thinks, Cowork executes office work, Code acts inside my projects. Two agents (HL and Cobra), skills for procedures, connectors for tools.
- The loop that makes it all grow: every error becomes a rule, every session becomes a capture. And one golden rule: the AI proposes, the human validates.
1. The principle: context is everything
When you're starting out, you think quality comes from the prompt — the right formula, the magic phrase. That's wrong, or rather it's 20% of the story. The other 80% is context: everything Claude knows before you write your first line. Who you are, what you do, how you like to be answered, what's already been decided, what's already broken.
The craft has had a name since 2025: context engineering. That's what my method is — organizing what Claude knows, in two layers that don't mix:
- How to work with me → the CLAUDE.md files (section 2).
- What we know → the Brain, my private wiki (section 3).
The first layer rarely changes (tone, rules, principles). The second changes all the time (projects, decisions, the state of ongoing work). Keeping them apart stops the rules from drowning in the facts, and the facts from hardening into rules.
Today's conversationThe request, the attached files, the tool results. Ephemeral. The CLAUDE.md files — “how to work with me”Tone, format, principles, hard rules, extensions by domain. Stable, versioned. The Brain — “what we know”Entities, building blocks, projects, method, notes, sessions. Living, dated, private. Skills and connectorsThe procedures loaded on demand, and the tools plugged in (Shopify, Drive, GitHub…).
2. The CLAUDE.md files: “how to work with me”
The historical core of the system hasn't moved: .md files (Markdown, plain text) that Claude reads at startup. A main CLAUDE.md that sets my tone (informal, direct, no preamble), my four working principles (Karpathy-style), my behavior rules (honesty, web search on anything that may have changed, “I don't know” rather than making things up) and context management.
Then extensions, loaded depending on the domain:
- CLAUDE-strat.md — strategy, marketing, communications, business.
- CLAUDE-dev.md — the generic coding conventions (discipline, deliverables, framed autonomous loops).
- CLAUDE-dev-cobra.md — the Cobra-specific rules (surgical Odoo deploys, Shopify sync, topics in progress).
What's changed since May: these files no longer live only in a chat's “Project Instructions.” They're versioned in the repositories (a docs/ folder, a CLAUDE-{domaine}-{projet}.md naming convention), read automatically by Claude Code, and re-read on a fixed schedule — because a wrong context file is worse than no file at all. I told the story of the refresh that exposed stale critical points (hosting, deploy workflow, number of modules): Claude was starting every session with a wrong mental model of the infrastructure.
Every brand also has its own DNA file: history, positioning, what we say and what we don't. An hour of writing with Claude, and everything it produces about the brand goes up a level.
→ The dedicated guide: Writing a good CLAUDE.md.
3. The Brain: “what we know”
This is the real new thing of summer 2026. Until then, what I knew about my projects lived in Claude project documents, not shareable between tools, and in my head. Since August, all of it lives in a Brain: a private git repository of Markdown files with a small header (type, title, description, tags, date, confidentiality), organized in seven folders:
- entities — the group's organizations (Cobra, Haute Fidélité, HiFi Lovers, HL Consulting…): what it is, where it lives online, my position, what runs on it;
- building blocks — the systems under construction, with their living specifications and their dated decisions;
- projects — anything with a beginning and an end;
- method — how I work (prescriptive: a rule to follow);
- notes — what I think (revisable: an opinion to cite, with its “what could take it down” section);
- sessions — the raw log;
- personal — always private.
The format is called OKF (Open Knowledge Format), an open specification published by Google Cloud in June 2026 that formalizes the “LLM wiki” popularized by Andrej Karpathy. Nothing to install: Markdown, links between files, an index at the root. My Claude instances read it through a plain GitHub connector, starting from the index and following the links. No vector database, no server — as long as navigation is enough. The day “find me what we said about order dedup” no longer surfaces the right document, that'll be the signal to build the index. Not before.
Two rules hold the Brain together:
- A stale brain is worse than an empty brain. A missing document triggers a search; a wrong document triggers a decision. Hence the capture ritual (section 7), which updates the reference pages and not just the log.
- We never invent the content of a shell (empty placeholder page). An empty doc that says it's empty is honest. A doc filled in by guesswork is a trap that goes off six months later, exactly when you trust it.
The Brain stays private. This Knowledge Hub is its curated version, rewritten to be read by humans and cited by AIs. Moving from one to the other is an editorial act, never a sync.
→ The dedicated guide: What is a Brain (and the OKF format) · the journal entry: The Brain, my private wiki read by all my Claude instances.
4. Chat, Cowork, Code: who does what
Three doors into the same Claude, and a split that structures all my work:
ChatWrite, thinkIn my setupAngle, text, tone, strategy. It has my voice. We stop at Markdown: no HTML, no git.ExampleWriting this page, framing a spec, settling a positioning. CoworkDelegate office workIn my setupFiles, spreadsheets, presentations, built-in browser, scheduled tasks — no terminal. On desktop, web and mobile since summer 2026.ExamplePreparing a deck, going through a file, running a Monday routine. CodeAct inside projectsIn my setupReads and edits files, runs commands, deploys, updates the internal linking. In the terminal, on the web or from my phone.ExampleAn Odoo module, this page live a minute after the push, an internal app. The boundary rule is simple and I stick to it: Chat writes, Code executes. A Chat session produces a validated Markdown; Code turns it into a deliverable (HTML page, JSON-LD, sitemap, llms.txt, commit, push). The two halves have different success criteria — the accuracy of the argument on one side, conformance to the template on the other. Mixing them in one session means losing both.
→ The dedicated guide: Chat, Cowork or Code: which one to use.
5. Two agents, two accounts
I run two Claude instances, deliberately kept apart:
- Claude · HL — my personal account: steering, strategy, editorial, method, this site, the group's building blocks. Extension CLAUDE-strat.md.
- Claude · Cobra — the company account: Odoo and Shopify development, purely technical. Extension CLAUDE-dev.md + Cobra. It knows the codebase by heart and never talks about my personal projects.
Both write in the same journal (the Claude · HL and Claude · Cobra badges on each entry) and read the same Brain — but the Cobra Claude only writes to the Cobra pages, the sessions and the technical building blocks. Not a technical permission: a governance rule, so as not to mix two perimeters in a base read from both sides.
6. Skills and connectors: the procedures and the arms
Two building blocks have taken up a lot of room this year.
Skills. A skill is a procedure packaged in a folder (a SKILL.md file, sometimes scripts) that Claude loads when the situation calls for it. In my setup, three do most of the work:
- kh-post-brief — at the end of a session, with any AI, produce the brief for a journal entry: title, vertical, tags from the whitelist, sections, sanitization guardrails. I paste the brief into Claude Code, which publishes the FR + EN entry and all the internal linking.
- brain — read, search and update the Brain, with a strict write gate: never a write without an explicit instruction.
- wiki-capture — the end-of-session ritual (section 7).
A skill's strength: it's portable. The text of kh-post-brief works pasted into ChatGPT or Gemini. It's written method, not magic.
Connectors. Claude plugged into my tools through the MCP standard: Shopify (both stores), Google Drive, Gmail, GitHub, Qonto, the host of my apps, Odoo through code. Result: it works on my real tools, not on a demo — and it can now send an email or move a file, under validation. One non-negotiable rule: the assistant never has more rights than the person talking to it.
→ The guides: What is a skill (and a hook, a subagent) · What is MCP.
7. The loop: every error becomes a rule, every session a capture
The guiding principle is still Compound Engineering: when Claude trips over a recurring point, I don't grumble, I add the rule. The file improves with use, and all future work benefits. An Odoo production release that broke several things became a hard rule in CLAUDE-dev-cobra.md; an agent burning through its budget in a loop became a standard guardrail.
Since August, the loop has a second level. At the end of a session, the capture skill does four things, in this order: re-read the session and identify the entity and the topic; write the sessions/ entry in the OKF format; propose targeted changes to the reference pages affected (building blocks, entities); run the confidentiality filter and propose the commit. The third point is the one you're tempted to skip — so it's the one at the top of the procedure. Without it, the log grows while the pages go stale in silence.
The trigger isn't automatic, and that's deliberate: no mechanism fires reliably on “the conversation is getting long” across every client. Instead, a rule in the CLAUDE.md: when the conversation gets long, Claude offers to wrap up with a handoff brief — and to capture into the Brain. It works everywhere, including on mobile, with no infrastructure.
Do→ Spot the error or the lesson→ Rule in CLAUDE.md+ Capture in the Brain→ Next session, higher up every session → The guide: Compound Engineering.
8. The guardrails: the AI proposes, the human validates
The more Claude acts, the more the framework matters. The rules I apply everywhere, from the smallest script to my internal systems:
- An agent has four things before it's launched: an explicit goal (“we'll know it's good when…”), a budget cap, a bounded frequency, a measurable success criterion.
- Automatic reads, validated writes. Reading, refreshing, proposing: automatic. Changing a price, a stock level, a campaign, an email, a publication: human validation. The standard flow: request → analysis → preview of the change → validation → execution → log → measurement.
- Three regimes depending on the nature of the action: mechanical = automatic; factual reply = generated then validated with one button; judgment = human draft, always.
- Check before coding. My Odoo change-request pipeline has the AI review every request in two passes: it asks structured questions, the server checks them against the real database in read-only mode, the AI concludes. It has already requalified a development request into ten minutes of configuration.
- No secrets in the code or in the Brain, surgical deploys (never a whole branch, always the exact commit), no cron that publishes on its own.
→ The guide: The AI proposes, the human validates: the guardrails that hold.
9. Where to start
Look at existing files for inspiration, but don't copy them — they're tuned to a context that isn't yours. My recommendation, in order:
- Create a Project on claude.ai and ask Claude to build your CLAUDE.md with the prompt below. One hour, and you stop re-explaining yourself.
- Write the DNA file for your company or brand. That's where communications and content go up a level.
- Open a minimal Brain: a folder with an index.md, one page per organization (“what it is, where it is, my position, what runs on it”) and one method page. Markdown, a private repository, a connector. The rest fills in session after session — and never invent a page you don't know how to fill in.
- Move to Code or Cowork when you want Claude to do, not just answer. And set the four guardrails before the first agent.
The prompt to copy and paste to generate your files:
Prompt — generate your CLAUDE.md and your starter BrainI want to build my context system for Claude: a CLAUDE.md file, a DNA file for my organization, and a minimal Brain. I'm attaching CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE-strat.md and CLAUDE-dev.md files as references. Read them to understand the structure, the expected level of detail and the overall logic — but don't copy them: they're tuned to another context, not mine. What I want to build: 1. A main CLAUDE.md that covers: - My tone and preferred format (formal or informal? prose or lists? how long should answers be?) - My professional context: what I do, my company, my industry, my role - The behavior rules to enforce (web search on anything that may have changed, honesty, no flattery, “I don't know” rather than making things up, push back if my idea is bad) - What I DON'T want (preambles, end-of-answer summaries, frameworks I didn't ask for, over-complication) - Context management: when the conversation gets long, offer to wrap up with a handoff brief - The logic for calling the extension files: this file must know when to load the others depending on the context 2. A [NameOfMyOrganization].md file that describes its DNA: - History and context - What we do, for whom, why - Positioning and values - Brand tone: what we say, what we don't say - This file will be loaded whenever Claude produces content related to this organization 3. A minimal Brain: an index.md and, for each important organization in my professional life, a Markdown page with a header (type, title, description, tags, timestamp, confidentialite) that answers four questions — what it is, where it lives online, what my position is, what systems run on it. If you don't know how to fill in a section, leave it empty and ask me: don't make anything up. 4. If I have recurring technical or business needs, we'll create the appropriate extensions (the equivalent of CLAUDE-dev.md or CLAUDE-strat.md) once the foundation is in place. Method: ask me ONE question at a time. We build section by section. When we've covered everything, you generate each complete file in Markdown, separately. That's all you need to get started. The rest builds itself through use: every friction becomes a rule, every session becomes a capture, and your system gets better on its own.
10. What's changed since May 2026
For those who read the first version of this page — or who want to gauge how fast the ways of working are moving:
- The CLAUDE.md files are versioned in the repositories and split by convention (generic / specific), instead of living in a chat.
- The Brain exists (August 2026): knowledge has moved out of project documents to become a private wiki, readable by all my tools.
- Cowork has become a real third door: desktop, web, mobile, built-in browser, memory unified with the chat, scheduled routines.
- Skills have replaced reusable prompts. A procedure lives in a folder, not in a notepad.
- Connectors act, not just read: sending an email, managing a file — under validation.
- The Claude 5 family (Sonnet 5 in June, Opus 5 in July, Fable 5.1 on September 1) has changed the math: the right model is still the cheapest one that does the job, but “the job” has become much longer and more autonomous.
- Guardrails have become systems, not instructions: validation before writing, log, measurement after action.
Starting from scratch with AI?
Before the method, get the basics without jargon: what generative AI is, what an “LLM” is, who the big players are and what they can't do.

My system, in detail and dated
The journal tells every step: the birth of the CLAUDE.md system (May), its refresh and its split (June), the adoption of the Brain in the OKF format (August) and HL OS, the system that builds on all of this (September).

WHAT IS A “BRAIN” (A PRIVATE WIKI IN THE OKF FORMAT), AND WHY IT'S MY REAL ASSET
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-un-brain-okf.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

A Brain is the durable memory of what you know and decide, in Markdown files readable by all your AIs. The open OKF format (Google Cloud, June 2026), the seven folders of mine, reading through a GitHub connector with no database or server, the capture ritual, and the rule that holds it all together: a stale brain is worse than an empty brain.

Home › Guides › What is a Brain?
Guides · Method
What is a “Brain”,and why it's my real asset
A Brain is the durable memory of everything you know and decide, written in text files that all your AIs can read. Mine is in the open OKF format, in a private repository. Here's what it is, how it fills up, and the rule that holds it together: a stale brain is worse than an empty brain.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~7 min read Brain OKF méthode Claude vulgarisation
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- A Brain is a folder of Markdown files (plain text + a small header) that describes your organizations, your projects, your decisions and the way you work. Your AIs read it before answering you.
- The OKF format (Open Knowledge Format, Google Cloud, June 2026) standardizes this “LLM wiki”: a single required field, links between files, an index. Zero software to install.
- What holds it together isn't the tech: it's the update ritual, and two rules — a stale brain is worse than an empty brain; we never invent a page we don't know how to fill in.
1. The problem: AI has a short memory, and a siloed one
An AI assistant only “retains” what fits in its context window — the current conversation, plus whatever you've given it to read. Close the conversation, and everything starts from zero. The assistants' memory features help with your preferences, but they're tied to one tool, opaque, and impossible to re-read or correct by hand.
In my case, the symptom was clear: what I knew about Cobra, Haute Fidélité and the building blocks under construction lived in Claude project documents (not shareable between tools), in conversation threads, and in my head. Two Claude instances, a personal account and a work account, that didn't know the same things. And with every new piece of work, ten minutes of re-explaining.
2. What it is, concretely
A Brain is a private git repository full of Markdown files. Each file starts with a header (YAML: a few key: value lines) followed by a free-text body. Mine fits in seven folders:
entitiesThe organizationsCobra, Haute Fidélité, HiFi Lovers, HL Consulting… Four questions per page: what it is, where it lives online, my position, what runs on it. building blocksThe systems under constructionA living spec, a dev plan with success criteria, a dated Decisions section. projectsWhat has an endA site, a trip, a redesign. As opposed to entities, which carry on. methodHow I workPrescriptive: a rule an agent must follow. Chat vs Code, compound engineering, capture. notesWhat I thinkRevisable: an opinion to cite, with a status (draft, held, revised, abandoned) and its “what could take it down” section. sessionsThe raw logOne entry per work session that produced something. The raw material for this site's public entries. personalOutside businessAlways private. How things work, never the data: no credentials, no third-party names. Seven folders, an index at the root, links between pages: that's the graph. Method and notes look alike and don't serve the same purpose — one is applied, the other is cited.
The format is called OKF — Open Knowledge Format. It's an open specification published by Google Cloud in June 2026 that formalizes the “LLM wiki” popularized by Andrej Karpathy: Markdown, a YAML header with a single required field (type) and a few optional fields (title, description, resource, tags, date), Markdown links between documents. An OKF bundle can be read in any editor, renders on GitHub, and any search tool knows how to index it.
I kept six fields, plus two of my own: confidentialite (prive or publiable — private or publishable) — the guardrail made machine-readable — and auteur (me, Claude HL or Claude Cobra), because without it, there's no way six months later to judge how reliable a page on a given topic is. A small checking script (a linter) verifies all of this before every commit: fields present, links that exist, no secrets, note-specific rules.
# At the top of every file — YAML, then the text --- type: Brique # Entité | Brique | Projet | Perso | Méthode | Note | Session title: Knowledge description: One sentence. The one that makes you want to open it. tags: [knowledge, okf] timestamp: 2026-08-21T23:34:30Z confidentialite: prive # prive | publiable auteur: claude-hl # hugo | claude-hl | claude-cobra ---
3. How my AIs read it
Here's a decision that saved me weeks of work: no database, no server, no semantic search. The repository is private on GitHub; my Claude clients have the GitHub connector plugged in; they read the Brain directly, starting from the index.md and following the links. That's exactly what OKF's “progressive disclosure” is meant to allow.
Honesty: it works by navigation, not by search. That's enough as long as the bundle stays within a few dozen documents. I wrote down the switch criterion rather than building the step: the day “find me what we said about order dedup” no longer surfaces the right document, that'll be the signal to build a search index (embeddings + vector database). Not before. Writing down the signal that will tell you it's time to build almost always beats building as a precaution.
Brain (OKF) Claude · HLChat, Cowork, Code — personal account Claude · CobraOdoo / Shopify dev — work account Other assistantsAny client with a GitHub connector MeA text editor, anywhere A format, not a service: OKF doesn't sync anything, doesn't search anything. What lets one wiki serve several AIs is the access layer — and a GitHub connector is enough as long as the bundle is small.
4. How it fills up (and doesn't go stale)
This is the part that matters. A knowledge base runs at two speeds: the log grows on its own (writing an entry is rewarding and risk-free), and the reference pages go stale in silence (updating them means re-reading what you wrote and admitting it has moved). Nothing flags the gap. An agent querying the base sees a structured, dated, authoritative document — and answers with it.
Hence the conviction that structures everything: a stale brain is worse than an empty brain. A missing document triggers a search; a wrong document triggers a decision. And the better the rest of the bundle is kept, the more you trust it, the more a stale page costs.
The remedy is a ritual, not a tool. At the end of a session, a capture skill does four things, in this order:
- re-read the session, identify the entity and the topic;
- write the sessions/ entry in the OKF format;
- propose targeted changes to the reference pages affected — that's the point you're tempted to skip, so it sits at the top of the procedure;
- run the confidentiality filter, then propose the commit.
Three rules complete the ritual:
- We never invent the content of a shell (empty placeholder page). A document tagged “to fill in” opens with a box that says so and asks questions instead of answering them. An empty doc that says it's empty is honest; a doc filled in by guesswork is a trap that will go off six months later, at the precise moment you trust it.
- A conviction without a counter-argument isn't a conviction, it's a reflex. Every note carries a “what could take it down” section. If there's nothing to put there, we say so, rather than writing a hollow section.
- A document we no longer believe is never deleted: it moves to abandoned status. Knowing why you were wrong is reusable; a hole in the base isn't.
5. Brain, CLAUDE.md, Knowledge Hub: who does what
Three things that look alike and shouldn't be confused:
CLAUDE.md
How to work with me
- Tone, principles, hard rules
- Rarely changes
- Loaded at every session
- Private, versioned with the code
+ Brain (OKF)
What we know
- Entities, projects, decisions, method, notes
- Changes all the time
- Read on demand, by navigation
- Private — a connector, not a sync
And this Knowledge Hub is the third thing: the curated version of the Brain, rewritten to be read by humans and cited by AIs. Nothing marked prive can end up here, and even for a publiable document, it takes a human action. Moving from one to the other is an editorial act, never a sync. A good Brain contains things that will never get out — that's what makes it useful.
6. Where to start
Small. A private repository, an index.md that lists the folders, and three to five pages: one per important organization in your professional life (the four questions), one method page with your working rules. Plug the GitHub connector into your assistant, and check the criterion that matters: from any conversation, does a question about a project surface the right document?
Then, the ritual: at the end of every session that produced something, a session entry and an update of the pages affected. Three to five dictated lines are enough; the rest formats itself. And remember the rule that argues even harder for pruning than for updating: a base of fifteen living pages beats a base of two hundred half-dead ones.
Going further
- → What is context (and why it's everything) — the context window, what goes into it, and why the Brain is a chosen memory.
- → Writing a good CLAUDE.md — the other layer of context, the one that rarely changes.
- → Compound Engineering — the loop that fills the Brain instead of letting it go stale.
Real case. Adopting the format and the decisions made that day → The Brain: my private wiki in the OKF format, read by all my Claude instances. The OKF spec, at Google Cloud → How the Open Knowledge Format can improve data sharing.

WHAT IS AN AI'S "CONTEXT," AND WHY IT'S EVERYTHING (CONTEXT WINDOW, COMPACTION, MEMORY)
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-le-contexte.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

Context is everything the model sees at the moment it answers: instructions, files, history, tool results — nothing else. The context window explained simply (up to a million tokens on Claude 5, but attention gets diluted), what goes into it by layers (CLAUDE.md, Brain, skills, connectors, conversation), what happens when it overflows (compaction, handoff brief, capture), the difference from memory, and four context engineering reflexes.

Home › Guides › What is context?
Guides · Method
What is "context,"and why it's everything
We all started out looking for the right prompt. The real lever is elsewhere: in everything the AI knows at the moment you talk to it — and in what it no longer knows once the conversation drags on. Context explained simply: the window, what goes in, what falls out, and the four reflexes that change the quality of everything.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read contexte méthode LLM vulgarisation
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The visual body
- 3 Going further
In 30 seconds
- Context is everything the model "sees" at the instant it answers: your instructions, the context files, the attached documents, the conversation history, the results of its tools. Nothing else. It has no hidden memory.
- It all fits in a limited window (up to a million tokens on Claude 5 models). The fuller it gets, the more attention gets diluted: a long conversation gets worse, not better.
- The craft is called context engineering: organizing what the AI knows (CLAUDE.md, Brain, skills), splitting things up (one conversation per topic, subagents for heavy reads), and knowing when to close with a handoff brief.
1. The context window: the workbench
Picture a workbench. Everything laid out on it, the model can read and use to answer. Everything that isn't on it doesn't exist for the model — even if you told it yesterday, even if it's in another thread. That bench is the context window, and it's measured in tokens (fragments of words).
It's big — a million tokens on recent models, several books' worth — but two things make it less comfortable than it looks. First, everything laid out on it is re-read at every response: a long conversation costs more and answers more slowly. Second, the model's attention gets diluted: the more cluttered the bench, the more likely it is to miss the detail that matters, mix up two instructions, or reopen a decision you'd already settled three hours earlier. A conversation that drags on is not a conversation that gets better.
The base instructionsHow the tool works, then your CLAUDE.md: tone, principles, rules. Always there, has to stay short. What's loaded on demandA skill when your request matches, a page from the Brain, an attached document, the connected tools (connectors). The conversation historyEverything that's been said, by you and by it. That's what grows — and what ends up overflowing. The tool resultsA web search, a file read, a command run. Often the bulkiest, rarely the most useful after the fact. Everything on the bench is re-read at every response. Context engineering is deciding what goes on it, and when you clear it.
2. What goes into the context (by layers)
The right way to think about it is in layers, from the most stable to the most volatile:
- The rules — the CLAUDE.md. How to work with me. Changes little, loaded every time: hence the obsession with keeping it short.
- The knowledge — the Brain. What we know. Changes all the time, loaded on demand: the page for the entity at hand, not the whole wiki.
- The procedures — the skills. Loaded only when the request matches, so they don't pollute conversations that don't need them.
- The tools — the connectors. Every connected tool adds its description to the context; plugging in forty connectors "just in case" costs space at every response.
- The conversation — today's request, the attached documents, the history.
This hierarchy is the same as the one in my method. That's no coincidence: the method is a way of organizing context.
3. When it overflows: compaction, handoff brief, capture
When the bench is full, the tool compacts: it replaces the beginning of the conversation with a summary. It's automatic in Claude Code and in the API. It's useful, and it's risky: the summary keeps what's essential according to the model, not necessarily according to you. I've already seen a session pick back up after compaction having forgotten a constraint I'd set at the start — it was in the summarized part, and the summary had smoothed it over.
My answer is twofold, and it's in my CLAUDE.md:
- The handoff brief. When the conversation drags on, Claude offers to close with a brief: where things stand, what's decided, what's left, the constraints. I start over in a fresh conversation with that brief. A clean bench, and nothing forgotten — because I'm the one who validated what had to stay.
- The capture. Whatever durable thing the session produced (a decision, a lesson, a project status) doesn't stay in the history: it goes in the Brain. Tomorrow's context gets built today.
4. What about "memory"?
Assistants have memory features: Claude retains your preferences and the context of your projects from one conversation to the next — and since August 2026, that memory is shared between chat and Cowork. It's handy for what's implicit (your style, your ongoing projects). But it's a memory you never re-read, that's hard to correct, and that stays inside one tool.
The Brain is chosen memory: explicit, re-readable, versioned, correctable by hand, read by all my tools. The two coexist. The rule I apply: whatever commits a decision or describes a project goes in the Brain; whatever is about convenience ("he prefers short lists") can stay in the tool's memory.
5. The four reflexes
Reflex 1One conversation per topicNew topic, new conversation. Mixing the fall strategy and an Odoo bug in the same thread degrades both. Reflex 2Load the right file, not everythingThe page for the entity at hand, the matching skill, the useful document. Not "the whole folder just in case." Reflex 3Delegate heavy readsA long report, an entire repo: a subagent reads and returns the conclusion. The main conversation stays light. Reflex 4Close with a handoff briefBefore it overflows: a brief validated by you, a fresh conversation, a capture in the Brain.
6. From the prompt to the system
Eighteen months ago, the fashionable skill was prompt engineering: finding the formula. It hasn't gone away — a good prompt still counts — but it has become the small part of the job. What separates someone who "uses ChatGPT" from someone who ships things to production with AI is what they've built around the conversation: stable rules, up-to-date knowledge, filed procedures, framed tools, and the discipline of clearing the bench.
The right mental model: you're not writing prompts, you're managing the attention of a very competent, very distractible collaborator who only knows what you've put in front of them.
Going further
- → Writing a good prompt — the conversation layer, done right.
- → Writing a good CLAUDE.md — the rules layer.
- → What is a Brain — the knowledge layer.
- → How much does AI cost — why a cluttered context is expensive.
Real case. A post-compaction restart that nearly went wrong → Shopify collections SEO fix.

WHAT IS A "SKILL" (AND A HOOK, A SUBAGENT, A PLUGIN)?
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-un-skill.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

A skill is a procedure written in a folder (a SKILL.md file, sometimes scripts) that Claude loads on its own when your request matches; a hook is an automatic, deterministic script; a subagent is a delegated Claude with its own context; a plugin is the package that installs it all. What each one does, my three everyday skills, and how to choose between an instruction, a skill, a hook and a connector.

Home › Guides › What is a skill?
Guides · Getting set up
What is a "skill"(and a hook, a subagent, a plugin)?
When you're explaining the same procedure to Claude for the third time, that's a skill in disguise. A skill is a procedure written in a folder, which Claude loads on its own when the situation calls for it. Around it, three words that keep coming up: hook, subagent, plugin. Here's what each one does, and which to pick.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read skill Claude Code agent vulgarisation
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The visual body
- 3 Going further
In 30 seconds
- A skill = a folder with a SKILL.md file (the procedure, in text) and sometimes scripts. Claude loads it on demand, when your request matches. It's packaged know-how, portable from one tool to another.
- A hook = a script that fires automatically at a specific moment (before a command, after a change). Deterministic: it doesn't "think," it checks or blocks.
- A subagent = a Claude delegated to a subtask, with its own context. A plugin = the package that installs skills, hooks, subagents and connectors in one go.
1. The problem: the procedure you keep re-explaining
Publishing an entry on this site takes about twenty steps: the page, its English twin, the journal index, the homepage teaser, the sitemap, the llms.txt, the search index, the counters, a consistency check. The first six times, I explained it to Claude at the start of the session. The seventh time, I realized the problem wasn't Claude: it was me keeping the procedure in my head instead of writing it down.
The CLAUDE.md takes care of general rules (tone, principles, pitfalls). But a twenty-step procedure has no business there: it would weigh down every conversation, including the ones that don't need it. I needed a place for procedures, loaded only when useful. That's the skill.
2. The skill: a procedure in a folder
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file: at the top, a name and a description (that's what Claude reads to decide whether the skill applies to your request); below, the procedure in plain text, with its rules, its examples and its guardrails. Optionally, scripts or reference files alongside. Nothing else.
Three skills do the bulk of my work:
- kh-post-brief — at the end of a session, with any AI, produce the brief for a journal entry: title, vertical, author, tags from the whitelist, status, sections (context, what was done, what was hard, stack, what it illustrates), visuals to attach, and the sanitization guardrails (no secrets, no sensitive financial figures, no internal app URLs). I paste the brief into Claude Code, which publishes the FR + EN entry and all the cross-linking.
- brain — read, search and update my Brain, with a strict write gate: read freely, write only on explicit instruction ("note that in my Brain"), never turn a discussion into a write.
- wiki-capture — the end-of-session ritual: the session entry and the update of the reference pages.
Name + descriptionOne sentence that says when this skill applies. It's the trigger: Claude compares it to your request. The procedureThe steps, in order, in plain text. With a filled-in example: one example is worth ten lines of explanation. The guardrailsWhat we never do (secrets, amounts, internal URLs), the cases where we stop and ask. Scripts and references (optional)A check script, a template, a whitelist. Loaded only if the procedure needs them. A skill isn't magic: it's written method, filed in the right place and loaded at the right moment.
The property that matters: a skill is portable. The text of kh-post-brief is written to be pasted into ChatGPT or Gemini at the end of a session; the AI returns the brief, and Claude Code publishes. A well-written skill survives a change of tool. And since summer 2026, the Claude Cowork app even lets you teach a skill by recording your screen while narrating: Claude turns it into a reusable skill, without writing a line.
3. The hook: an automatic reflex
A hook is a script that fires automatically at a specific moment in Claude's work: before a command is run, after a file has been modified, when the conversation gets compacted, when a session ends. The fundamental difference from a skill: a hook doesn't think. It checks, blocks, formats, logs — deterministically, every time, no exceptions.
Useful examples for a merchant: refusing any command that would push code straight to production; running a consistency checker after every change to a data file; forbidding a file containing a secret from being added to the repo. What I used to entrust to a CLAUDE.md rule ("never merge the whole branch") can become a hook that makes the mistake physically impossible. A rule gets read; a hook gets executed.
Honest limit: hooks run in Claude Code (the terminal, or its web and desktop versions). In a Chat conversation or on mobile, they don't exist — hence, in my setup, a duplicate instruction rule for whatever has to work everywhere.
4. The subagent: delegating a subtask
A subagent is a Claude that the main agent hands a subtask to, with its own context, its own instructions, sometimes its own tools. It works — in the background by default, since summer 2026 — and returns a result. Three uses:
- Parallelize: translate twenty pages, audit ten files, check five sources at the same time.
- Isolate context: a heavy read (a long document, an entire repo) doesn't clutter the main conversation; only the conclusion comes back up.
- Specialize: a "reviewer" subagent with adversarial instructions, a "verifier" subagent that only confirms or refutes.
Workflows (available in Claude Code since June 2026) are the layer above: a small script that orchestrates several subagents deterministically — a review per dimension, then a check of each finding, for example. Useful, but reserve it for tasks that deserve a dozen agents. The default reflex is still: start without.
5. The plugin: the package
A plugin bundles skills, subagents, commands, hooks and connectors into a versioned package, installable in one command. It's the way to share complete know-how with a team — or to install it at home from a marketplace. The code security checker I use before every delivery is a plugin; my publishing pipeline will become one the day someone other than me has to publish here.
6. Instruction, skill, hook or connector: which to choose
A general ruleCLAUDE.mdTone, principles, pitfalls turned into rules. Short, always loaded. "Keep it casual," "never a whole branch in prod." A procedureSkillSteps, a template, guardrails. Loaded when the request matches. "Publish an entry," "capture the session." A systematic checkHookHas to happen every time, no judgment. "Block any push to main," "run the check after every change." Access to a toolConnector (MCP)Read or act in Shopify, Drive, Gmail, GitHub. The arms — to be framed by permissions. The test: is it a rule (CLAUDE.md), a procedure (skill), a reflex that must always run (hook), or a tool to plug in (connector)?
7. And without a terminal?
Skills aren't reserved for developers. Claude Cowork (the desktop app, also on the web and on mobile) installs them from a marketplace and loads them into ordinary office work: preparing a deck, going through a file, running a routine. And learning by screen recording is the simplest way there is to turn know-how into a procedure: you do the task once while narrating, Claude writes it up.
My advice for getting started: take the procedure you explain most often — not the most impressive, the most repeated — and write it in ten lines with a filled-in example. If Claude gets it right three times in a row without your help, it's a skill. If not, the procedure wasn't clear, and you just learned that.
Going further
- → Writing a good CLAUDE.md — the general rules, the other half.
- → What is an MCP — the connectors, the arms.
- → What is an AI agent — the basic loop that subagents multiply.
Real cases. The publishing skill → this site's redesign, published with it · the adversarial review of a dev request → the AI checks what it assumes.

AI PROPOSES, HUMANS VALIDATE: THE GUARDRAILS THAT HOLD (AGENTS, WRITES, DEPLOYS)
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/lia-propose-lhumain-valide.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

The guardrails Hugo Lahutte applies everywhere after three real incidents: automatic reads but validated writes, three autonomy regimes (mechanical, factual, judgment), the request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement flow, the four things before launching an agent, having the AI check a request before coding, and the non-negotiable locks (permissions, secrets, no cron that publishes on its own, surgical deploys). Why the framework lets you automate more.

Home › Guides › AI proposes, humans validate
Guides · Decide
AI proposes, humans validate:the guardrails that hold
The more AI acts, the more the framework matters. I've broken a production deploy, let an agent burn its budget in a loop, and discovered a pricing overhaul "already in prod" while testing it. Each incident became a rule. Here are the guardrails I apply everywhere — from the smallest script to my internal systems — and why they set you free more than they hold you back.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~7 min read agent sécurité strat méthode
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The visual body
- 3 Going further
In 30 seconds
- Automatic reads, validated writes. Read, refresh, analyze, propose: automatic. Change a price, a stock level, a campaign, an email, a post: human validation, log, measurement.
- Three regimes depending on the nature of the action: mechanical → automatic; factual → generated then validated with one click; judgment → human draft, always.
- Four things before launching an agent: an explicit objective, a budget cap, a bounded frequency, a measurable success criterion. And the AI checks what it assumes before coding.
1. Three incidents, three rules
I'm not theorizing. Every rule below has an incident behind it:
- May 2026 — the production deploy that broke everything. An entire branch merged into production, with mixed developments (mine and the integrator's). Several things broken. Hard rule, carved into my dev context file the next day: never a whole branch, always the specific commit, and a mandatory question before any deploy. → the entry.
- The agent stuck in a loop. An agent that relaunched itself every day, ate its budget and produced nothing usable. Rule: objective, budget, frequency, success criterion — or no agent. → the agent guide.
- August 2026 — the overhaul discovered while testing it. An overhaul of the per-variant pricing system was already in production, without formal confirmation; a discrepancy between Odoo and the site revealed it. Rule: test for real rather than trust the docs — and a system where the AI checks what it assumes before writing a line. → the entry.
It's Compound Engineering applied to safety: the incident doesn't just get fixed, it hardens the system so it can't happen again.
2. The three autonomy regimes
Not everything is equal. The right question isn't "how much autonomy?" but "what kind of action?":
Regime 1 · mechanicalAutomaticRead, refresh, deduplicate, format, log. No judgment, no irreversible consequence. A cron can do it. Regime 2 · factualGenerated, then validated with one clickA factual answer backed by a verified observation, a price computed by a rule, a product page extracted from a price list. The AI prepares, a person hits the button. Regime 3 · judgmentHuman draft, alwaysAn opinion under a magazine's byline, a LinkedIn post in your own name, a commercial trade-off. The AI can propose; it never signs. The regime is decided per action, not per tool. The same agent can be automatic on reads and draft-only on judgment.
3. The standard flow of an action
In my internal systems, every action that touches the real world follows the same path, whatever the building block:
Request→ Analysisevidence, freshness→ Previewwhat's about to change→ Validationhuman→ Executionidempotent→ Log+ measurement Three details that make the difference:
- The preview before validation. You validate a change you can see ("these 300 prices are going from X to Y"), not an intention ("align the prices"). My price-alignment engine first ran for weeks in observation mode — it simulated — before I switched product families to live, one by one.
- Idempotent execution. Running the same action twice must not produce two effects. That's what makes mistakes recoverable.
- Measurement after the action. A recommendation without measurement doesn't close the loop: it isn't "learned." The result is fed back into the next recommendation.
4. The four things before launching an agent
- An explicit objective — "we'll know it's good when…". A weak criterion = guaranteed wasted time.
- A hard budget cap — in euros or in calls. My daily hi-fi watch is capped at a few euros a month and picks its model automatically: it can no longer break on an update or run away.
- A bounded frequency — no permanent loop. A recurring task of under three days is a loop that expires on its own; a permanent task is a real scheduled task, monitored.
- A measurable success criterion — and an alert when it isn't met (a source dead for three days, an expected import that never arrives).
5. Have it checked before coding
The most profitable guardrail of the year isn't in the deploy, it's before: at the moment of the request. Odoo change requests used to arrive as a single line — no where, no what-happens-on-click, no "what must not change." My internal pipeline now frames them: a guided form (eight fields, dictation possible), screenshots and a transcribed video, then a two-pass AI review — it asks structured questions, the server checks them in the real database in read-only mode, the AI concludes.
Result on the first cases: a development request requalified as ten minutes of configuration, and a "solution" the AI showed didn't remove the supplier calls it claimed to avoid. About a hundred seconds and a few cents per review. The lesson: the AI doesn't code my request, it checks what it assumes. → the entry.
6. The non-negotiable locks
- The assistant never has more permissions than the person talking to it. A whitelisted login, roles, and no possible escalation from within a conversation.
- No secrets in the code, nor in the Brain, nor in a context file. Keys live in server-side environment variables; a scan blocks any commit that would contain one.
- No cron that publishes on its own. A publication is an explicit, idempotent action, with a readable error.
- Hard-blocking embargo, restricted people excluded from social queues (minors included), LinkedIn as draft only, never a judgment under the magazine's byline — the Content Machine locks.
- Surgical deploys. The specific commit, never the whole branch; a parallel session always restarts from the up-to-date version; in case of conflict, reapply only your own files.
- No automated engagement on social networks. No likes, no follows: inbound is a reader relationship, not growth hacking.
7. Why guardrails set you free
Guardrails are often presented as a brake. It's the opposite. Because the pricing engine can't sell at a loss and ignores absurd offers, I can let it run on six product families without watching it. Because the invoice agent can only attach an invoice to an order that exists, I can let it read my emails every fifteen minutes. Because Growth changes nothing without validation, I can plug all my tools into it.
The framework isn't what keeps you from automating. It's what lets you automate more — while you sleep.
Going further
- → What is an AI agent — the basic loop and its four guardrails.
- → What is HL OS — the request → measurement flow, applied to a whole system.
- → Is my data safe? — the other side: where the data goes.
Real cases. The pricing engine, from observation mode to live · The invoice agent in production · A code review handled point by point.

WHAT IS HL OS: AN OPERATING SYSTEM FOR RUNNING A GROUP WITH AI
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-hl-os.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

HL OS is the shared foundation (database, AI layer, identity and permissions, action log) and the five building blocks (Zéro, Knowledge, Content Machine, Growth, AI Core) that Hugo Lahutte has been building since June 2026 to run Cobra, Haute Fidélité and his projects with AI. One core, several contexts, and a single flow: request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement.

Home › Guides › What is HL OS?
Guides · My systems
What is HL OS:an operating system for running a group with AI
A store, a magazine, a brand, a personal venture — and ten tools that don't talk to each other. HL OS is the name I give to what I've been building since June 2026 to run all of it with AI: a shared foundation, five building blocks, and one rule — the AI proposes, the human validates. The map, without jargon.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~8 min read HL OS agent strat Claude Code
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- HL OS = a shared foundation (a database, an AI layer, identity and permissions, an action log) + five building blocks that plug into it: Zéro (mail and tasks), Knowledge (the Brain), Content Machine (publish), Growth (decide), AI Core — Socle IA — (write, search, secure).
- One core, several contexts: Cobra and Haute Fidélité share the engines, never the accounts, the data or the rules.
- Every action follows the same flow: request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement. Reading is automatic; writing is validated.
1. Why an “OS”
My daily life is Odoo for sales, margin and stock; Shopify for the stores; Google Analytics, Ads, Search Console and Merchant Center for visibility; Brevo for email; the social networks; one mailbox per organization; a magazine to produce. Every tool knows how to produce its own dashboard. None of them answers, on its own, the question that matters: what deserves my time today?
Until 2025, the answer was “hire, or buy a suite.” In 2026, AI changes the scale of what a business owner who knows what they want can have built. So I stopped stacking tools and started building the layer above — the one that reads every tool, reconciles the facts, proposes actions and keeps the record. An operating system, in the literal sense: what everything else runs on.
The word is a bit big for an organization my size. I own it: the day I started calling this an OS, I stopped thinking of it as a collection of scripts.
2. The foundation
Everything rests on four shared things:
- A shared database, inherited from HF-OS, the publishing ERP I built in five days in June: a single application (a headless CMS + a web framework + PostgreSQL) that serves the dashboard, the admin and the API. The building blocks don't reinvent storage: they plug into it.
- A shared AI layer — the AI Core (Socle IA): writing in my voice (several voices, actually: the magazine, me in the first person, the travel journal), embeddings for search, a router that picks the model by tier (small, large, fallback) and logs every call, and a pattern of secrets encrypted server-side — never in the code, never in the Brain.
- Identity and permissions: Google sign-in restricted to a whitelist, roles, and the rule that governs everything — the assistant never gets more rights than the person talking to it.
- An action log: every write leaves a usable trace, idempotent whenever the connector allows it.
3. The five building blocks
A building block is a perimeter, a living specification, a development plan with success criteria (“we'll know it's good when…”) and a dated Decisions section. The five:
HL OS foundation ZéroMail + tasks. Sorts, summarizes, turns an email into a task. The Brain's daily source of signal. KnowledgeThe Brain and its index: everything about me becomes queryable by my AIs. Content MachineOne capture, N destinations: field capture, magazine repurposing, validated publishing. GrowthAction-first decisions: reconciles sales, acquisition, SEO, web, email and social, and proposes the next useful piece of work. AI CoreWriting in my voice, embeddings, model router, encrypted secrets. The other building blocks call it, they don't reimplement it. Five building blocks, one foundation. The boundary is clean: Growth measures and recommends, the Content Machine makes and publishes, Knowledge preserves, Zéro feeds, the AI Core serves the others.
Growth — from ten dashboards to a queue of actions
The most advanced building block. It automatically pulls the facts available (Odoo, Shopify, Analytics, Ads, Search Console, Merchant Center, web health checks, email, social), reconciles them, and proposes a handful of actions ranked by impact, confidence, effort and risk. A short home page, a single bar to ask a question or prepare an action, and the expert views behind it, as evidence. A missing data point shows up as exactly that — never a silent zero. Details in the journal entry.
Content Machine — one capture, N destinations
It doesn't produce content, it carries a presence: a few photos, a voice memo, at a place, at a time, by an identified person — and the machine proposes the renderings (post, article, print page) to the right destinations, without ever publishing on its own. Dedicated guide: Content Machine.
Knowledge — the Brain
The durable memory, in the OKF format, read by all my AIs. Dedicated guide: What is a Brain.
4. One core, several contexts
The most important architecture decision, made from the start: Cobra and Haute Fidélité share the intelligence, never the accounts, the secrets, the data or the operating rules. The first Growth instance runs for Cobra; a Haute Fidélité instance will reuse the same core with its own accounts, data and goals — an isolated context inside HL OS. The Content Machine works the same way: a context (the provenance — where, when, why) is not a destination (where it publishes), and one context deploys to several destinations.
The benefit isn't only technical. It's what makes it possible to run a work account and a personal account, a Claude Cobra and a Claude HL, without ever mixing two perimeters in a base read from both sides.
5. The flow of an action
Whatever the building block, an action that touches the real world (a price, a stock level, a campaign, an email, a publication) follows the same path:
Requesta question, an intent→auto Analysisfacts, sources, freshness→auto Previewwhat's about to change→human Validationone button, one person→auto Executionthrough the connector→auto Log + measurementbefore / after, fed back in Reading and refreshing can be automatic. Writing to Shopify, Odoo, an ad platform, the email tool or a social network stays behind required validation as long as no finer explicit permission exists. And a recommendation without a measurement after execution doesn't close the loop: it hasn't been “learned.”
6. Where it stands (September 2026)
Dated snapshot · September 1, 2026
- Growth — in production for Cobra since September 1: action-first home, main bar, evidence views, reads from every connected source. Current priority: making audience measurement reliable before allowing any budget-shift recommendation. One particularity: this block was built with ChatGPT and Codex, with Claude involved only at the margins (the story and architecture).
- Content Machine — v2 spec (July 30), foundation in place; the September 1 pivot unifies field capture, magazine repurposing and “publish this idea” into a single system. Next step: capture in under ten seconds, then a first Instagram rendering. Deadline: the Haute Fidélité show, late September.
- Knowledge / Brain — in place since August 21; read through a GitHub connector; search index postponed until the signal.
- Zéro and AI Core — in progress; the specifications are migrating into the Brain.
This status is a snapshot, not a lasting truth: figures and statuses live in the tools and in the Brain, never copied here as permanent.
7. What it illustrates
Three things I believe transfer to any small or mid-sized business:
- The value isn't in one more dashboard. It's in no longer having to open ten interfaces to piece together a situation — and in having a queue of actions with their evidence.
- The hard work wasn't the code. It was deciding which source to believe (Odoo carries the actuals, Shopify the web flow, the ad platforms their self-reported attribution) and preventing misleading reconciliations. The AI hammered out the code; the trade-offs stay human.
- Build rather than wait for a quote, when the business is specific and the cost of customization collapses. The core of Growth was framed over a weekend and put into production on the Tuesday — built, for this block, with ChatGPT and Codex rather than Claude. The question “do you still need to buy?” now applies to the steering layer, not just the ERP.

- → Content Machine: one capture, N destinations — the publishing building block.
- → What is a Brain — the Knowledge building block.
- → The AI proposes, the human validates — the guardrails that make all of this possible.
- → Do you still need to buy an ERP? — HF-OS, the technical foundation, built in five days.
Real cases. HL OS: five building blocks, one foundation · Growth: replacing ten dashboards with a queue of actions · HF-OS: the foundation, deployed.

CONTENT MACHINE: ONE CAPTURE, N DESTINATIONS
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/content-machine-une-capture-n-destinations.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

Hugo Lahutte's Content Machine doesn't produce content, it carries a presence: the basic unit is the attested observation (media, place, time, person), and the post or the article are only renderings of it. Three inputs (Telegram capture in under ten seconds, repurposing of the Haute Fidélité magazine, “publish this idea” from the Brain), locks before publication, disposable or permanent destinations, and one rule: the machine proposes, the human validates.

Home › Guides › Content Machine
Guides · My systems
Content Machine:one capture, N destinations
Anyone can generate content with AI — which is precisely why it's no longer worth anything. My content machine does the opposite: it doesn't produce content, it carries a presence. A photo, a voice memo, a place, a time, a person — and the machine proposes where and in what form it should land. Without ever deciding on its own.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~8 min read Content Machine marketing GEO agent
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- The basic unit isn't the article, it's the attested observation: a few media files, a note, a place, a time, an identified person. A post, an article, a print page are only renderings of it.
- Three inputs, one shared log: field capture (Telegram, under ten seconds), repurposing of the magazine (issues and archives whose rights I hold), and “publish this idea” from the Brain.
- The machine never decides: it proposes a destination along with its reasoning, the human settles it with one button. And provenance is the product — it's what search engines and AIs reward.
1. The problem: generated content is no longer worth anything
In 2026, producing ten posts, a blog article and a newsletter takes five minutes. Everyone does it; the feeds are full of smooth texts that nobody actually lived. For a magazine, a brand or a retailer, that's not just useless: it's dangerous, because it dilutes the only thing that still sets you apart — having been there.
My problem was concrete. A print magazine (Haute Fidélité) and its archives, an editorial brand (HiFi Lovers), a family travel journal, this Knowledge Hub, a LinkedIn account, a trade show coming up. A huge amount of raw material, and every time the same friction: capturing is easy, formatting eats time, and nothing connects what was seen to what gets published.
2. The principle: carrying a presence
The Content Machine doesn't produce content. In it, AI is the logistics between what was observed in the field and the place where it needs to land. Four rules, non-negotiable:
- The basic unit is the attested observation: a few photos, a voice memo or a note, at a place, at a time, by an identified person. The post, the article, the print page are only renderings of it.
- Witnessed and documented are kept separate, in the database and in the form. What I saw doesn't have the same status as what I read, and the reader must be able to see it.
- The machine never decides. It proposes a destination along with its reasoning; the human settles it with one button.
- Provenance is the product. Who, where, when: that's the first-hand experience signal that search engines and answering AIs reward.
3. Three inputs, one shared log
Input 1 · witnessedField captureFrom Telegram, in under ten seconds, offline if needed: photos, a voice memo, a text. Posting in the right topic states the context — zero manual tagging. Input 2 · documentedMagazine repurposingThe PDFs and HD visuals of the issues — current and archived — whose rights I hold as the publisher, turned into renderings for the social networks and the site. The magazine is the reserve of authority. Input 3 · documented“Publish this idea”A Brain document marked publiable (publishable) becomes an entry on this Knowledge Hub, written in my voice, validated with one tap, live a minute later. Three raw materials, a single governance and a single rendering system. What was scattered across three projects has become one building block.
4. Context ≠ destination
The distinction that unlocked everything. The context is the provenance: where, when, why. The destination is where it publishes. One context deploys to several destinations, and each has its own rules:
- Personal — public and indexed: journal, personal Instagram, book. Its own rules: location metadata stripped, a delay before publishing a position, no indexing of minors.
- Professional, in my own name — private, step by step: LinkedIn as draft only, never auto-published. The only place where judgment is legitimate — so nothing automatic.
- Haute Fidélité — public, with a hard embargo: site, Instagram, newsletter, print. Judgment forbidden under the magazine's byline; facts and vintages checked.
Technically, it's a single Telegram group with one topic per context. Posting in a topic is enough; inferring from the content is only a suggestion. Capture stays under ten seconds, which is the only way to really capture.
5. The locks, before any publication
- Embargo as a hard block. A release date is a lock, not content: door closed until the date.
- Visibility lock. A media file showing a restricted person — minors included — is excluded from the social queues; only a manual override naming the person unlocks it.
- Witnessed / documented kept separate in the database and in the form.
- LinkedIn = draft only.
- Never a judgment under the magazine's byline.
- Publication on an explicit action, idempotent, with a readable error in Telegram. No cron that publishes on its own.
On the social networks, the engagement rule is just as strict: DMs and replies to comments are a reader relationship, not automated growth. No automatic likes, no automatic follows. Three regimes: mechanical = automatic; factual reply = generated then validated with one button; judgment = human draft.
6. Destinations and their life cycle
Not all destinations have the same lifespan, and that's what dictates the build order:
Disposable
Immediate
- Instagram, stories
- LinkedIn (draft)
- A bad output costs nothing
→ Evolving → permanent
It stays
- Magazine site, journal, this Knowledge Hub (evolving)
- Newsletter (derived)
- Print, book (permanent, dated, calibrated to a character count)
The social layer is deliberately pluggable: a replaceable publishing adapter behind a single interface. The site remains the source of truth, the social networks are satellites. Measurement, for its part, doesn't depend on the publishing provider: Growth reads the platforms' native statistics directly. You can switch publishing tools without losing the history.
7. The build order (and where it stands)
Social → web → print. You validate the engine where a bad output costs nothing, before trusting it with what's permanent. The stages: the irreversible foundation (domains, URLs, data schemas, media storage); timed Telegram capture; the documentation (entities, embeddings, model router); a first Instagram rendering to prove the adapter and the isolation of spaces; the duplicable journal — including the Atlas of Asia (Atlas d'Asie), our travel journal from this summer, as the hand-made pilot; the magazine site and LinkedIn; print; the book.
Dated snapshot · September 1, 2026
The v2 spec dates from July 30; the foundation (collections, sign-in, indexing guardrail, entity page with structured data) is in place; the September 1 pivot brought field capture, repurposing and “publish this idea” together into a single building block and settled the publishing tool (self-hosted, replaceable) rather than services billed per account. Next steps: capture in under ten seconds, first Instagram rendering. External deadline: the Haute Fidélité show, late September 2026. Still open: the dedicated name and domain for the magazine site and the journals.
8. What it changes for getting cited by AIs
GEO — getting cited in an AI's answer — rewards three things the machine produces by construction: one page per entity with its structured data (schema.org), explicit provenance (who, where, when — the first-hand experience signal), and a server-rendered site, readable without JavaScript, with an llms.txt. Mass-generated content has none of these three attributes. An attested observation has all of them.
In other words: the Content Machine isn't a machine for producing more. It's a machine for publishing only what was actually lived — and making it readable by humans and machines alike.

- → The AI proposes, the human validates — the locks, in detail.
- → Being visible in AI: GEO — why provenance is the product.

WHAT'S AI, AND WHAT'S AN “LLM”?
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-ia-llm.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

Generative AI and LLMs explained without jargon: what they do, who the big players are (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral…), and above all what they can NOT do.

Home › Guides › What's AI and an LLM?
Guides · The entry point
What's AI,and what's an “LLM”?
Generative AI and “LLMs” explained without jargon, to decide fast: what they do, who the big players are (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral…), and above all what they can't do.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read IA LLM vulgarisation meta
- 1 30-second take
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
30-second take
- Generative AI is a family of software that produces text, code or images from a simple instruction written in plain language.
- The engine behind assistants like ChatGPT or Claude is called an LLM (large language model): a model trained on enormous amounts of text, whose only real talent is predicting the most plausible continuation of what you write to it — and that's enough to do stunning things.
- The big players today: OpenAI (ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Meta, Mistral (the French one), xAI (Grok), the Chinese open models (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen), plus Microsoft (Copilot) and Perplexity. Versions change every month; the roles, much less.
1. Are AI and an LLM the same thing?
No — and that's the first confusion to clear up. People say “AI” about everything, but there are two very different things behind it.
“Classic” AI has existed for decades: it's the algorithms that recommend you a product, filter spam or optimize a delivery route. Useful, but specialized: each system does a single task, the one it was coded for.
The recent breakthrough is generative AI: a single system can write an email, summarize a 40-page PDF, translate, code, analyze a sales spreadsheet — without having been programmed for each of those tasks. That versatility is what changes the game. And the LLM is precisely the engine of that generative AI for text: a subset of the big word “AI,” not a synonym.
AI Machine Learning Deep Learning LLM
- AIAny system that imitates an “intelligent” task — since the 1950s.
- Machine LearningAI that learns from examples, rather than from hand-written rules.
- Deep LearningMachine learning based on large neural networks.
- LLMA neural network specialized in language. The engine of assistants like ChatGPT or Claude.
“LLM” is a precise subset of the buzzword “AI” — not a synonym.
2. What's an LLM, concretely?
An LLM is a model that has “read” a gigantic share of what's written online, and has learned a single thing: guessing the next word. You give it a beginning, it predicts the most probable continuation, word after word.
Seen like that, it looks like your phone's autocomplete. The difference is scale: by ingesting so much text, the model ends up “understanding” enough of the structure of language to summarize, argue, translate or write code — capabilities that emerge without having been explicitly programmed.
“The customer wants an amp   …”
Next word — candidates ranked by probability
- powerful41%
- home-theater28%
- second-hand11%
The model doesn't “know” what comes next: it ranks the continuations by probability, picks one, then starts again. Token after token.
The right mental model to keep: an LLM doesn't recite a database, it generates. It doesn't go “look up” an answer stored somewhere — it rebuilds it on the fly. That's its strength (it adapts to any request) and its weakness (it can rebuild it wrong, see below).
3. What are the best-known LLMs?
The market has settled around a few families. Versions follow one another fast (every few months) — what matters is knowing who does what:
- OpenAI — ChatGPT: the best known to the general public, the one that launched the wave in late 2022. GPT-5.6 family since July 2026, and “ChatGPT Work,” an agent for professional tasks.
- Anthropic — Claude: focused on reliability, reasoning and “serious” work (writing, code, analysis, agents). Claude 5 family since summer 2026 (Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1). It's the one I build everything on (see the dedicated guide).
- Google — Gemini: integrated into the Google ecosystem (and into its AI overviews in search), very strong on long documents, video and multimodal; also publishes open models (Gemma).
- Meta: long the champion of “open weights” (Llama, which you can host yourself); in 2026, low-cost agentic models (Muse Spark) and an emphasis on advertising and assistants inside its apps.
- Mistral: the French/European champion, partly open — the sovereignty argument when hosting your data in Europe matters. A thousand employees in 2026, very good on specialized building blocks (document reading, robotics), a notch behind the frontier on general-purpose models.
- The Chinese open models — DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen: open, formidable on performance per dollar, and closing the gap with the leaders at every release (but raising confidentiality questions when you use their online services).
- xAI — Grok: Elon Musk's model, plugged live into X, which in 2026 became a serious option for agents thanks to its performance/price ratio (Grok 4.6).
- Microsoft — Copilot: the AI built into Windows and the Office suite. Under the hood, mostly partner models (OpenAI, and Claude on its Azure cloud), plus its first in-house models.
- Perplexity: less a model than an answer engine — it searches the web and answers with its sources cited; and since 2026 a “Computer,” an agent that executes tasks by orchestrating other people's models.
OpenAI ChatGPT The general public, the broadest ecosystem. GPT-5.6. 🇺🇸Closed Anthropic Claude Reliability, reasoning, code, agents. Claude 5 family. 🇺🇸Closed Google Gemini Multimodal, video, long documents, built into Google. 🇺🇸Closed Meta Llama · Muse Spark Historic open weights; low-cost agents in 2026. 🇺🇸Open Mistral Mistral / Le Chat The European champion; sovereignty, documents, robotics. 🇫🇷Open DeepSeek DeepSeek · GLM · Kimi · Qwen The Chinese open models: unbeatable performance per dollar (watch your data). 🇨🇳Open xAI Grok Plugged into X; very competitive for agents. 🇺🇸Closed Microsoft Copilot Built into Windows/Office; partner + in-house models. 🇺🇸Closed Perplexity Perplexity Answer engine and “Computer” agent. 🇺🇸Closed A dated snapshot (September 2026), not a benchmark: rankings change every month. “Open” = model weights downloadable / self-hostable.
4. What can an LLM NOT do?
This is the part people skip too often, and it's the one that avoids nasty surprises.
- It's not a search engine or a database. Because it generates instead of retrieving, an LLM can make up a wrong answer with total confidence — that's called a hallucination. On a number, a product reference, a date: you check.
- By default, it's connected neither to the internet in real time nor to your data. For it to read your email, your Shopify or your ERP, you have to explicitly connect it (that's the whole point of another guide).
- It's a copilot, not an oracle. Used well, it saves a crazy amount of time; used with blind trust, it does damage. The whole method is right there.

- → Is my data safe?
Real-world case. Every morning, an LLM writes me a press review of worldwide hi-fi news from 64 sources. Not a demo — something that runs in production. → Daily HiFi news watch Telegram bot

WHAT IS CLAUDE, AND WHY DID I BUILD EVERYTHING ON IT? (THE CLAUDE 5 FAMILY, SEPTEMBER 2026)
