================================================================

Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, explained simply: who makes it, the lineup in September 2026 (Fable 5.1, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Haiku), the products behind the name (Chat, Cowork, Code), why it's at the top of the pack, and why it became the foundation of all my projects — for real, not in a demo.

Home › Guides › What is Claude?
Guides · General
What is Claude,and why did I build everything on it?
Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, explained simply: who makes it, what the lineup looks like in September 2026 (the Claude 5 family), the products behind the name, why it's at the top of the pack — and why I made it the foundation of all my projects, for real, not in a demo.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026 · Updated September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read Claude Anthropic IA meta
- 1 30-second take
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
30-second take
- Claude is the AI assistant developed by Anthropic, an American lab that has made reliability and safety its obsession.
- Since summer 2026, it's the Claude 5 family: Fable 5.1 (the most capable, released September 1), Opus 5 (the everyday high end), Sonnet 5 (the balanced one), and Haiku (the fast one). Four tiers, one rule: the cheapest one that gets the job done.
- Behind the name, several products — Chat, Cowork, Code — and, in my setup, a single foundation: Cobra, Haute Fidélité, the daily briefs, this site, my Brain. Everything runs through Claude.
1. What Claude is, and who makes it
Claude is Anthropic's AI — a lab founded by former OpenAI researchers, with a clear guiding principle: models that are as reliable and predictable as possible, built for serious work rather than flashy performance.
In practice, Claude isn't one model but a family, available in sizes you pick based on what you need. The version name changes every few months — what stays constant is the "very powerful / powerful / balanced / fast" logic.
The class above Fable The most capable model released to the public: hard problems, autonomous work lasting several hours. Saved for what deserves it. The powerhouse Opus The everyday high end: long reasoning, big builds, demanding code. My default model in Claude Code. The balanced one Sonnet The best power-to-price ratio, covering the vast majority of needs — and running my agents. The fast one Haiku The ultra-fast lightweight: for volume and simple tasks where speed and price come first. Four sizes, one family. You pick based on the task — no need to know the version numbers.
2. The lineup in September 2026: the Claude 5 family
A dated reference point, because everything moved this summer. In three months, Anthropic renewed the entire lineup:
- Claude Sonnet 5 (June 30) — "the most autonomous Sonnet yet": it plans, and uses the browser and the terminal on its own. Its launch price ($2 / $10 per million tokens in / out) became permanent in August. It's the workhorse of agents.
- Claude Opus 5 (July 24) — gets close to Fable 5's level for half the price ($5 / $25), and is presented as the model most resistant to prompt injection — an important point as soon as an agent reads the web or emails.
- Claude Fable 5.1 (September 1) — successor to Fable 5 (released June 9), same tier, same price ($10 / $50), a one-million-token context window, cheaper cache reads, and refined cybersecurity guardrails (fewer false refusals). Its version without certain guardrails, Mythos 5.1, remains reserved for trusted-access programs. I told the whole story — including the June episode when the US government suspended Fable 5 for three weeks — in Fable, Mythos, Glasswing.
- Claude Haiku 4.5 — still the fast one and the cheapest ($1 / $5), for volume.
What it changes for the user: the rule doesn't move — the right model is the cheapest one that gets the job done — but "the job" has become much longer and more autonomous. A Sonnet 5 does today what an Opus did in the spring. The details on prices and plans are in How much does AI cost.
3. The products behind the name
"Claude" is also several ways of using it, which I detail in Chat, Cowork, or Code:
- Claude (Chat) — the conversation, on the web, in the app, and on mobile, with memory, projects, and connectors (Gmail, Drive, Shopify…).
- Claude Cowork — the desktop assistant that carries out a job end to end, without a terminal: files, spreadsheets, a built-in browser, scheduled routines. On desktop, web, and mobile.
- Claude Code — the agent that acts inside a project: reads, edits, runs, deploys. Terminal, web, desktop app, mobile.
- And around them: Claude Design (mockups), Claude Science (research), Claude in Slack (a team member you mention), the API for developers, and hosted agents that run at Anthropic on a schedule.
Every paid plan includes Chat, Cowork, and Code. What sets the plans apart is usage volume, not access to the tools.
4. Why it's one of the champions right now
No BS: no model is "the best at everything," the right choice depends on the task, and the competition is fierce — OpenAI, Google, xAI, and the Chinese open models ship a major version every month. But a few objective signals put Claude at the top of the pack:
- It powers the pros' coding tools. The AI editors developers use most rely on Claude; Anthropic even said in June that more than 80% of the code merged into its own codebase is now written by Claude.
- It attracts the best. In May 2026, Andrej Karpathy — co-founder of OpenAI, former head of AI at Tesla, one of the field's greatest teachers — joined Anthropic. When someone of that caliber picks a home, it says a lot.
- It's built for serious work. Writing, analysis, reasoning, code, and — new this year — resistance to manipulation when an agent reads outside content. That's exactly what a business needs.
- The know-how spreads. Free training (Claude Academy, August 2026), open documentation, a connection standard (MCP) adopted by the whole market.
5. Why I, of all people, built everything on it
The real proof isn't a benchmark, it's what runs in my setup. I'm not a developer — strategy, marketing, purchasing, that's my trade — and yet, with Claude:
- Cobra runs on management modules I framed and had written (purchasing, stock imports, shop sync, pricing system), an internal app hub, an engine that aligns prices against the competition, an agent that processes supplier invoices, and since September Growth, the action queue that replaces ten dashboards.
- Haute Fidélité has its press ERP (HF-OS, built in five days), its online store, and its logistics set up the same way.
- Two daily briefs land every morning — global hi-fi and AI news — written automatically from dozens of sources.
- This site, bilingual, is written and published with Claude. And my Brain, the memory of all this, is read by every one of my Claudes.
The common thread: a non-technical person shipping to production things that used to take a team. That's the click.
Claude CobraOdoo modules, internal apps, pricing, invoices, Growth Haute FidélitéHF-OS, store, logistics Daily briefsHi-fi (64 sources) + AI Knowledge HubThis site, written & published, FR + EN BrainThe memory, in OKF format A single foundation: the same assistant feeds every project, from dev to editorial — and remembers everything thanks to the Brain.

WHY AI REALLY CHANGES THE WAY WE WORK: DO, STEER, FRAME (2026)
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/pourquoi-lia-change-le-travail.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

Generative AI is a general-purpose technology, like electricity. In 2026 it acts inside your tools: work climbs three steps — do, steer, frame a system that proposes. The cost of customization collapses (an ERP in five days, an action queue in a weekend), the skills that matter change, and what doesn't change: judgment, responsibility, customer relationships, validation.

Home › Guides › Why AI changes the way we work
Guides · General
Why AI really changes the way we work
Not just another fad. Why generative AI is a shift of the same order as electricity, what it concretely changes for a business owner or a retailer in 2026 — three steps, not one — and what it does not change.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026 · Updated September 2, 2026 · ~8 min read IA strat vulgarisation meta
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- Generative AI isn't one more tool: it's a general-purpose technology, like electricity — a layer that slips in everywhere, into every line of work.
- In 2026, it no longer just answers: it acts inside your tools and chains steps on its own. Work climbs three steps: do → steer → frame a system that proposes.
- The cost of customization collapses: an ERP for a magazine in five days, an action queue in a weekend. What doesn't change: judgment, responsibility, customer relationships — and validation before any sensitive action.
1. A general-purpose technology
The right analogy isn't “a new piece of software.” It's electricity. The phrase “AI is the new electricity” is Andrew Ng's (2017), and it hits the mark: electricity didn't improve one industry, it transformed all of them, because it plugged in everywhere.
Generative AI has that same horizontal character: the same tool writes an email, analyzes a sales spreadsheet, writes code, translates a contract — and, since this year, sorts the inbox, reads invoices, and aligns prices. It's not one profession that changes, it's every profession that gains a new layer.
- Steam enginelate 18th c.
- Electricitylate 19th c.
- Computing & internetlate 20th c.
- Artificial intelligencetoday
A rare category: technologies that don't transform one sector, but all of them at once.
2. The signals that this isn't hype
September 2026 benchmarks — names and amounts date quickly; it's the logic that matters, not the details.
The “revolution” talk is easy. What doesn't lie is where the people and the money of those with the most to lose are going:
- Code writes itself, at scale. Anthropic reports that more than 80% of the code merged into its own codebase is now written by Claude; at Cursor, more than half of merged changes come from agents in the cloud. This is no longer a demo: it's the production output of the people who build the tools.
- The best are switching houses for it. Andrej Karpathy joined Anthropic; CTOs of companies valued in the billions agreed to go back to being researchers. Jeff Bezos came out of semi-retirement to co-found an AI company.
- Infrastructure is absorbing unprecedented sums. A quarter of nearly $100 billion in revenue for the leading chipmaker, hundreds of billions in commitments. The bottleneck is no longer the model, it's what runs it.
- It has become a matter of state. The labs are preparing to go public; a model was suspended for three weeks by a government on national-security grounds. You don't suspend a fad.
The reading rule: when those with the most to lose reallocate their time and their capital to a subject, the subject is serious.
3. Three steps: do, steer, frame
In May, I described a shift: from “doing” to “steering and verifying.” Three months later, there's one more step, and it's the most important one.
Doyou produce everything by hand: research, write, format, fix Steeryou describe, the AI executes, you verify — one task at a time Frameyou write the context and the rules; a system reads, proposes, and waits for your validation ← 20242026 ↑ The 2026 shift: your time no longer goes to execution, nor only to verification — it goes to the frame.
- Do → steer. You describe what you want and you verify, instead of doing everything by hand. A non-technical person does technical things: I've shipped management modules and advanced SEO without being a developer. The brake is no longer execution, it's knowing what to ask.
- Steer → frame. When the AI acts inside your tools — reads the emails, prepares the product pages, proposes a price — you're no longer checking a function, you're framing a system: what it knows (the context), what it's allowed to do (the permissions), when it has to stop and ask you (the validation). That's what I built with HL OS: an action queue that says what to handle, with the evidence, and a button to validate.
4. The cost of customization collapses
This is the least visible and the deepest change for a small business. Custom software used to cost months and an agency; it now costs a few days and a good specification. Two examples at my place: HF-OS, the ERP of the Haute Fidélité magazine, built from scratch in five days with Claude Code; Growth, Cobra's action queue, framed over a weekend and in production on Tuesday — with ChatGPT and Codex, this time. The question “should you still buy software?” is no longer rhetorical: it comes up for every management layer.
The flip side: what costs now is knowing what you want and keeping it up to date. The specification, the context, the rules. Code has become the easy part.
5. The skills that matter now
Not “learning to code.” Four things, all within reach of a business owner or a retailer:
1 Write context Your business, your rules, your tools, in files the AI reads before every session. The guide. 2 Set a success criterion “We'll know it's good when…” Without that, an AI acting on its own doesn't know when to stop. 3 Judge a result Read a diff, proofread an email, check a number: business expertise becomes central again, it just moves to a different moment. 4 Decide what stays human Which action goes through validation, which relationship can't be delegated. The guardrails. Value moves toward those who know how to state the problem, frame the system, and verify the result.
6. What it does NOT change (and the pitfalls)
- It doesn't replace judgment. AI proposes, you decide. It can be confidently wrong (see the guide on LLMs) — and an AI that acts gets things wrong faster than an AI that answers.
- Responsibility can't be delegated. A price changed, an email sent, an order placed: that's you. Hence the rule that holds everything together at my place: automatic reads, validated writes.
- The customer relationship stays human. The AI prepares the answer; it doesn't replace the contact, the goodwill gesture, the advice on the store floor.
- The new trap: context debt. An AI framed with stale rules decides confidently on false premises. The frame has to be kept up to date like inventory — that's the subject of Compound Engineering.
- The advantage goes to those who start early. Not in theory: by practicing, on real cases, with one specific chore to start.
Going further

- → What's an “AI agent”? — the “steer → frame” step, explained.
- → What is Claude — the model I do all of this on.
Real-world cases. How AI entered my daily work → Claude joins the Cobra workflow · how it spread to the team → Colleagues start using Claude · the third step → HL OS: five building blocks, one foundation.

WHAT'S AN “AI AGENT”? FORMS IN 2026, WHAT RUNS ON MY SIDE, AND THE GUARDRAIL
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-un-agent-ia.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

An AI agent is Claude handed a goal and the means to act on its own, in a loop, until the result. The assistant / agent difference, the four forms of an agent in 2026 (in the session, subagents, routines, hosted agents), the six agents in production on my side (news watches, invoices, supplier price lists, pricing, dev request review, Growth), and the essential guardrail: goal, budget, frequency, criterion — and automatic reads, validated writes.

Home › Guides › What's an AI agent?
Guides · General
What's an “AI agent”?
An AI agent is Claude handed a goal and the means to act on its own, in a loop, until the result. What it makes possible, the forms it takes in 2026 (subagents, routines, hosted agents), what runs on my side — and the guardrail without which it spirals out of control.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026 · Updated September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read agent IA vulgarisation
- 1 30-second take
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
30-second take
- An assistant answers; an agent acts: it chains steps on its own toward a goal (search, decide, execute, check, start again).
- Plugged into your tools, it runs tasks without you: news watch, invoices, supplier price lists, pricing, monitoring numbers. In 2026, it multiplies (subagents), schedules itself (routines) and lives in the cloud.
- The trap: without guardrails (clear goal, capped budget, limited frequency, success criterion), an agent loops and spirals out of control. I learned that the hard way. And the rule that makes it all possible: AI proposes, the human validates.
1. Assistant or agent: the real difference
When you chat with Claude, it's an assistant: you ask, it answers, you take back control. An agent is the step above: you set it a goal, and it chains the steps on its own — it searches, decides, acts, checks its result, and starts again if needed, until it delivers.
The key ingredient is autonomy in a loop + access to tools to act (the connectors).
Goal → Act → Observe → Adjust → Deliver start again until the result What makes an agent: the autonomous loop, running until the goal is reached.
2. The forms of an agent in 2026
A year ago, “an agent” meant a script calling a model in a loop. Today, it takes four forms, from the closest to you to the most autonomous:
- The agent in your session — Claude Code or Cowork chaining the steps of a task while you watch (or don't). Since the Claude 5 models, that can last for hours: it delivers a tested feature, not a function.
- Subagents — a main agent delegating subtasks to copies of itself, in parallel, in the background, each with its own context. Translate twenty pages, audit ten files, check five sources. Details in What's a skill.
- Routines — a scheduled agent (every morning, every Monday), run in the cloud without your machine. This summer's novelty. See Loops, routines and scheduled tasks.
- Hosted agents — an agent living on a server (yours, or at Anthropic's), plugged into your tools through the API, running 24/7 with its own secrets and its own log. That's the form of my invoice agent and my news watches.
3. What runs on my side
Not a list of intentions — what's in production as of September 1, 2026:
- Two daily news watches (worldwide hi-fi across 64 sources, AI news) that read, sort, write and publish every morning on Telegram and here. Repaired and hardened in August: model picked automatically, alert if a source dies for three days, cost capped.
- Cobra's supplier invoice agent: it reads the inbox every fifteen minutes, extracts each invoice, attaches it to the right purchase order and pushes it for validation. It can only attach to an order that exists — that's what keeps it from drifting.
- The app that reads supplier price lists: extracting references and prices, matching against the database, detecting duplicates, human validation before any write. No created product is published online automatically.
- The price alignment engine: it recomputes target prices against the competition at each data delivery, never at a loss, in observation mode first and then live, family by family — going live remaining a human decision.
- Dev request review: the AI asks questions, checks its hypotheses against the real database in read-only mode, and concludes — before a single line of code is written.
- Growth: the action queue that brings together sales, acquisition, visibility, email and social, and proposes the next useful piece of work with its evidence. Automatic reads, validated writes.
What they have in common isn't the technology. It's that each one has a scope, a budget, and a clear line between what it does alone and what it submits.
4. The essential guardrail
An agent without a frame is a robot let loose. I had one that kept relaunching itself in a loop and burned its budget every day without producing anything usable. The lesson, now a rule on my side: every agent needs four things before it's launched —
- an explicit goal (“we'll know it's good when…”),
- a hard budget cap,
- a limited frequency (not a permanent loop),
- a measurable success criterion.
And a fifth, since agents started acting inside tools: automatic reads, validated writes. An agent reads, proposes, prepares; a person validates anything that changes a price, a stock level, a campaign, an email, a publication. That's not excessive caution: it's what lets me keep six agents running while I sleep. The details — three autonomy regimes, the flow of an action, the locks — are in AI proposes, the human validates.
One threat specific to agents, worth knowing: an agent that reads a web page or an email can run into booby-trapped instructions there (a prompt injection). The 2026 models resist it far better, but the real protection is still limited permissions: an agent that can't send money can't be manipulated into doing it.
Assistant
Question → answer
- You ask
- It answers
- You take back control
→ Agent (framed)
Autonomous loop
- You set a goal
- It acts in a loop
- Frame: goal · budget · frequency · criterion
- It reads on its own, it writes under validation
An agent without a frame spirals out of control. The frame (on the right) is not optional.
5. Where to start
Small. A single agent, a single task, read-only first (it watches and alerts, it touches nothing), and you prove it's reliable before giving it a button — then a second agent. The “agents everywhere” big bang is the best way to break everything. My news watch ran for months before I let an agent write into Odoo.

- → AI proposes, the human validates — the guardrails, in detail.
- → What's an MCP — what gives the agent its arms.
- → Loops, routines and scheduled tasks — the agent that comes back to check.
- → My AI Watch agent — a real agent, online, that you can subscribe to.
Real-world cases. An invoice agent framed before a single line of code → the architecture, then in production · supplier price lists → An app that reads price lists for me · the action queue → Growth.

FABLE, MYTHOS, GLASSWING: WHY ANTHROPIC RELEASED TWO VERSIONS OF THE SAME MODEL
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/fable-mythos-glasswing.html
Published: 2026-06-10
================================================================

On June 9, 2026, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5, the first model in a new “Mythos” class above Opus — and restricted the unguarded version, Mythos 5, to vetted cyberdefenders. What it changes, explained simply.

Home › Guides › Fable, Mythos, Glasswing
Guides · General
Fable, Mythos, Glasswing: why Anthropic released two versions of the same model
On June 9, 2026, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 — the first model in a new class, above Opus. And it made an unusual choice: keeping the unguarded version, Mythos 5, for a small circle of cyberdefenders. Here's the story, jargon-free.
By Hugo Lahutte· June 10, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026·~5 min read IA vulgarisation actualité
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- Fable 5 is the most powerful model Anthropic has ever made publicly available — the first building block of a new “Mythos” class, one notch above Opus.
- Mythos 5 is the same model without some of the safeguards: it's only accessible to vetted cyberdefenders and infrastructure operators, through Project Glasswing.
- Pricing: $10/$50 per million tokens (double Opus 4.8). Included free for Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise subscribers from June 9 to 22.
Update · September 1, 2026
Fable's eventful summer, in five dates
- June 12 — three days after launch, the US government suspends access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 through an export-control directive. Anthropic disables both models for everyone; developers fall back on Opus 4.8.
- July 1 — Fable 5 returns, worldwide, with new classifiers targeting malicious cyber uses; some routine coding tasks fall back to Opus 4.8. The access included in subscriptions is extended, then reorganized on July 20: included in the higher plans with a reduced quota, on usage credits for the others.
- July 24 — Opus 5 ships: close to Fable 5 for half the price, and the most resistant to prompt injection. For the vast majority of uses, it's the one that made Fable optional.
- August 7 — Fable 5's biology safeguards are loosened: about 85% fewer false refusals on everyday health questions, with dual-use topics still routed to a more restricted model.
- September 1 — Fable 5.1 succeeds Fable 5: same tier, same price ($10 / $50 per million tokens), a one-million-token context window, cheaper cache reads, refined cyber safeguards (60% fewer false positives, according to Anthropic). Mythos 5.1 stays reserved for the trusted-access programs (cybersecurity, life sciences).
The rest of this guide is the June 10 story, kept as is: the logic of “one class above, two versions of the same model” hasn't moved. What has moved is that power carries a political price as much as an economic one.
1. What happened on June 9
A few days after publicly warning that AI was becoming “too dangerous” to release without precautions, Anthropic launched… its most powerful model. The paradox is only apparent: it's exactly the same decision, seen from both sides. Claude Fable 5 shipped on June 9, 2026, presented as exceeding “any model ever made generally available” by Anthropic — state-of-the-art on nearly every benchmark: software engineering, knowledge work, vision, scientific research.
The news isn't just about power: it's the lineup structure that changes, and the way Anthropic handles the risk that comes with it.
2. Mythos: a class above Opus
For years, the Claude lineup has come in three sizes: Haiku (fast, cheap), Sonnet (balanced), Opus (top of the line). I explain all of this in What is Claude. Fable 5 opens a fourth floor: the Mythos class, above Opus.
Before
3 sizes
- Opus — the most capable
- Sonnet — the balance
- Haiku — the fast one
→ Since June 9
4 floors
- Mythos — the class above (Fable 5)
- Opus · Sonnet · Haiku
Fable 5 is not an “Opus 4.9”: it's the first model of a brand-new class.
On the technical side, for those who care: a one-million-token context window, up to 128,000 output tokens, and “adaptive” reasoning the model doses itself according to difficulty.
3. Why two versions of the same model
This is the heart of the story. Under the hood, Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are the same model. The difference is the safeguards:
- Fable 5, the public version, ships with reinforced protections around cybersecurity and biology. Concretely, sensitive requests (biology, chemistry) are redirected to Opus 4.8, which answers instead. Anthropic says the tuning is deliberately cautious — it sometimes catches harmless requests — but it triggers in fewer than 5% of sessions.
- Mythos 5, the version without some of those limits, is not for sale: it's reserved for a small group of cyberdefenders and critical-infrastructure operators, vetted one by one, under Project Glasswing.
The logic: a model at this level is genuinely useful for defending systems (finding flaws before attackers do) — but the same capabilities can be used to attack. Rather than choosing between “publish everything” and “publish nothing”, Anthropic splits the difference: the general public gets the power with brakes, vetted defenders get the power without them.
4. What it changes for you
Three concrete things:
- The price. Fable 5 costs $10 per million input tokens, $50 per million output — double Opus 4.8 ($5/$25). For the orders of magnitude, see How much does AI cost.
- The free window. From June 9 to 22, 2026, Fable 5 is included at no extra cost for Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise subscribers. It's the moment to test the top of the line on your real cases — exactly what I did: Fable 5 reviewed this site the day after its release.
- The right reflex. Since then, the golden rule hasn't changed: the right model is the cheapest one that does the job. Emails, product sheets, routine analysis → Sonnet or Opus are enough. Save Fable for the hard problems where the marginal intelligence is worth its price.

- → How much does AI cost — subscriptions vs API, the orders of magnitude.
- → Fable 5 reviews this site — my first full-scale test, in production the same day.

CHAT, COWORK, OR CODE: WHICH TO USE (AND THE FAMOUS “TERMINAL”)
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/chat-cowork-code-terminal.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

Three ways to use Claude depending on the task: Chat (talk), Cowork (delegate office work, on desktop, web, and mobile), and Code (act on your files and your site, in the terminal, the browser, or your phone). The truth about the terminal, the one-command install, why you don't need a big computer, and what changed in 2026: routines, built-in browser, cloud sessions, Auto mode.

Home › Guides › Chat, Cowork, or Code
Guides · General → practical
Chat, Cowork, or Code: which to use (and the famous "terminal")
Three ways to use Claude depending on the task — talk, delegate, act — and the truth about the "terminal," which looks scary but installs with one command. Along with what changed in 2026: Cowork everywhere, Code in the browser and on mobile, and routines that run without your machine.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026 · Updated September 1, 2026 · ~7 min read Claude Claude Code infra vulgarisation
- 1 30-second take
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
30-second take
- Chat: you talk, it produces text, analyses, ideas — with its memory and your connected tools. The interface you already know.
- Cowork: you delegate real office work to it (prepare a doc, dig through files, fill out a form in its built-in browser, run a routine) — designed for non-developers, on desktop, web, and mobile.
- Code: it acts directly on your files, your project, your site — the most powerful option. In the "terminal" (one command to paste), but also in the browser, the app, or your phone, where the session runs in the cloud.
1. Chat, Cowork, Code: which for what
They're three doors into the same Claude, to pick based on what you want to do:
- Chat (web, mobile, app) — the conversation. To think, write, analyze a document, prepare a strategy. 90% of people start and stay here, and that's perfectly fine. In my setup, that's where everything in my voice gets written — and we stop at the validated text: no HTML, no publishing.
- Cowork — an assistant that carries out office work end to end, for someone who doesn't code. It handles files, a spreadsheet, a presentation; it opens a browser in its panel to fill out a form or finish an online process; it runs scheduled routines; it shares its memory with chat. The step between "talking" and "delegating."
- Code — the agent that gets its hands dirty: it reads and edits your files, runs commands, manages a code repository, deploys a site, updates all the cross-links of a page. That's what I run Cobra with and how I publish this site. Not reserved for devs: it's just the "it acts, it doesn't just answer" level.
ChatTalk What it's forThink, write, analyze, decide. An exampleFrame a spec, summarize a PDF, write a text in your voice. Who it's forEveryone — the starting point. CoworkDelegate What it's forHand off office work end to end, no terminal. An exampleBuild a deck, go through a file, a Monday-morning routine. Who it's forNon-developers who want to delegate. CodeAct What it's forEdit files, run, deploy, maintain. An exampleA management module, a site live a minute later, an internal app. Who it's forAnyone who wants it to act, devs or not. From left (talk) to right (act). You move up a notch when you want Claude to do, not just answer.
My boundary rule, which structures all my work: Chat writes, Code executes. A Chat session produces a validated text; Code turns it into a deliverable. The two halves don't share the same success criterion — the accuracy of the message on one side, conformity to the template on the other — and mixing them in a single session means losing both. Details in my method.
2. What "the terminal" is, and why it shouldn't hold you back
The terminal is just a window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons. It has a "hacker movie" vibe that intimidates, but it's an interface like any other.
And above all: you don't need to master it. The strategy is dead simple — you copy, you paste, you hit Enter. If a command gets stuck, you paste the error to Claude and it tells you what to do. You learn by doing, no course required.
— bash — 80×24 $ curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash It looks impressive, but it's just a window where you paste one line.
3. Installing Claude Code, really easily
No need to install anything else anymore: a single command to paste in the terminal.
On Mac (or Linux) — open Terminal, paste, Enter:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
On Windows — open PowerShell, paste, Enter:
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
Then you check, and you launch:
claude --version claude
On first launch, it opens your browser to sign in to your Claude account. You need a paid subscription — and good news: every paid plan includes Claude Code and Cowork, from the Pro plan (about twenty dollars a month) to the Max plans; what changes between them is usage volume.
And if the terminal really puts you off, you have three other doors: the desktop app (Mac/Windows), which runs Claude Code without a terminal, Claude Code in the browser (the session runs in the cloud, on a copy of your project, nothing to install), and the mobile app — I launch fixes from my phone, and check them live a minute later.
Official details: code.claude.com/docs/en/setup.
4. Do you need a big computer? (No.)
Let's demystify: all the computation happens on Anthropic's servers, not on your machine. You do not need a gamer graphics card or a monster — your computer only sends and receives text.
A year ago, I recommended a machine that stays on 24/7 to host your automations. That's less and less necessary: Claude Code on the web and Cowork run in the cloud, and scheduled routines run without your machine. My little always-on Mac is now only used for what genuinely has to run at my place. The real comfort of a good computer is running several sessions in parallel without lagging — not computing power.
Your computer (or your phone) sends / receives text Internet Anthropic servers where the computing happens — and where cloud sessions and routines run No GPU needed
Your machine is just a remote control: the engine runs elsewhere.
5. What changed in 2026
For those who read the first version of this guide, in May:
- Cowork left the desktop. Desktop, web, and mobile for every paid plan (August); a built-in browser to finish an online process; the ability to teach Claude a skill by recording your screen; memory shared with chat; scheduled routines; a plugin marketplace.
- Code left the terminal. Browser, desktop app, mobile — the session runs in the cloud. Auto mode (Claude decides routine permissions on its own, with protections against manipulation) became the default in August. Subagents work in the background, workflows orchestrate several agents, Artifacts produce shareable pages from a session, and a cleanup command tidies up unused skills and context files.
- Chat acts. Connectors no longer just read: Claude can send a reply in Gmail or file a document in Drive, with validation on the actions that matter.
- The models. The Claude 5 family — Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1 — made Code capable of autonomous tasks lasting several hours. It's no longer "it writes a function," it's "it ships a feature, tested."

- → GitHub — the free thing that backs everything up on its own, and that Code works on.
- → What is a skill — the procedures Cowork and Code load on demand.
- → What is Claude — the models behind these three doors.
Real cases. Why I run two separate Code sessions → Double Claude Code: Cobra vs HL · how I document my setup to pass it on → Claude setup: documentation and onboarding · the Chat / Code split in my method.

WHAT IS GITHUB, AND WHY IS IT FREE AND KIND OF MAGICAL
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-github.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

GitHub for non-devs: the vault that backs up your work, keeps the full history, and once connected, updates itself automatically. Free to get started.

Home › Guides › What is GitHub?
Guides · General
What is GitHub, and why is it free and kind of magical
GitHub for non-devs: the vault that backs up your work, keeps the full history, and once connected, updates itself automatically. Free to get started.
By Hugo Lahutte· May 31, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026·~5 min read GitHub infra vulgarisation
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Going further
In 30 seconds
- GitHub is an online home for your project (a site, some code, files), with the complete history of every change.
- Once connected, your tools sync themselves: you never re-upload anything by hand.
- It's free for the essentials, and it's the global standard — every contractor you work with knows how to use it.
1. What it is, in one image
Think of Google Drive for your project, but with total memory. Every time something changes, GitHub keeps a dated snapshot of the previous state. Nothing gets lost, and you can roll back to any version with one click if a change breaks everything.
That's what changes everything: you work without fear. You test, you break things, you roll back. A mistake is no longer a drama.
- May 31 · 09:12Initial version
- May 31 · 14:03Homepage redesign↩ roll back here
- May 31 · 16:40Added pricing section
- Jun 1 · 10:05Change that breaks everything 😬
Every change = a dated snapshot. If the latest one breaks everything, you roll back to a healthy version with one click.
2. Why it's free (and not a gimmick)
GitHub is owned by Microsoft, and its free tier comfortably covers the needs of a freelancer or a small business. It's not a stripped-down "just to try it" version: entire companies run on it. The paid plans only matter for advanced team use.
Another advantage: it has become the standard. When you hand a piece of work to a developer or an agency, "it's on GitHub" is all you need to say — everyone speaks the same language.
3. "Once connected, it updates itself"
This is the click. You connect once: your site, say, or your shop's theme. After that, every change pushed to GitHub deploys automatically online. No FTP, no "let me re-upload the right file."
At my place, it's gotten wild: my site, my Shopify theme, and even automations tied to Odoo all live on GitHub. Claude Code pushes the changes there, and they're live a minute later. I almost never open the hood.
My projectyour files, your site →push GitHubhistory + source of truth →auto Livedeployed on its own Connected once: the last arrow is automatic. You push, it's live.
4. You don't need to understand all of it
Good news for non-technical people: you don't need to master GitHub. Claude Code handles version control for you (backups, history, deployment); you approve. GitHub runs in the background like a safety net.
Update · September 1, 2026
GitHub has become the place where Claude works
Three things have moved since May. Claude Code now works directly on a GitHub repository, from the browser or the phone: the session runs in the cloud, on a copy of the project, and pushes its changes as a pull request for you to review. My Brain lives on GitHub too, in a private repository my Claudes read through a connector: the same safety net (full history, rollback) protects my memory the way it protects my code. And automated checks (the "CI": lint, tests, build on every change) have become my norm, even for a static site — a weekly consistency check makes sure counters, indexes, and the sitemap stay aligned with the files.
Going further
- → What is MCP: connecting Claude to your tools
- → Chat, Cowork, or Code — Code is the one that drives GitHub for you.
Real case. This very site lives on GitHub and deploys itself with every change → This Knowledge Hub itself.

WHAT'S AN “MCP,” AND HOW TO PLUG CLAUDE INTO YOUR TOOLS (CONNECTORS, PERMISSIONS, ACTIONS)
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-mcp-connecter-claude.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

The four ways to plug Claude into your tools (copy-paste, browser, API, MCP), what MCP is — Anthropic's open standard, a universal socket adopted by Shopify, Meta, GitHub and everyone else —, what changed in 2026 (Claude no longer just reads: it sends an email, files a document, under validation), the two permission rules, what's connected on my side, and the difference between an MCP (the arms) and a skill (the know-how).

Home › Guides › What's an MCP?
Guides · General
What's an “MCP,” and how to plug Claude into your tools
API, MCP, browser, copy-paste: the four ways to plug Claude into your tools (Shopify, Gmail, Drive…), from the simplest to the most powerful. Why MCP changed everything — and, since 2026, why Claude no longer just reads: it acts, under your validation.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026 · Updated September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read MCP Claude infra vulgarisation
- 1 30-second take
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
30-second take
- By default, Claude can't see your tools. It reasons, but touches nothing until you plug it in.
- Four ways to connect it, from the simplest to the beefiest: copy-paste / screenshot → browser → API → MCP. In the Claude apps, a connected MCP is called a connector.
- MCP is a standard socket that lets Claude read and act in Shopify, Gmail, Drive, GitHub… It turns the assistant into a colleague plugged into your business — hence one rule: it never has more permissions than you, and the actions that matter get validated.
1. The starting point: a head without arms
Claude on its own is a brilliant brain with no hands. It can analyze what you show it, but it knows nothing about your Shopify or your email until you open the door. “Connecting” Claude means giving it arms.
2. The 4 levels of connection
From the simplest to the most powerful:
- Copy-paste / screenshot — zero setup. You paste a text, a photo of a screen, an export. Perfect to get started.
- The browser — you let Claude drive a browser to go click and read on a site for you. Cowork has had one built in since August 2026, in its side panel.
- The API — a programmed pipe between a service and Claude. More technical, but automatable.
- MCP — the standard socket (see below). The cleanest and most durable connection.
Copy-pastescreenshot / export BrowserClaude clicks for you APIprogrammed pipe MCPthe standard socket ← less setup effortmore power → The higher you climb, the more powerful and durable it gets — but starting at the bottom is perfectly fine.
3. What an MCP is, concretely
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It's an open standard created by Anthropic in late 2024 and adopted since by the whole market: think of a universal socket, like USB. Any MCP-compatible tool plugs into Claude — or into another assistant — with no custom tinkering. You “connect” Shopify, Google Drive, Gmail… and Claude can then read inside them and act, within the limits you allow.
The point: instead of re-coding an integration for each tool, everyone speaks the same socket. In 2026, vendors publish their own socket: Shopify for stores, Meta for ad accounts, hosting providers, online banks, invoicing tools. In the Claude apps, it's simply called a connector, switched on from a menu.
Claude Shopifyorders, products, collections Google Drivefiles, spreadsheets Gmailread — and reply, under validation GitHubthe code, the repos, the Brain Bank, hosting…invoices, deploys, logs A standard socket (USB-style): every MCP-compatible tool plugs in without a custom integration.
4. Read, then act: what changed in 2026
In the spring, connectors were mostly for reading: cross-checking sales, finding a document, summarizing an inbox. Since the summer, Claude acts: it drafts and sends a reply in Gmail, files or creates a document in Drive, updates a product page, opens a change request on a code repository — with control over the actions that require your validation.
It's a change in kind, and it imposes two rules I don't negotiate:
- The assistant never has more permissions than the person talking to it. A connector inherits your account, not an admin account. On my side, each Claude has its own connectors: the Cobra Claude sees Odoo and the Cobra store, the HL Claude sees my projects and my Brain — never the other way around.
- Automatic reads, validated writes. Reading and proposing: automatic. Sending, editing, publishing: a preview, then a button. The details of these regimes are in AI proposes, the human validates.
One more reason to be strict: an agent that reads outside content (a web page, an email) can run into booby-trapped instructions there — what's called prompt injection. The 2026 models resist it far better (Anthropic says it has nearly neutralized the problem with Opus 5 and Claude Code's Auto mode), but limited permissions remain the real protection: an assistant that can't wire money can't be manipulated into doing it.
5. What's connected on my side
Concretely: my two Shopify stores (Cobra and Haute Fidélité) live, my Drive and my email, GitHub — which holds my code, this site and my Brain —, the online bank for invoices and statements, the host of my apps to read logs and redeploy, and Odoo through code. The result: Claude works on my real tools, not a demo. That's the difference between “a nice chatbot” and “an operational colleague.”
Two examples from a typical week: cross-checking the store's orders against Odoo's all-channel sales for one brand, in a single question; or, from my phone, asking Claude Code to fix a page on this site and seeing it live a minute later.
6. MCP or skill? The arms and the know-how
The two get mixed up all the time. An MCP gives access to a tool: it's an arm. A skill describes a procedure: it's know-how. Publishing an entry on this site takes both — the GitHub connector to write, and the skill that knows in what order to update the twenty files. An arm without a procedure does anything, fast; a procedure without an arm stays a document.
Go deeper
- → What's an AI agent — once connected, Claude can act on its own.
- → What's a skill — the know-how that goes with the arms.
- → Is my data safe? — connecting means opening an access.
Real-world cases. Cross-checking Shopify and Odoo sales → Shopify/Odoo audit, 803 products · Dynaudio sales analysis · driving a deploy from the session → HF-OS: the foundation deployed.

WHAT IS A “LOOP”? AGENT LOOPS, ROUTINES, AND SCHEDULED TASKS
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-une-loop.html
Published: 2026-06-10
================================================================

A loop is a prompt re-run at a regular interval by an agent, to monitor or check something without you. Three tools depending on how long you need it: the Claude Code loop (ephemeral, expires on its own), the routine (scheduled, run in the cloud on Claude's side, without your machine), and the homemade scheduled task (cron, GitHub Actions). The concept, how to choose, the uses for a merchant, and the framing: a recurring task reads and alerts, it doesn't write on its own.

Home › Guides › What is a loop?
Guides · Setting up
What is a "loop"? Loops, routines, and scheduled tasks
A classic agent works toward a goal and then stops. A loop is the level above: the same task re-run at a regular interval — monitor, check, alert — without you. Since summer 2026, there are three ways to do that, from the most ephemeral to the most durable. The concept, the three tools, and the framing.
By Hugo Lahutte · June 10, 2026 · Updated September 1, 2026 · ~5 min read agent automatisation Claude Code
- 1 30-second take
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
30-second take
- A loop = a prompt re-run at a regular interval by an agent (every 5 min, every hour…), to monitor or check something without you.
- Three tools depending on how long you need it: the loop (ephemeral, inside your Claude Code session, expires on its own), the routine (scheduled, runs in the cloud on Claude's side, without your machine), the homemade scheduled task (cron, GitHub Actions, a server — for what has to run forever).
- Simple rule: need it for a few hours → loop; recurring need that can live at Claude's → routine; production infrastructure → scheduled task. And always a frame: goal, budget, frequency, criterion.
1. The loop, the level above the agent
In What is an AI agent, I explained the assistant/agent difference: the assistant answers, the agent acts in a loop until the result — then stops. The loop adds the time dimension: the entire task is re-run at a regular interval. The agent no longer works once toward a goal, it comes back to check — again and again.
It's the natural pattern for everything that is monitoring: you never "finish" monitoring a deployment or an order flow; you look, you compare with the expected state, you alert if it drifts, and you come back later.
Check → Compare → Alert if needed → Wait → Expire at every interval, until expiry The loop: a monitoring loop bounded in time — not an infinite loop.
2. The loop in Claude Code
Claude Code (see Chat, Cowork, or Code) ships with a /loop command: you give it a prompt and an interval, and it re-runs that prompt at every due time, inside your session. Without an interval, it sets the pace itself based on what it's waiting for — an eight-minute deployment deserves one check, not eight.
The detail that made me adopt it: the guardrail is built in. A loop expires automatically after a few days — it runs one last time, then deletes itself. A forgotten loop can't run indefinitely or silently burn a budget. It's exactly the kind of frame I demand for any agent (goal, budget, frequency, success criterion) — except here, the boundary is set by the tool itself.
3. Loop, routine, or scheduled task?
All three re-run a task at a regular interval; what differs is the lifespan and where it runs.
A few hoursLoopTied to your work session. Created in one line, expires on its own. To watch a deployment this afternoon. Recurring, no infraRoutineScheduled (every morning, every Monday) and run in the cloud on Claude's side — Claude Code on the web, Cowork, or a hosted agent — without your machine. For a weekly report, a seven-day watch. ForeverHomemade scheduled taskCron, GitHub Actions, a small server. Real production infrastructure, logged, with its secrets on the server side. For what has to run every day, without depending on a subscription. From ephemeral to durable. Routines are the new thing in 2026: the missing link between "I'm watching for three hours" and "I'm setting up infrastructure."
In my setup, all three coexist. My two daily briefs (hi-fi and AI) are scheduled tasks: they have to run every morning, forever, with their secrets on a server. The seven-day watch on my audience measurement — comparing each morning the real orders, the web flow, and the analytics, read-only, without changing anything — is a routine. Checking that an Odoo deployment goes well this afternoon is a loop: useful for three hours, forgettable afterwards.
4. What it's good for, for a merchant
Everything that gets checked at a regular interval:
- Orders: check every 30 minutes that the morning's orders are going out to fulfillment, alert if a status is stuck.
- Production release: after a deployment, check every 10 minutes that the key pages respond and that nothing breaks.
- Supplier feeds: monitor that an expected stock import has arrived and integrated properly.
- Prices: my alignment engine recalculates target prices with each new delivery of competitor prices, several times a day — in observation mode first, then live, family by family.
- Sources: my daily brief alerts me when a source has stopped responding for three days. Monitoring of the monitoring.
One cross-cutting rule, whatever the form: a recurring task reads and alerts; it doesn't write on its own into a production tool without a human having validated the action. Details in AI proposes, the human validates.
Go deeper
- → What is an AI agent — the basic loop, and the four guardrails.
- → Chat, Cowork, or Code — where loops and routines live.
- → Case study: the AI watch bot — a real, durable scheduled task, from A to Z.
Real cases. A daily brief that monitors its own sources → HiFi watch: 64 sources, alert when a source dies · an engine re-run with every price delivery → Automatic competitive alignment.

WHAT IS A "SKILL" (AND A HOOK, A SUBAGENT, A PLUGIN)?
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-un-skill.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

A skill is a procedure written in a folder (a SKILL.md file, sometimes scripts) that Claude loads on its own when your request matches; a hook is an automatic, deterministic script; a subagent is a delegated Claude with its own context; a plugin is the package that installs it all. What each one does, my three everyday skills, and how to choose between an instruction, a skill, a hook and a connector.

Home › Guides › What is a skill?
Guides · Getting set up
What is a "skill"(and a hook, a subagent, a plugin)?
When you're explaining the same procedure to Claude for the third time, that's a skill in disguise. A skill is a procedure written in a folder, which Claude loads on its own when the situation calls for it. Around it, three words that keep coming up: hook, subagent, plugin. Here's what each one does, and which to pick.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read skill Claude Code agent vulgarisation
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The visual body
- 3 Going further
In 30 seconds
- A skill = a folder with a SKILL.md file (the procedure, in text) and sometimes scripts. Claude loads it on demand, when your request matches. It's packaged know-how, portable from one tool to another.
- A hook = a script that fires automatically at a specific moment (before a command, after a change). Deterministic: it doesn't "think," it checks or blocks.
- A subagent = a Claude delegated to a subtask, with its own context. A plugin = the package that installs skills, hooks, subagents and connectors in one go.
1. The problem: the procedure you keep re-explaining
Publishing an entry on this site takes about twenty steps: the page, its English twin, the journal index, the homepage teaser, the sitemap, the llms.txt, the search index, the counters, a consistency check. The first six times, I explained it to Claude at the start of the session. The seventh time, I realized the problem wasn't Claude: it was me keeping the procedure in my head instead of writing it down.
The CLAUDE.md takes care of general rules (tone, principles, pitfalls). But a twenty-step procedure has no business there: it would weigh down every conversation, including the ones that don't need it. I needed a place for procedures, loaded only when useful. That's the skill.
2. The skill: a procedure in a folder
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file: at the top, a name and a description (that's what Claude reads to decide whether the skill applies to your request); below, the procedure in plain text, with its rules, its examples and its guardrails. Optionally, scripts or reference files alongside. Nothing else.
Three skills do the bulk of my work:
- kh-post-brief — at the end of a session, with any AI, produce the brief for a journal entry: title, vertical, author, tags from the whitelist, status, sections (context, what was done, what was hard, stack, what it illustrates), visuals to attach, and the sanitization guardrails (no secrets, no sensitive financial figures, no internal app URLs). I paste the brief into Claude Code, which publishes the FR + EN entry and all the cross-linking.
- brain — read, search and update my Brain, with a strict write gate: read freely, write only on explicit instruction ("note that in my Brain"), never turn a discussion into a write.
- wiki-capture — the end-of-session ritual: the session entry and the update of the reference pages.
Name + descriptionOne sentence that says when this skill applies. It's the trigger: Claude compares it to your request. The procedureThe steps, in order, in plain text. With a filled-in example: one example is worth ten lines of explanation. The guardrailsWhat we never do (secrets, amounts, internal URLs), the cases where we stop and ask. Scripts and references (optional)A check script, a template, a whitelist. Loaded only if the procedure needs them. A skill isn't magic: it's written method, filed in the right place and loaded at the right moment.
The property that matters: a skill is portable. The text of kh-post-brief is written to be pasted into ChatGPT or Gemini at the end of a session; the AI returns the brief, and Claude Code publishes. A well-written skill survives a change of tool. And since summer 2026, the Claude Cowork app even lets you teach a skill by recording your screen while narrating: Claude turns it into a reusable skill, without writing a line.
3. The hook: an automatic reflex
A hook is a script that fires automatically at a specific moment in Claude's work: before a command is run, after a file has been modified, when the conversation gets compacted, when a session ends. The fundamental difference from a skill: a hook doesn't think. It checks, blocks, formats, logs — deterministically, every time, no exceptions.
Useful examples for a merchant: refusing any command that would push code straight to production; running a consistency checker after every change to a data file; forbidding a file containing a secret from being added to the repo. What I used to entrust to a CLAUDE.md rule ("never merge the whole branch") can become a hook that makes the mistake physically impossible. A rule gets read; a hook gets executed.
Honest limit: hooks run in Claude Code (the terminal, or its web and desktop versions). In a Chat conversation or on mobile, they don't exist — hence, in my setup, a duplicate instruction rule for whatever has to work everywhere.
4. The subagent: delegating a subtask
A subagent is a Claude that the main agent hands a subtask to, with its own context, its own instructions, sometimes its own tools. It works — in the background by default, since summer 2026 — and returns a result. Three uses:
- Parallelize: translate twenty pages, audit ten files, check five sources at the same time.
- Isolate context: a heavy read (a long document, an entire repo) doesn't clutter the main conversation; only the conclusion comes back up.
- Specialize: a "reviewer" subagent with adversarial instructions, a "verifier" subagent that only confirms or refutes.
Workflows (available in Claude Code since June 2026) are the layer above: a small script that orchestrates several subagents deterministically — a review per dimension, then a check of each finding, for example. Useful, but reserve it for tasks that deserve a dozen agents. The default reflex is still: start without.
5. The plugin: the package
A plugin bundles skills, subagents, commands, hooks and connectors into a versioned package, installable in one command. It's the way to share complete know-how with a team — or to install it at home from a marketplace. The code security checker I use before every delivery is a plugin; my publishing pipeline will become one the day someone other than me has to publish here.
6. Instruction, skill, hook or connector: which to choose
A general ruleCLAUDE.mdTone, principles, pitfalls turned into rules. Short, always loaded. "Keep it casual," "never a whole branch in prod." A procedureSkillSteps, a template, guardrails. Loaded when the request matches. "Publish an entry," "capture the session." A systematic checkHookHas to happen every time, no judgment. "Block any push to main," "run the check after every change." Access to a toolConnector (MCP)Read or act in Shopify, Drive, Gmail, GitHub. The arms — to be framed by permissions. The test: is it a rule (CLAUDE.md), a procedure (skill), a reflex that must always run (hook), or a tool to plug in (connector)?
7. And without a terminal?
Skills aren't reserved for developers. Claude Cowork (the desktop app, also on the web and on mobile) installs them from a marketplace and loads them into ordinary office work: preparing a deck, going through a file, running a routine. And learning by screen recording is the simplest way there is to turn know-how into a procedure: you do the task once while narrating, Claude writes it up.
My advice for getting started: take the procedure you explain most often — not the most impressive, the most repeated — and write it in ten lines with a filled-in example. If Claude gets it right three times in a row without your help, it's a skill. If not, the procedure wasn't clear, and you just learned that.
Going further
- → Writing a good CLAUDE.md — the general rules, the other half.
- → What is an MCP — the connectors, the arms.
- → What is an AI agent — the basic loop that subagents multiply.
Real cases. The publishing skill → this site's redesign, published with it · the adversarial review of a dev request → the AI checks what it assumes.

HOW TO TALK TO AI PROPERLY IN 2026: FROM PROMPT TO BRIEF
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/ecrire-un-bon-prompt.html
Published: 2026-05-31
================================================================

The recipe for a good prompt (context, task, format, constraints) still holds. But when the AI works on its own, the prompt becomes a brief: a goal, a success criterion, context provided rather than described, checkpoints. The reflexes of 2026, a real brief, and the three places an instruction lives (prompt, CLAUDE.md, skill).

Home › Guides › Writing a good prompt
Guides · General → practice
How to talk to AI properly in 2026: from prompt to brief
A good prompt makes a good answer. A good brief makes good work — when the AI chains steps together on its own, what you write beforehand matters more than ever. The recipe that still holds, what's changed, and what you should stop retyping.
By Hugo Lahutte · May 31, 2026 · Updated September 2, 2026 · ~7 min read prompt méthode vulgarisation
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- The basic recipe hasn't moved: context + task + format + constraints, and an example of the result you want.
- What's changed: the AI no longer just answers, it works (reads your files, acts in your tools, chains steps together). The prompt becomes a brief: a goal, a success criterion, checkpoints.
- The real lever is no longer the magic phrase: it's what the AI knows before your request. An instruction you keep retyping is a rule in disguise; a procedure you keep re-explaining is a skill in disguise.
1. The basic recipe (still true)
A prompt is the instruction you write to the AI. Nothing technical, but it's what changes an answer the most: the same AI returns generic mush or a clean deliverable depending on how you ask. No secret formula — clarity. Four building blocks are enough for a simple request:
ContextWho you are, the situation, who it's for. “I run a hi-fi shop, I'm writing to an unhappy customer…” TaskWhat you want, in one action verb: “write,” “summarize in five points,” “compare these two options.” FormatThe output shape: a list, a table, an email ready to send, three paragraphs max. ConstraintsThe frame: length, tone, language, what to avoid. “Warm tone, no jargon, 120 words.” Context + task + format + constraints. Add an example of the result you want and you go up one more notch.
2. From prompt to brief: what's changed
In May, a request to the AI produced an answer. In September 2026, it often triggers a piece of work: Claude reads a folder, fixes twenty files, sends an email pending your approval, runs for an hour in the background. Claude Code's default mode chains actions without asking your permission at every step; Cowork does the same on your desktop. A one-line instruction that was enough for an answer becomes dangerous for a mission.
Hence the shift from prompt to brief. Two more building blocks, and a change of nature for the first one:
- Context is provided, no longer described. Instead of explaining your business, you hand over the files, the folder, the connector. “Here's the sales spreadsheet” beats three paragraphs about your sales. What's permanent (tone, rules, tools) no longer even belongs in the prompt: it lives in a CLAUDE.md.
- The goal and the success criterion. “We'll know it's done when…”: all 175 pages share a consistent tone, the script runs without errors, the email fits in 120 words. An AI acting on its own needs to know when to stop — otherwise it keeps going, or stops too early.
- The checkpoints. For a long mission: “propose a plan before you start,” “show me the diff before pushing,” “one question at a time if something's ambiguous.” You keep control at the moments that matter, not on every line.
Goal+ “it's done when…” → Context providedfiles, folder, connector → Task broken downsteps, order → Format & constraintswhat stays untouched → Checkpointsplan, preview, validation The 2026 brief: the four building blocks of the prompt, with a measurable goal up front and checkpoints at the end.
3. Vague prompt, precise prompt, brief
The same need, three levels. The second is enough for an answer; the third is what I write when the AI has to deliver on its own.
Vague
“Write me an email for a customer”
- No context
- No clear goal
- Generic result, to be redone
→ Precise
Context + task + format
- “Customer unhappy about a delivery delay”
- “Write a reply that apologizes and offers a gesture”
- “Warm tone, 120 words, ready to send”
Same AI, same topic: precision makes all the difference on an answer.
And the brief, for a mission — a real one here, for an invoice check handed to Claude Code:
Goal: check that every invoice in the /factures-aout folder matches an Odoo order. We'll know it's done when: a table lists each invoice with the order number found, or “to check” with the reason. Context: the invoices are PDFs; Odoo access is read-only. Rules: change nothing in Odoo; never guess an amount. Steps: 1) read the folder and propose a 5-line plan, wait for my OK; 2) process the invoices; 3) deliver the table + the list of doubtful cases. If something is ambiguous, ask ONE question, then continue.
Notice what's missing: no explanation of what an invoice is, no instruction about tone, no naming rule. All of that is already in the permanent context. The brief only contains what's specific to this mission.
4. The reflexes of 2026
- Give an example. Showing a model of the result is worth ten lines of explanation. For a recurring deliverable, the example ends up in a skill.
- Ask for the plan before execution. On anything beyond ten minutes of work: “propose a plan, wait for my OK.” Claude Code has a dedicated mode for this; elsewhere, the sentence is enough. It's the “think before acting” principle of the four principles.
- One question at a time. Allow the AI to ask you one question when something's ambiguous — and forbid the burst of ten. You avoid off-target answers without getting grilled like at the police station.
- Iterate on the result, not on the sentence. “Too long,” “keep the second paragraph, cut the rest,” “show me what you changed.” Back-and-forth is normal; hunting for the perfect wording on the first try is not.
- Break it down. A big mission into steps, with a checkpoint between each one. For a long project, a plan file the AI ticks off as it goes.
- Say what must not be touched. “Only change this file,” “read-only on Odoo,” “don't push anything without showing me.” With an AI that acts, the negative constraint counts as much as the positive instruction.
- Close cleanly. When a conversation gets long, ask for a handoff brief: where things stand, what's left, the decisions made. The next session picks up from there instead of re-explaining everything.
5. The three places an instruction lives
The question to ask about every instruction: am I going to write it again? If so, it's not in the right place.
The promptwhat's specific to this request The CLAUDE.mdwhat's true all the time: tone, rules, tools The skilla procedure you repeat: steps, template, checks ← one-offreused ↑ The more an instruction comes back, the higher it climbs: from prompt to rule, from rule to procedure.
In my setup, the casual tone (“tu” in French), “no preamble,” “one question at a time” or “flag it, don't change it on your own” are never typed anymore: they're in the CLAUDE.md. Publishing a journal entry (page, index, sitemap, feeds, translation) is no longer explained: it's a skill. This very guide was born from a two-line brief, because everything else was already known. That's the central idea of the guide What is “context”, and why it's everything: the prompt is 20%; the context is the rest.
6. Depending on the tool: Chat, Cowork, Code
- In Claude Chat — the basic recipe is enough. For a recurring topic, create a project with its instructions and documents: the context is provided once and for all.
- In Cowork — point to the folder or the connector (Gmail, Drive, Shopify…) rather than describing what it contains, and say explicitly what must be validated before being sent or changed. The guide AI proposes, the human validates spells out the rule.
- In Claude Code — write a brief (goal, criterion, steps, checkpoints), ask for the plan, let it run, review the diff. For a task that comes back every day, it's no longer a prompt: it's a routine.
Choosing the tool itself is covered in Chat, Cowork, or Code.
Going further
- → What is “context”, and why it's everything — why what the AI knows beforehand matters more than the sentence.
- → Writing a good CLAUDE.md — when your instructions become permanent.
- → What is a “skill” — when a procedure deserves better than a prompt.
Real-world cases. A brief so Claude works on its own → Mission brief: invoice verification · a pipeline that restates every request before coding → AI doesn't code my request — it verifies what it assumes.
