WHAT IS HL OS: AN OPERATING SYSTEM FOR RUNNING A GROUP WITH AI
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/cest-quoi-hl-os.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

HL OS is the shared foundation (database, AI layer, identity and permissions, action log) and the five building blocks (Zéro, Knowledge, Content Machine, Growth, AI Core) that Hugo Lahutte has been building since June 2026 to run Cobra, Haute Fidélité and his projects with AI. One core, several contexts, and a single flow: request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement.

Home › Guides › What is HL OS?
Guides · My systems
What is HL OS:an operating system for running a group with AI
A store, a magazine, a brand, a personal venture — and ten tools that don't talk to each other. HL OS is the name I give to what I've been building since June 2026 to run all of it with AI: a shared foundation, five building blocks, and one rule — the AI proposes, the human validates. The map, without jargon.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~8 min read HL OS agent strat Claude Code
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- HL OS = a shared foundation (a database, an AI layer, identity and permissions, an action log) + five building blocks that plug into it: Zéro (mail and tasks), Knowledge (the Brain), Content Machine (publish), Growth (decide), AI Core — Socle IA — (write, search, secure).
- One core, several contexts: Cobra and Haute Fidélité share the engines, never the accounts, the data or the rules.
- Every action follows the same flow: request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement. Reading is automatic; writing is validated.
1. Why an “OS”
My daily life is Odoo for sales, margin and stock; Shopify for the stores; Google Analytics, Ads, Search Console and Merchant Center for visibility; Brevo for email; the social networks; one mailbox per organization; a magazine to produce. Every tool knows how to produce its own dashboard. None of them answers, on its own, the question that matters: what deserves my time today?
Until 2025, the answer was “hire, or buy a suite.” In 2026, AI changes the scale of what a business owner who knows what they want can have built. So I stopped stacking tools and started building the layer above — the one that reads every tool, reconciles the facts, proposes actions and keeps the record. An operating system, in the literal sense: what everything else runs on.
The word is a bit big for an organization my size. I own it: the day I started calling this an OS, I stopped thinking of it as a collection of scripts.
2. The foundation
Everything rests on four shared things:
- A shared database, inherited from HF-OS, the publishing ERP I built in five days in June: a single application (a headless CMS + a web framework + PostgreSQL) that serves the dashboard, the admin and the API. The building blocks don't reinvent storage: they plug into it.
- A shared AI layer — the AI Core (Socle IA): writing in my voice (several voices, actually: the magazine, me in the first person, the travel journal), embeddings for search, a router that picks the model by tier (small, large, fallback) and logs every call, and a pattern of secrets encrypted server-side — never in the code, never in the Brain.
- Identity and permissions: Google sign-in restricted to a whitelist, roles, and the rule that governs everything — the assistant never gets more rights than the person talking to it.
- An action log: every write leaves a usable trace, idempotent whenever the connector allows it.
3. The five building blocks
A building block is a perimeter, a living specification, a development plan with success criteria (“we'll know it's good when…”) and a dated Decisions section. The five:
HL OS foundation ZéroMail + tasks. Sorts, summarizes, turns an email into a task. The Brain's daily source of signal. KnowledgeThe Brain and its index: everything about me becomes queryable by my AIs. Content MachineOne capture, N destinations: field capture, magazine repurposing, validated publishing. GrowthAction-first decisions: reconciles sales, acquisition, SEO, web, email and social, and proposes the next useful piece of work. AI CoreWriting in my voice, embeddings, model router, encrypted secrets. The other building blocks call it, they don't reimplement it. Five building blocks, one foundation. The boundary is clean: Growth measures and recommends, the Content Machine makes and publishes, Knowledge preserves, Zéro feeds, the AI Core serves the others.
Growth — from ten dashboards to a queue of actions
The most advanced building block. It automatically pulls the facts available (Odoo, Shopify, Analytics, Ads, Search Console, Merchant Center, web health checks, email, social), reconciles them, and proposes a handful of actions ranked by impact, confidence, effort and risk. A short home page, a single bar to ask a question or prepare an action, and the expert views behind it, as evidence. A missing data point shows up as exactly that — never a silent zero. Details in the journal entry.
Content Machine — one capture, N destinations
It doesn't produce content, it carries a presence: a few photos, a voice memo, at a place, at a time, by an identified person — and the machine proposes the renderings (post, article, print page) to the right destinations, without ever publishing on its own. Dedicated guide: Content Machine.
Knowledge — the Brain
The durable memory, in the OKF format, read by all my AIs. Dedicated guide: What is a Brain.
4. One core, several contexts
The most important architecture decision, made from the start: Cobra and Haute Fidélité share the intelligence, never the accounts, the secrets, the data or the operating rules. The first Growth instance runs for Cobra; a Haute Fidélité instance will reuse the same core with its own accounts, data and goals — an isolated context inside HL OS. The Content Machine works the same way: a context (the provenance — where, when, why) is not a destination (where it publishes), and one context deploys to several destinations.
The benefit isn't only technical. It's what makes it possible to run a work account and a personal account, a Claude Cobra and a Claude HL, without ever mixing two perimeters in a base read from both sides.
5. The flow of an action
Whatever the building block, an action that touches the real world (a price, a stock level, a campaign, an email, a publication) follows the same path:
Requesta question, an intent→auto Analysisfacts, sources, freshness→auto Previewwhat's about to change→human Validationone button, one person→auto Executionthrough the connector→auto Log + measurementbefore / after, fed back in Reading and refreshing can be automatic. Writing to Shopify, Odoo, an ad platform, the email tool or a social network stays behind required validation as long as no finer explicit permission exists. And a recommendation without a measurement after execution doesn't close the loop: it hasn't been “learned.”
6. Where it stands (September 2026)
Dated snapshot · September 1, 2026
- Growth — in production for Cobra since September 1: action-first home, main bar, evidence views, reads from every connected source. Current priority: making audience measurement reliable before allowing any budget-shift recommendation. One particularity: this block was built with ChatGPT and Codex, with Claude involved only at the margins (the story and architecture).
- Content Machine — v2 spec (July 30), foundation in place; the September 1 pivot unifies field capture, magazine repurposing and “publish this idea” into a single system. Next step: capture in under ten seconds, then a first Instagram rendering. Deadline: the Haute Fidélité show, late September.
- Knowledge / Brain — in place since August 21; read through a GitHub connector; search index postponed until the signal.
- Zéro and AI Core — in progress; the specifications are migrating into the Brain.
This status is a snapshot, not a lasting truth: figures and statuses live in the tools and in the Brain, never copied here as permanent.
7. What it illustrates
Three things I believe transfer to any small or mid-sized business:
- The value isn't in one more dashboard. It's in no longer having to open ten interfaces to piece together a situation — and in having a queue of actions with their evidence.
- The hard work wasn't the code. It was deciding which source to believe (Odoo carries the actuals, Shopify the web flow, the ad platforms their self-reported attribution) and preventing misleading reconciliations. The AI hammered out the code; the trade-offs stay human.
- Build rather than wait for a quote, when the business is specific and the cost of customization collapses. The core of Growth was framed over a weekend and put into production on the Tuesday — built, for this block, with ChatGPT and Codex rather than Claude. The question “do you still need to buy?” now applies to the steering layer, not just the ERP.
Going further

- → What is a Brain — the Knowledge building block.
- → The AI proposes, the human validates — the guardrails that make all of this possible.

CONTENT MACHINE: ONE CAPTURE, N DESTINATIONS
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/content-machine-une-capture-n-destinations.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

Hugo Lahutte's Content Machine doesn't produce content, it carries a presence: the basic unit is the attested observation (media, place, time, person), and the post or the article are only renderings of it. Three inputs (Telegram capture in under ten seconds, repurposing of the Haute Fidélité magazine, “publish this idea” from the Brain), locks before publication, disposable or permanent destinations, and one rule: the machine proposes, the human validates.

Home › Guides › Content Machine
Guides · My systems
Content Machine:one capture, N destinations
Anyone can generate content with AI — which is precisely why it's no longer worth anything. My content machine does the opposite: it doesn't produce content, it carries a presence. A photo, a voice memo, a place, a time, a person — and the machine proposes where and in what form it should land. Without ever deciding on its own.
By Hugo Lahutte · September 1, 2026 · ~8 min read Content Machine marketing GEO agent
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body, visual
- 3 Go deeper
In 30 seconds
- The basic unit isn't the article, it's the attested observation: a few media files, a note, a place, a time, an identified person. A post, an article, a print page are only renderings of it.
- Three inputs, one shared log: field capture (Telegram, under ten seconds), repurposing of the magazine (issues and archives whose rights I hold), and “publish this idea” from the Brain.
- The machine never decides: it proposes a destination along with its reasoning, the human settles it with one button. And provenance is the product — it's what search engines and AIs reward.
1. The problem: generated content is no longer worth anything
In 2026, producing ten posts, a blog article and a newsletter takes five minutes. Everyone does it; the feeds are full of smooth texts that nobody actually lived. For a magazine, a brand or a retailer, that's not just useless: it's dangerous, because it dilutes the only thing that still sets you apart — having been there.
My problem was concrete. A print magazine (Haute Fidélité) and its archives, an editorial brand (HiFi Lovers), a family travel journal, this Knowledge Hub, a LinkedIn account, a trade show coming up. A huge amount of raw material, and every time the same friction: capturing is easy, formatting eats time, and nothing connects what was seen to what gets published.
2. The principle: carrying a presence
The Content Machine doesn't produce content. In it, AI is the logistics between what was observed in the field and the place where it needs to land. Four rules, non-negotiable:
- The basic unit is the attested observation: a few photos, a voice memo or a note, at a place, at a time, by an identified person. The post, the article, the print page are only renderings of it.
- Witnessed and documented are kept separate, in the database and in the form. What I saw doesn't have the same status as what I read, and the reader must be able to see it.
- The machine never decides. It proposes a destination along with its reasoning; the human settles it with one button.
- Provenance is the product. Who, where, when: that's the first-hand experience signal that search engines and answering AIs reward.
3. Three inputs, one shared log
Input 1 · witnessedField captureFrom Telegram, in under ten seconds, offline if needed: photos, a voice memo, a text. Posting in the right topic states the context — zero manual tagging. Input 2 · documentedMagazine repurposingThe PDFs and HD visuals of the issues — current and archived — whose rights I hold as the publisher, turned into renderings for the social networks and the site. The magazine is the reserve of authority. Input 3 · documented“Publish this idea”A Brain document marked publiable (publishable) becomes an entry on this Knowledge Hub, written in my voice, validated with one tap, live a minute later. Three raw materials, a single governance and a single rendering system. What was scattered across three projects has become one building block.
4. Context ≠ destination
The distinction that unlocked everything. The context is the provenance: where, when, why. The destination is where it publishes. One context deploys to several destinations, and each has its own rules:
- Personal — public and indexed: journal, personal Instagram, book. Its own rules: location metadata stripped, a delay before publishing a position, no indexing of minors.
- Professional, in my own name — private, step by step: LinkedIn as draft only, never auto-published. The only place where judgment is legitimate — so nothing automatic.
- Haute Fidélité — public, with a hard embargo: site, Instagram, newsletter, print. Judgment forbidden under the magazine's byline; facts and vintages checked.
Technically, it's a single Telegram group with one topic per context. Posting in a topic is enough; inferring from the content is only a suggestion. Capture stays under ten seconds, which is the only way to really capture.
5. The locks, before any publication
- Embargo as a hard block. A release date is a lock, not content: door closed until the date.
- Visibility lock. A media file showing a restricted person — minors included — is excluded from the social queues; only a manual override naming the person unlocks it.
- Witnessed / documented kept separate in the database and in the form.
- LinkedIn = draft only.
- Never a judgment under the magazine's byline.
- Publication on an explicit action, idempotent, with a readable error in Telegram. No cron that publishes on its own.
On the social networks, the engagement rule is just as strict: DMs and replies to comments are a reader relationship, not automated growth. No automatic likes, no automatic follows. Three regimes: mechanical = automatic; factual reply = generated then validated with one button; judgment = human draft.
6. Destinations and their life cycle
Not all destinations have the same lifespan, and that's what dictates the build order:
Disposable
Immediate
- Instagram, stories
- LinkedIn (draft)
- A bad output costs nothing
→ Evolving → permanent
It stays
- Magazine site, journal, this Knowledge Hub (evolving)
- Newsletter (derived)
- Print, book (permanent, dated, calibrated to a character count)
The social layer is deliberately pluggable: a replaceable publishing adapter behind a single interface. The site remains the source of truth, the social networks are satellites. Measurement, for its part, doesn't depend on the publishing provider: Growth reads the platforms' native statistics directly. You can switch publishing tools without losing the history.
7. The build order (and where it stands)
Social → web → print. You validate the engine where a bad output costs nothing, before trusting it with what's permanent. The stages: the irreversible foundation (domains, URLs, data schemas, media storage); timed Telegram capture; the documentation (entities, embeddings, model router); a first Instagram rendering to prove the adapter and the isolation of spaces; the duplicable journal — including the Atlas of Asia (Atlas d'Asie), our travel journal from this summer, as the hand-made pilot; the magazine site and LinkedIn; print; the book.
Dated snapshot · September 1, 2026
The v2 spec dates from July 30; the foundation (collections, sign-in, indexing guardrail, entity page with structured data) is in place; the September 1 pivot brought field capture, repurposing and “publish this idea” together into a single building block and settled the publishing tool (self-hosted, replaceable) rather than services billed per account. Next steps: capture in under ten seconds, first Instagram rendering. External deadline: the Haute Fidélité show, late September 2026. Still open: the dedicated name and domain for the magazine site and the journals.
8. What it changes for getting cited by AIs
GEO — getting cited in an AI's answer — rewards three things the machine produces by construction: one page per entity with its structured data (schema.org), explicit provenance (who, where, when — the first-hand experience signal), and a server-rendered site, readable without JavaScript, with an llms.txt. Mass-generated content has none of these three attributes. An attested observation has all of them.
In other words: the Content Machine isn't a machine for producing more. It's a machine for publishing only what was actually lived — and making it readable by humans and machines alike.
Going further
- → What is HL OS — the Content Machine is one of the five building blocks.
- → The AI proposes, the human validates — the locks, in detail.
- → Being visible in AI: GEO — why provenance is the product.
Real cases. Content Machine: the September 1 pivot · HiFi Lovers Instagram strategy · Anatomy of the special issue's cover.

SHOULD YOU STILL BUY AN ERP? I BUILT MY OWN WITH CLAUDE CODE
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/faut-il-encore-acheter-un-erp.html
Published: 2026-06-14
================================================================

A build-in-public deep dive: in 5 days and 96 pull requests, I built HF-OS, my magazine&#x27;s internal ERP (CRM, ad sales, invoicing, payment reminders), with Claude Code. The real question: should you still buy an ERP when you can build your own — in your own colors — with AI?

Home › Guides › Should you still buy an ERP?
Deep dive · Build in public
Should you still buy an ERP when AI lets you build your own?
A build-in-public deep dive: in 5 days and 96 pull requests, I built HF-OS, my magazine's internal ERP (CRM, ad sales, invoicing, payment reminders), with Claude Code. The real question: should you still buy an ERP when you can build your own — in your own colors — with AI?
By Hugo Lahutte· June 14, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026· 12 min read erp hf-os claude-code strat In 30 seconds
- In 5 days and 96 pull requests, I built HF-OS — the internal ERP of my magazine Haute Fidélité: CRM, ad sales, invoicing, payment reminders, emails. It replaces a pile of Excel + emails + Qonto + Shopify. Alone, part-time, the code written by Claude Code, me at the helm.
- In parallel, at Cobra, I extend an existing Odoo almost every day with Claude (plus homemade dashboards on the side).
- The thesis: a custom ERP, in your own colors, is no longer a €200k, 18-month project. Two paths — build (HF-OS) or extend an off-the-shelf ERP (Odoo) — are now within reach of a business owner who knows how to steer AI.
1. The ERP, a wall for a long time
For an SMB, getting management software “of your own” long meant: a heavy budget, months of integration, and a lasting dependency on a vendor or an agency. The result — you do without, and the company runs on a pile of tools that don't talk to each other: a shared Excel file, emails, a Drive, an improvised CRM, the bank on one side, the store on the other. Everything is re-keyed by hand.
The question this deep dive asks is simple, and it's getting serious in 2026: should you still buy an ERP, when you can build a custom one — in your own colors — by steering AI? I have two pieces of proof in hand, opposite and complementary.
2. HF-OS: a publishing ERP, started from scratch
HF-OS is the internal OS of Haute Fidélité: a single application that brings together ad sales, editorial, upcoming AI agents, and settings/roles. The stated goal from day one: automation at the core, end to end — create an invoice → send it → follow up → see the sales — and a tool that grows the back-office team (roles, access).
- Mon. 8Foundation: single app, SSO, database, deployment
- Wed. 10Product foundation: migrations, Ad Sales model
- Thu. 11Integrations: Qonto, Brevo, CRM, imports
- Fri. 12The peak: invoicing, reminders, roles (43 PRs)
- Sat. 13Live ad sales, Shopify, multi-title (31 PRs)
96 PRs over 5 active days (June 8 → 13, 2026). Friday alone: 43 PRs.
3. What it replaces: the production Excel file
Today, a magazine's real team tool is a shared Excel workbook: the flatplan (the page-by-page skeleton, in signatures), the table of contents, the list of product tests, awards, the ad plan, archives, calibration rules. Central, but isolated (connected neither to the website nor to invoicing), manual, and where the business rules are “kept in people's heads.”
Before
One Excel workbook, ~25 tabs
- Isolated: no website, no bank, no invoicing
- Manual re-keying, copy-paste
- Business rules not encoded (signatures, double-page spreads)
- No roles, no reliable history
→ With HF-OS
Connected software
- Ad sales connected to the CRM and to Qonto (invoices)
- Single source of data, automatic sync
- Business rules encoded (state machine for insertions)
- Roles, access, history, in your own colors
The ad block is already absorbed (Insertions collection + Kanban). The editorial core (web flatplan) is the next project.
4. The architecture (deliberately simple)
A single application serves three faces: the business dashboard, the admin, and the API. Stack: Next.js 16 + Payload 3 (TypeScript), managed PostgreSQL, homemade Google SSO auth, Render deployment (auto-deploy from main, CI lint+typecheck+build). External integrations are read-only by default, with graceful degradation: a page never breaks if a service goes down.
HF-OS · single app PostgreSQLinternal source of truth Qontoinvoices & balances (read) Brevoemails & reminders (read) Shopifystore (OAuth) Webfloweditorial import Internal cronsQonto sync · reminders · nightly backup One deployment, shared types, the admin “for free” with Payload. When a source of truth already exists (Qonto issues the invoices), HF-OS doesn't reinvent it.
In my own colors · the “HL Quiet UI” design system
The whole ERP runs on a homemade design system — teal, the Good Times typeface, light/dark — with HL Média's identity, not a vendor's. That's the whole point of custom-built. See the style board →
5. What's already running
- CRM — single database of Companies + Contacts + Tags, CSV import, deduplication & merge, rich records, SIREN/VAT enrichment. Done.
- Ad sales / Invoicing — Qonto sync (source of truth, daily cron), dashboard (outstanding / collected / overdue), sales mining. Done.
- Reminders & emails — Brevo KPIs, per-invoice reminders (FR/EN), daily robot, IMAP/SMTP mailboxes. Done.
- Ad tracking — Insertions collection (state machine), tracking screen (KPIs + Kanban), Excel-style editable table. Done.
- Auth & roles — restricted Google SSO, Admin / Ad Sales / Editorial / Reader roles. Done.
- Editorial (Webflow import) and Shopify (OAuth) — in progress. AI / agents — planned, to be scoped.
6. Two paths to your own custom ERP
HF-OS is the “build from scratch” path. But it's not the only one, and it's not always the right one. The other path, I practice in parallel at Cobra: start from an off-the-shelf ERP — Odoo — and extend it. There, I modify/add modules almost every day with Claude Code, and I build homemade dashboards on the side for what Odoo doesn't do well (see the build in public and the Cobra sessions in the journal: Shopify wizard, product creation agent, catalog integration).
Build vs. extend — the right reflex
Extend an existing ERP (Odoo) when the business is standard (accounting, purchasing, inventory) and you want to lean on a proven foundation. Build custom (HF-OS) when the business is specific (producing a magazine) and no off-the-shelf software models it — or not in your colors. In both cases, AI makes the cost of customization collapse.
7. The cadence (what AI really changes)
The most telling number isn't the line count, it's the rate of complete PRs (each PR = code + migration + checks, green CI):
Mon 82 Wed 107 Thu 1113 Fri 1243 Sat 1331 Record day: 43 PRs on Friday (≈ 1 PR every 12 minutes of active time).
- 96merged pull requests
- ~20,000lines of code
- 12data collections
- ~16 hof cumulative effective work
- ~6/hPRs merged on average
- 1person, part-time
How the numbers were made: PR count, merge dates and code volume measured (GitHub API + git). The “before AI” comparisons and the fine breakdown of lines are orders of magnitude, flagged as such.
8. How it gets built (the method)
- One feature = one PR, mandatory CI (lint + typecheck + build), never a direct push to main.
- Parallel sessions, always restarted from a freshly fetched origin/main; in case of conflict, reapply only your own files.
- Render MCP plugged in to drive deployments and read logs from the session.
- The human role: product framing, architecture calls, prioritization — not typing the code. A solo operator who steers a team-sized delivery capacity.
On the safety side: no secrets in the repo (gitleaks scan in CI, env variables on the hosting side), a GDPR guardrail (never commit personal data), allowlisted access. Operating cost: a few dozen euros a month (hosting + managed database + backup storage), plus the Claude subscription. An order of magnitude — nowhere near an ERP license.
9. So, should you still buy an ERP?
Honest answer: it depends — but the needle has moved.
- Buying (or extending standard software) remains the right choice when the need is generic and critical: accounting, payroll, regulated inventory. You don't rewrite an accounting system.
- Building custom becomes rational as soon as the business is specific, off-the-shelf tools force you to “fit into boxes,” or you want your UX and your brand identity. What used to be expensive — customization — is now where AI makes the biggest difference.
What doesn't change: you still need someone to decide (architecture, scope, guardrails) and to verify. AI hasn't removed the builder's craft — it has removed the cost wall. For a business owner who knows their trade, that's exactly the good news.
Update · September 1, 2026
HF-OS has become a foundation
Three months after this deep dive, HF-OS is no longer just the magazine's ERP: its database and its application serve as the shared foundation for the building blocks I'm building for the whole group — the memory (the Brain), the content machine, and Growth, the action queue that replaces ten dashboards at Cobra, scoped over a weekend and put into production on Monday. The question “should you still buy?” now applies to the steering layer, not just the ERP. → What is HL OS

- → An AI product-creation agent + its spec (the “extend Odoo” path at Cobra).
- → A website + an AI bot, without knowing how to code (same method, different terrain).

ODOO OR A CUSTOM ERP: WHICH ONE TO CHOOSE IN 2026?
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/odoo-vs-erp-maison.html
Published: 2026-06-16
================================================================

Odoo or a custom ERP built with AI? A criterion-by-criterion comparison (cost, time to launch, flexibility, dependency) by someone who practices both: Odoo extended at Cobra, a homemade ERP built in 5 days.

Home › Guides › Odoo vs homemade ERP
Guides · Comparison
Odoo or a custom ERP: which one to choose in 2026?
The question keeps coming back: pick an off-the-shelf ERP like Odoo, or build your own now that AI makes the cost of development collapse? I practice both in parallel — Odoo extended daily at Cobra, and a homemade ERP built from scratch in 5 days. Here's the verdict, criterion by criterion, with no religion.
By Hugo Lahutte· June 16, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026·~7 min read comparatif erp odoo strat The 30-second verdict
- Pick Odoo (or an off-the-shelf ERP) when the business is standard and regulated — accounting, payroll, inventory, purchasing. A proven foundation covers 80% of the need from day one, and you don't rewrite an accounting system.
- Pick custom-built when the business is specific, when no software models it without forcing you to “fit into boxes,” or when you want your UX and your brand identity. That's where AI changes everything.
- The trap to avoid: reasoning on the license price instead of the total cost (integration, customization, maintenance, dependency). And falling into “everything custom” for generic functions the market already does very well.
1. The match in one table
The decision isn't about “which one is better” in the absolute, but about the weight you give to each criterion. Here are the eight that really matter.
Odoo vs. custom ERP — criterion-by-criterion comparison (2026). Criterion Odoo (buy / extend) Custom ERP (build with AI) Upfront cost Per-user/month license (Enterprise) + integration days. Community is free but limited. Almost nothing in licenses. The cost = your framing time + the AI subscription. Development collapses. Total cost over 3 years (TCO) Grows with the number of users and the customization. Maintenance of custom modules to plan for. Hosting + managed database = a few dozen €/month, stable whatever the number of users. Time to launch Fast on the standard: existing modules run right away (accounting, CRM, inventory). Everything has to be built — but much faster than before: a working core in days, not months. Business flexibility Good within Odoo's framework; beyond it, you have to develop modules and live with the imposed data model. Total. The software fits your exact business, not the other way around. No box you're forced into. Maintenance & updates Core maintained by the vendor, but every version upgrade can break your custom modules. 100% on you — but a smaller codebase, in your hands, and AI speeds up fixes too. Dependency Vendor (roadmap, pricing, terms) + often a partner integrator. You / your team. No license ransom, but the knowledge has to stay documented and shared. Compliance (accounting, payroll) Covered and kept up to date by the vendor (standards, tax rules). A huge advantage on the regulatory side. Not to be reinvented. The right reflex: let an external source of truth handle the regulatory part. Risk / reversibility Low technically (proven product), but a costly exit once locked into the ecosystem. Quality risk if nobody verifies; but you own your code and your data, so it's reversible.
2. Odoo in detail
Odoo is a very complete modular management suite (CRM, sales, purchasing, inventory, accounting, HR…), available as an open-source Community edition and a paid Enterprise edition. It's an excellent default for the vast majority of SMBs: the standard is solid, the community huge, and the essentials of a classic business are covered without writing a line of code.
Where Odoo wins: a quick start on generic functions, accounting and tax compliance maintained for you, an ecosystem of modules and integrators, and a “clean” exit as long as you stay within the framework. At Cobra, that's exactly my choice: an Odoo I extend almost every day with Claude Code, rather than rewriting everything.
Where it gets stuck: as soon as your business steps outside the framework, you develop modules, you live with Odoo's data model, and every version upgrade becomes a regression test of your customizations. Community's “free” quickly melts into integration and maintenance costs.
3. The custom ERP in detail
Building your own is no longer the six-figure, 18-month project of yesteryear. With AI at the keyboard and a human at the helm, a working core gets built in days. The point isn't to “do Odoo, but worse”: it's to model exactly your business, with your UX and your brand identity.
Where custom-built wins: total flexibility, a near-fixed operating cost (no per-user license), ownership of the code and the data, and an experience tailored to your team — not a generic compromise. Decisive for a business the market doesn't model.
Where it gets stuck: everything rests on your ability to decide and verify. No vendor safety net: quality, backups, security, regulatory compliance are your responsibility. And above all, don't rewrite what's generic and critical (accounting) just for the pleasure of custom-built.
4. Who should choose what
Rather Odoo
Standard business, a team to equip fast
- Accounting, payroll, inventory, purchasing at the heart of the need
- Strong regulatory compliance requirements
- Non-technical team, no in-house AI pilot
- Growth through modules that already exist
· Rather custom-built
Specific business, UX requirements
- Processes the market doesn't model (or models badly)
- You want your interface and your brand identity, not a vendor's
- A business owner / a team that knows how to steer AI
- A need for very specific dashboards and automations
And most of the time, the real answer is hybrid: an off-the-shelf foundation for the generic and the regulatory, custom pieces grafted alongside for what sets you apart. That's precisely what I do in practice.
My field experience
I didn't pick a side: I live both paths in parallel, which makes the comparison concrete.
Custom-built — I built HF-OS, the internal ERP of my magazine Haute Fidélité (CRM, ad sales, invoicing, payment reminders), in 5 days, 96 pull requests, ~20,000 lines and ~16 hours of effective work, alone, steering Claude Code. Operating cost: a few dozen euros a month. The full story and the numbers: Should you still buy an ERP?
Extending the market — at Cobra, I start from an existing Odoo that I modify and complete almost daily, with homemade dashboards on the side for what Odoo does badly. See the sessions product creation agent and Odoo catalog integration.
My conclusion from the field: the needle has moved. Custom-built becomes rational much earlier than before — but extending a standard remains the right reflex for everything generic and critical.
6. Frequently asked questions
Odoo or a custom ERP: which one to choose?
Odoo (or any off-the-shelf ERP) when the business is standard and regulated — accounting, payroll, inventory, purchasing: you don't rewrite an accounting system, and a proven foundation covers 80% of the need right away. A custom ERP when the business is specific, when no software models it without contortions, or when you want your own UX and brand identity. Now that AI makes the cost of customization collapse, custom-built becomes rational much earlier than before.
How much does a custom ERP built with AI cost?
The line item that collapses is development: HF-OS, a working publishing ERP (CRM, ad sales, invoicing, payment reminders), was built in ~16 hours of effective work over 5 days and 96 pull requests, by one person steering Claude Code. The operating cost comes to a few dozen euros a month (hosting + managed database + backups) plus the AI subscription. Compare that with per-user licenses and the integration days of an off-the-shelf ERP. The real remaining cost of custom-built isn't money: it's the time spent framing and verifying.
Is Odoo really free?
Partly. Odoo Community is open source and free when self-hosted, but limited (no full accounting and some apps missing). The Enterprise edition is paid, billed per user per month, and the real bill mostly comes from integration, customization and module maintenance. So “free” doesn't mean “no cost”: it's the total cost of ownership you have to look at, not the license price.
Do you need to know how to code to build your ERP with AI?
Not to write the code line by line — the AI takes care of that. But you need to know how to decide and verify: frame the scope, make the architecture calls, set the guardrails (backups, access, personal data), review. It's steering work, not typing. A business owner who knows their trade and learns to steer AI can produce the capacity of a small team; someone who doesn't want to verify anything shouldn't risk it on a critical tool.
Update · September 1, 2026
A third path, which has appeared since
At Cobra, the “extend Odoo” path has continued (pricing system, competitive alignment engine, order statuses), and a third path has been added: building the steering layer on top of the tools rather than inside one of them. Growth reads Odoo, Shopify, analytics, ad platforms and email, reconciles the facts and proposes actions — without replacing either the ERP or the store. Odoo remains the commercial truth; the decision is made elsewhere. → What is HL OS
Going further
- → Should you still buy an ERP? — the full deep dive on HF-OS, built in 5 days (the numbers-backed proof of “custom-built”).
- → AI in concrete terms, for a merchant or an SMB — where to start, without jargon.
- → Extending Odoo at Cobra — the “start from the market and complete it” path.
Sources. My direct experience of both approaches (HF-OS and Odoo at Cobra), measured via the GitHub API and git. The Odoo pricing elements are orders of magnitude, to be checked against the official price list when deciding.

CASE STUDY
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/etude-de-cas-dashboard-prix-concurrentiels.html
Published: 2026-07-13
================================================================

Build in public: the competitor price data (Wiser) was already in production, delivered by the integrator. What was missing was the steering layer — quoted at several weeks and left waiting. We built it in-house with Claude Code, in a few days: ABC scoring, competitor columns, an Align button. The most direct build-vs-buy case of the year.

Home › Guides › Case study — Competitive-pricing dashboard
Case study · Build in public · Cobra
A competitive-pricing dashboard,built in-house
The data was already there — competitor prices, collected through Wiser and integrated by our service provider, were running in production. What was missing was the steering layer to do something with it: a spec, quoted at several weeks, left waiting. We built it in-house with Claude Code, in a few days. The most direct build vs buy case of the year.
By Hugo Lahutte · July 13, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~8 min read build in publicbuild vs buyprixWiserOdooClaude Code The dashboard built in-house: price-position counters, filters, ABC scoring, per-product status against competitors (illustrative preview, sample data).
1. The need: steering your prices against the competition
In specialty retail, price is a permanent battlefield. Knowing, product by product, where you stand against competitors — cheaper, aligned, more expensive — isn't a comfort: it's the basis for deciding where to defend your margin and where to align so you don't lose the sale. But that information has to be readable and actionable, not drowned in an unreadable export you open once a quarter.
At Cobra, the raw material already existed. What was missing was the tool to look at it and act on it.
2. The data already existed — delivered by the integrator
The most technical building block — the import and matching of competitor prices through the Wiser tool (a pricing-intelligence platform that goes and collects the prices charged elsewhere and matches them to our catalog) — had already been delivered by our external integrator (Irokoo) and was running in production. Competitor prices were indeed landing in the system, attached to the right products.
In other words: the “data” part of the problem was solved, and solved well. The hole was elsewhere — in the layer above the data.
3. The quote left waiting
A spec had in fact been sent to the integrator on March 19, 2026 for that missing layer: a price-tracking dashboard (ABC scoring of products, an alignment rules engine, price history), estimated at several weeks of development. That spec stayed at the status “to be validated before development” — never launched, never invoiced.
Not a dramatic blocker: just a project waiting its turn, like dozens of others. Except that with Claude Code, “waiting its turn” no longer has quite the same opportunity cost.
4. Framing the gap precisely
Before building anything, we had to clearly separate what had already been delivered (the import / matching, phase 1) from what remained to be done (the steering, phase 2, never ordered) — to rebuild only the missing part, without starting from scratch or duplicating the integrator's work.
To frame precisely what the Wiser tool actually exposed (and therefore what the dashboard had to display), we went about it differently from yet another scoping workshop: thanks to Claude's built-in browser — a recent capability, Claude can now open a page and look at it — we had it watch a Wiser presentation video and extract the features and the data actually available. Enough to turn a demo into a list of concrete needs, without going back to the provider.
The reflex that changes everything
The question is no longer “how much does it cost to have this developed?” but “what already exists, and what's the smallest piece I'm really missing?”. Framing the gap well is already half the savings.
5. The foundation: a price that makes sense
A price-alignment dashboard is only worth something if “align a price” writes to the right place. That's the whole point of having, in parallel, overhauled the Odoo pricing system around a single field, the source of truth, that drives quotes, sales and the Shopify sync. Without that foundation, an “Align” button would be wishful thinking; with it, it changes the price, everywhere, at once.
6. What we built (first version)
Rather than requesting another external quote, the app was built directly with Claude Code — a first version, already being deployed:
- Sync of Odoo data to a dedicated local database.
- ABC scoring of products, reusing a module already in place rather than redoing it.
- A dashboard with clickable indicators and a product table groupable by brand / category, with the competitor columns alongside.
- A detail record per competitor, with an “Align” button wired to the price-alignment assistant that already existed on the Odoo side — so one click that really writes the new price.
- Excel export, standard Cobra brand identity, and deployment on our internal apps hub.
Nothing speculative: we built exactly the missing piece, leaning on everything that already existed (the Wiser data, the scoring, the alignment assistant, the overhauled pricing system).
7. Build vs buy: the real math
The spec talked about 3 to 4 weeks of development for the rules engine part alone. The first version was built in-house in a few days, a fraction of that time — and above all, keeping control: every iteration gets settled live, with no quoting back-and-forth.
The lesson isn't “never call an integrator again.” On the contrary: the integrator had delivered the hardest building block (the Wiser import / matching), and it's precisely because that base was solid that we could build fast on top of it. The real build vs buy math isn't “do everything yourself” — it's buy what's hard and standard, build what's specific and changing.
And after
This dashboard isn't an isolated object: it joins a small ecosystem of internal applications that's growing fast at Cobra (cash flow, purchasing, salesperson performance, reporting…), all built from the same mold — shared brand identity, shared Odoo connection, standardized deployment. That momentum deserves its own story: a dedicated guide is in the works.
See also
- The journal entry — the competitive-pricing dashboard
- The overhaul of the Odoo pricing system (cobra_price)
- Case study — An agent that processes supplier invoices
- Should you still buy an ERP when AI lets you build your own?
← All guides Let's discuss → Update · September 1, 2026
And after: the engine went live
The “first version” of this dashboard got its sequel in August 2026: a rules engine in Odoo reads competitor prices at every delivery, computes a target price (best valid competitor, bounded by a minimum margin), ran in observation mode, then was switched live family by family — six families and a few hundred prices realigned, the rest adjusting on its own. Going live remains a human decision. → Price tracking and automatic alignment · the shared guardrails → AI proposes, humans validate


================================================================
CASE STUDY
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/etude-de-cas-agent-facturation.html
Published: 2026-06-17
================================================================

Build in public: an autonomous agent that reads supplier emails, extracts the invoices, attaches them to the right purchase order in Odoo and pushes them for validation in Teams. Hosted on Scaleway, triggered every 15 min. The real gain isn&#x27;t speed: it&#x27;s a workflow that no longer drifts.

Home › Guides › Case study — Supplier invoice agent
Case study · Build in public · Cobra
An agent that processessupplier invoices
It reads the emails, extracts each invoice, attaches it to the right purchase order in Odoo, checks the prices, and pushes it for one-click validation in Teams. Hosted on a Scaleway instance, triggered every 15 minutes. The real gain isn't speed — it's a workflow that can no longer drift.
By Hugo Lahutte · June 17, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~10 min read build in publicagent IAOdooAPI ClaudeScalewayTeams The full flow: emails → extraction → line-by-line matching against the PO → Teams card → Odoo write. Design details in the “architecture” journal entry.
1. The real problem: not speed, discipline
Odoo has been in place at Cobra since February 2025. On paper, the accounting chain is crystal clear: sales order (SO) → purchase order (PO) → invoice → payment → SEPA batch. Each invoice should point to the order that triggered it — that's what enables the 3-way match (order / receipt / invoice) and therefore the automatic control of prices and quantities.
In real life, that chain was never applied properly. The accounts-payable staff in place never mastered the tool: invoices were entered “flat,” disconnected from their original order, payments rarely reconciled correctly. The result: an Odoo full of unreadable entries, and a chain impossible to read end to end.
The angle of this piece
A rushed human skips attaching the invoice to the order. Not out of stupidity — because it's the tedious step, and no alarm goes off when you forget it. Discipline doesn't hold over time. A coded rule does. That's the whole point of handing this to an agent: not to “go faster,” but to make the error impossible by construction.
2. The drift, in numbers
Before writing a single line, we measured the real state of the database (read-only, via XML-RPC). The numbers speak for themselves — out of 5,450 supplier invoices posted since February 2025:
Symptom of the driftCountAmount Invoices with no link at all to a purchase order (PO)1,524€2,032,524 incl. VAT Unpaid / partially paid for more than 2 months241€600,531 still to pay — of which prior to 2026 (5-6 months and older)130€371,762 In plain terms: ~€2M of supplier invoices entered off-chain, with no link to any order, and €600k of unpaid invoices dragging on for more than two months. That's the cost of the drift — and precisely what the agent prevents from happening again.
An honest nuance, because this site is build in public, not brochure mode: the drift is mostly historical. Among the invoices detached from an order, 1,379 are old (> 2 months) versus 145 recent. It improved over time — but 145 recent ones prove that without an automatic constraint, human entry drifts again, always.
Making the chain readable: the 3 statuses on the order
First building block, on the Odoo side: I added three fields on the purchase order (purchase.order) to expose the complete state directly from the PO — before, you had to dig through invoices and payments separately.
FieldMeaningOn confirmed POs DeliveredGoods received?complete 3,439 · partial 77 · no 309 InvoicedInvoice received and linked?complete 3,319 · partial 144 · no 362 PaidSettled?complete 3,003 · partial 147 · no 675 One glance at an order: delivered? invoiced? paid? The chain becomes readable again — which was impossible with invoices detached from their order.
Why the paid status is vital here
Cobra has almost no outstanding supplier credit: most suppliers are paid on receipt or on short terms. Knowing at any moment what is invoiced and paid, order by order, is therefore not accounting comfort — it's cash-flow steering. An invoice detached from its order is a payment you risk forgetting… or paying twice. That's exactly what these statuses, and their automatic tracking, make impossible.
The purchasing control tower in Odoo: each order shows its delivered / invoiced / paid state, and the tiles aggregate unpaid invoices in real time. With no supplier credit, this is the view that steers cash flow.
The detail of an order, augmented with the 3 statuses that make the chain readable end to end.
3. What the agent does (and why it can't drift)
The agent doesn't “help” you enter data better. It replaces data entry with a workflow it is incapable of not following. The journey of an invoice, end to end:
- Invoice collection (two sources). Every 15 minutes, the agent picks up invoices where they arrive: the PDFs already attached to orders in Odoo (source A), and above all the mailboxes where suppliers converge — including a catch-all — through the Microsoft Graph API (sources B/C). It spots the attachments and email bodies that are invoices, and deduplicates (SHA-256 + message ID).
- Extraction. Depending on the supplier, each invoice is read either by a dedicated parser (known, structured formats, highly reliable), or — the general case — by OCR + the Claude API (Opus 4.8 model). In both cases, the output is a clean structure, with a confidence score: supplier, number, date, lines, amounts, VAT, WEEE eco-fee, shipping.
- Line-by-line matching. Each line is matched to the exact order line (identification hierarchy: supplier code → EAN → name → price), handling the silent traps (pair/unit quantities, WEEE fee and shipping bundled in or on a separate line).
- Blocking checks. Duplicate? Price gap > 5%? Order not found? → the invoice doesn't go to draft: it's parked for human follow-up (the “intervention” channel, or “to sort” if there's no readable order reference in the document).
- Human validation in Teams. A card (Adaptive Card) summarizes the invoice and offers one-click actions. The human never touches the Odoo interface again, except for the weekly SEPA batch.
The four guardrails that make drift structurally impossible:
- Attachment guaranteed by construction. Each invoice line created points to the exact order line (purchase_line_id) and fills in the origin automatically. The agent doesn't know how to create a “free” invoice. 100% of what it creates is linked to its order — versus the 28% detached in the human-entered history.
- Anti-duplicate. It refuses to create if the supplier reference already exists, or if the order line is already invoiced.
- Price consistency. Invoice vs. order gap > 5% → block and request a corrected invoice from the supplier, before any write.
- Constancy. The same rules, every 15 minutes, on every invoice, indefinitely. Code doesn't get tired, never skips the tedious step.
The price-gap check, in code
The “price consistency” guardrail isn't wishful thinking: it's a coded rule, which blocks before any write to Odoo. Beyond a 5% gap between the invoiced price and the price negotiated on the order, the agent creates nothing — the invoice is parked and flagged.
TOLERANCE_PRIX = 0.05 # 5%: beyond that, we create NOTHING, the invoice goes to intervention def controle_ecart_prix(ligne_facture, ligne_commande): """Compare the invoiced unit price to the price negotiated on the purchase order (PO). ≤ 5% : minor gap (bundled shipping, rounding) → the invoice follows the normal flow. > 5% : blocking → no draft is created, the invoice is parked and flagged. The human then requests a corrected invoice from the supplier. """ prix_po = ligne_commande.prix_unitaire_ht if not prix_po: # line without an order reference: can't be checked here return Verdict(statut="non_controle") ecart = (ligne_facture.prix_unitaire_ht - prix_po) / prix_po if abs(ecart) <= TOLERANCE_PRIX: return Verdict(statut="ok", ecart_pct=round(ecart * 100, 1)) return Verdict( statut="bloquant", motif="ecart_prix", ecart_pct=round(ecart * 100, 1), message=( f"Invoiced price {ligne_facture.prix_unitaire_ht:.2f} € " f"vs order {prix_po:.2f} € ({ecart:+.1%}) — " f"beyond the {TOLERANCE_PRIX:.0%} tolerance" ), )
A bloquant (blocking) verdict goes up to the decision engine, which refuses to create the draft and routes the invoice to the “intervention” channel with its reason. That's anti-drift in one function: no human judgment call on every invoice, a rule that applies on its own, always.
An invoice extracted and matched to its order (here PO P06152, extraction confidence 95%), ready to process from Teams: Validate, Create payment, Reject or View in Odoo — one click = an Odoo write. On the left, the 3 channels To validate / To pay / Paid that track the payment state. Zero accounting interface.
4. The production architecture on Scaleway
The point that changes everything compared to the design phase: the agent exists outside my computer. It runs on a Scaleway instance (BASIC3-X2C-4G VM: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, Paris region), for ~€36/month. French hosting — that matters for accounting data.
- The batch: a cron every 15 minutes launches the agent loop (read emails → extraction → matching → Teams cards).
- The endpoint: a small Flask server, for its part, runs permanently (systemd service) to receive the clicks on the Teams card buttons and write back to Odoo. It's reachable through a dedicated subdomain (agent-factures.cobra.fr, DNS at Gandi) rather than a bare IP, with an HMAC signature on every incoming request.
- Reading emails: through Microsoft Graph (Microsoft 365 API, application flow), no IMAP. Reading emails directly at the source is what makes the agent autonomous: no human intervention to “forward it” an invoice.
- Odoo: Odoo 18 Enterprise, XML-RPC access + API key.
LayerTech ExtractionClaude API (Opus 4.8) · pdfplumber · Tesseract OCR (fr/en) · Poppler LogicPython 3.14 · pydantic (strict schema) Teams endpointFlask · HMAC signature · Adaptive Cards v1.5 via Power Automate EmailsMicrosoft Graph (application flow) HostingScaleway instance (Paris) · cron + systemd The email invoice-collection module (fetch_mail.py), written with Claude Code: Microsoft Graph application flow, anti-noise filters, SHA-256 deduplication, PDF drop-off. Build in public all the way down to the code.
Proof that the agent lives outside my computer: the Scaleway instance running, in Paris.
What a run looks like, for real
Here's the log of a real 15-minute cycle (37 seconds of execution). Nine invoices in the queue, and above all: every possible outcome shows up — validation, duplicate already booked, price gap that blocks, order not found, non-invoiceable document rejected. The agent does the sorting, applying the same rules to every line.
$ python agent_loop.py --write 2026-06-17 08:15:00 [INFO] agent_loop — ═══ Loop run 2026-06-17T08:15:00Z (write=True) ═══ 2026-06-17 08:15:03 [INFO] fetch_po — [A] Odoo POs: 261 POs scanned · 4 candidate attachments · 2 collected · 2 dedup 2026-06-17 08:15:10 [INFO] fetch_mail — [B/C] Graph: 3 mailboxes (***@cobra.fr) → 87 messages · 31 PDF attachments 2026-06-17 08:15:10 [INFO] fetch_mail — → 7 collected · 22 dedup · 2 ignored (delivery note / payment reminder) 2026-06-17 08:15:10 [INFO] agent_loop — 9 new invoices in the processing queue 2026-06-17 08:15:13 [INFO] extract — [1/9] FA-2026-04417 · Supplier-A → LLM ok (confidence 0.94 · 3 lines · excl. VAT 1,642.80 €) 2026-06-17 08:15:14 [INFO] orchestr. — [1/9] PO P06143 found · 3/3 lines matched · max price gap +1.2% → ✅ VALIDATE 2026-06-17 08:15:14 [INFO] orchestr. — draft 150148 created · PDF → LLM ok (confidence 0.91 · 6 lines · shipping 12.00 €) 2026-06-17 08:15:25 [WARN] orchestr. — [4/9] no PO ref in the document (email source) → ⏸️ TO SORT · parked · no card 2026-06-17 08:15:27 [INFO] extract — [5/9] AVR-1180 · Supplier-E → LLM ok (confidence 0.86) 2026-06-17 08:15:28 [WARN] orchestr. — [5/9] PO P05904 · line already fully invoiced (qty_invoiced ≥ qty) → 🟠 INTERVENTION (doublon) 2026-06-17 08:15:30 [INFO] extract — [6/9] FC-77310 · Supplier-F → LLM ok (confidence 0.92 · 2 lines) 2026-06-17 08:15:31 [WARN] orchestr. — [6/9] PO ref “P06210” not found in Odoo → 🟠 INTERVENTION (commande_introuvable) 2026-06-17 08:15:33 [INFO] orchestr. — [7/9] FA-2026-04420 · Supplier-A · PO P06151 · 2/2 matched · +0.4% → ✅ VALIDATE → draft 150149 2026-06-17 08:15:35 [INFO] orchestr. — [8/9] 26061002 · Supplier-B · PO P06160 · 1/1 matched · 0.0% → ✅ VALIDATE → draft 150150 2026-06-17 08:15:36 [INFO] orchestr. — [9/9] BL-99317 → non-invoiceable document (delivery note) → rejected 2026-06-17 08:15:37 [INFO] agent_loop — [PIPELINE] {'total': 9, 'valider': 3, 'deja_traite': 1, 'intervention': 3, 'a_trier': 1, 'rejete': 1, 'erreur': 0} 2026-06-17 08:15:37 [INFO] agent_loop — ═══ Run finished in 37s — 3 drafts created, 3 intervention cards ═══
Out of these 9 invoices: 3 validated and moved to an Odoo draft linked to their order, 1 already booked (payment mirror card), 3 parked in intervention (price gap, duplicate, order not found), 1 to sort (no order reference) and 1 rejected (delivery note, not an invoice). None slipped off-chain — which is precisely what human entry didn't guarantee.
A note on the channels: “To validate” is the human action queue — it groups both the clean drafts ready to validate in one click and the parked cases to handle (price gap, duplicate…). The “To pay” and “Paid” channels, for their part, track the payment state on the Odoo side.
5. The numbers: volume, time, ROI
Measured volume: ~349 supplier invoices/month, i.e. ~80/week.
The human time per invoice (import, line-by-line check, reconciliation) is in the range of 7 to 12 minutes with manual entry. Taking a median of 9 minutes over 80 invoices/week:
Human time / week Before the agent (entry + check + reconciliation)~12 h (≈ 0.35 FTE) With the agent (validating the Teams cards + intervention cases)~2 to 2.5 h Net time saved~9 to 10 h / week Honesty: measured volume, estimated minutes
The volume (80/week) is measured in Odoo. The minutes per invoice are a market range for manual accounts-payable entry — not a stopwatch measurement. To be adjusted with our real times. On the cost side: this task occupied a full-time position in accounts payable, of which only about ten hours were actually productive for lack of mastery of the tool; on top of that came “extra” time taken from other people and an external accounting firm. At ~€3k/month fully loaded for an equivalent position (market estimate), the agent pays back its hosting (~€36/month) several dozen times over.
6. What the agent does NOT do
To stay credible, the scope has to be clear. The agent guarantees the invoice → order attachment and price consistency. It does not do:
- Reconciliation / bank matching. Payment and the SEPA batch remain a human and banking step. What the agent brings on the payment side is visibility, not execution: three Teams sub-channels (To validate / To pay / Paid) reflect the Odoo payment state. But by delivering invoices that are clean and linked to their order, it makes downstream reconciliation trivial and reliable — where a detached invoice makes it manual and fragile.
- Updating Teams cards “in place.” At every state change, the agent posts a new mirror card in the right channel — it doesn't modify the existing card (a limitation of Power Automate webhooks). A true live update through a Teams bot is identified as the next step, not done yet.
- Cleaning up the past. The ~1,500 detached invoices and the 241 lingering unpaid ones remain a regularization project. The agent doesn't repair the history — it guarantees the future no longer gets dirty.
Point to harden (said honestly)
The secrets (API keys, Odoo access) currently live in a protected .env file on the instance, not in a dedicated secrets manager. It works, it's acceptable for a single-operator start — but it's the first hardening item on the list.
7. What this illustrates
The lesson isn't “AI processes invoices.” It's: when a business process drifts because it depends on human discipline, the right reflex isn't more training or more control — it's coding the rule so it applies on its own, always, without exception.
The agent isn't “faster than an accountant.” It is incapable of drifting. That's a different property, and it's the one that durably repairs an accounting chain, where no amount of human effort managed to.
Coming up / what's next
- Live update of Teams cards (Teams bot rather than webhook) for a card that updates in place.
- Secrets management through a dedicated vault.
- Regularization project for the history (detached invoices, lingering unpaid) — semi-automatable once the incoming flow is under control.
- Real measurement of before/after times to replace the market range with our own numbers.
See also
- Designing the agent: architecture, business rules, edge cases
- Case study — AI-watch bot: from idea to production
- What is an “AI agent”?
← All guides Let's discuss → Update · September 1, 2026
The same pattern, applied to price lists and prices
This agent's pattern — extraction, matching against reference data, human validation before writing — has become the norm at Cobra: an app reads supplier price lists and prepares product creation without publishing anything on its own; a pricing engine proposes then applies, family by family, on human decision. The shared guardrails are detailed in AI proposes, humans validate.
