Yes: in one weekend, without knowing how to code, I shipped a complete static website and a serverless AI-watch bot to production with Claude Code. The method, the guardrails, and two case studies with real numbers.

Home › Guides › A website + an AI bot in one weekend?
Build in public · The big question
A website + an AI botin one weekend?
Without knowing how to code. The short answer is yes — and the bottleneck is no longer technical. Here's how, and why it's within reach of a business owner or a merchant.
By Hugo Lahutte · June 1, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~6 min read build in publicClaude CodeGitHub Pagessans serveur
- 1 In 30 seconds
- 2 The body
- 3 Going further
In 30 seconds
Yes. In one weekend, without knowing how to code, I shipped two real things to production with Claude Code:
- a complete static website (journal, guides, glossary, search, dark mode, GEO) hosted for free on GitHub Pages;
- a serverless AI-watch bot that summarizes the news and publishes it every morning on Telegram + on the site.
The secret isn't technical. It's about deciding well (simple architecture, zero dependencies, a clear data contract) and letting the AI hammer out the code while I check the rendering and the facts.
1. Start with the need, not the tech
My trigger wasn't “I want to build a website.” It was: “I'm tired of re-explaining what I do with AI — I need one single place for it.” The need dictated the form.
2. Pick the dumbest possible stack
- Site: vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, zero framework, zero build. You open a .html, it works. Hosted on GitHub Pages (free, deploys on push).
- Bot: a Python script orchestrated by GitHub Actions (a free cron). No server to manage.
Why so simple? Because a non-dev has to be able to maintain their project alone. Every dependency you add is future debt.
3. Separate responsibilities
Two repos: the bot = data engine, the site = display. Connected by a single file (feed.json). Immediate benefit: the secrets (API keys, bot token) stay in the engine's private repo — the public site contains none of them.
4. Work in a visual loop with the AI
My rhythm: I describe → the AI codes and commits → I look at the rendering in the browser → I ask for an adjustment. On repeat. The AI holds the keyboard; I hold the choices (tone, structure, guardrails) and the verification (accurate facts, nothing made up).
5. Set guardrails from day one
- Budget: 1 run/day, strict caps on the volume collected, no runaway loops.
- Copyright: never copied content — always a rephrased summary + the source link.
- Security: never a published secret (placeholders everywhere), one dedicated token per use.
Takeaway. The bottleneck is no longer “I can't code.” The work that remains — deciding, framing, verifying — is exactly what a business owner or a merchant already knows how to do.
Update · September 1, 2026
Three months later: the answer is still yes, and the bar is even lower
What required a terminal in June is now done from a browser or a phone: Claude Code runs in the cloud on a copy of the project, and Cowork carries out office work without a single command line. The five principles of this guide haven't moved — and the fifth one (guardrails) has grown to the point of deserving its own guide.
Going further
- → Case study — the Knowledge Hub website: decisions, headaches (anti-FOUC, iOS cache), actual time spent. Token cost: zero.
- → Case study — the AI-watch bot: 2-repo architecture, cross-repo bridge, CI headaches. Real cost: ~a few cents a day.
- → Making-of: the story, from a dinner with friends to the “beautiful baby shipped in 2 days.”


================================================================
CASE STUDY
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/etude-de-cas-knowledge-hub.html
Published: 2026-06-01
================================================================

Build in public: how I ship and run a complete site (70+ pages, dark mode, GEO layer) in vanilla HTML/CSS/JS on GitHub Pages, with Claude Code. Decisions, headaches, real time spent, zero token cost.

Home › Guides › Case study — Knowledge Hub
Case study · Build in public
Knowledge Hub:from idea to production
How I ship and run a complete site with Claude Code. An honest account, orders of magnitude owned, zero made-up numbers.
By Hugo Lahutte · June 1, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~8 min read build in publicClaude CodeGitHub PagesGEOsite statique ⚠️ Honest framing
This account doesn't cover creating the site from scratch. The foundation already existed (43 journal entries, 4 verticals, search, encrypted vault, "HiFi Lovers" design system). This case study is about the editorial + UX layer added on top: evergreen guides, glossary, dark mode, nav redesign, GEO layer.
1. The spark / the initial need
The spark. Friday evening, May 29, 2026, dinner with friends. I'm talking again about what I do with AI — and since I'd already told the same story at lunch that day, I figure it's time to have one single place to show it all, rather than re-explaining it every time. Saturday morning, I launch the site. One thing leads to another, ideas pile up and go to production almost immediately: journal, glossary, tags, search, dark mode, AI Watch page, bot… a beautiful baby delivered in ~2 days.
The underlying need: the site already had a rich journal — 43 entries — but little evergreen content. And a journal lives in the moment and dates quickly. What I was missing was content that holds authority over time: readable by a human in a hurry, and citable by LLMs (the famous GEO, Generative Engine Optimization — being referenced by AIs when they answer).
Two drivers behind it, openly admitted:
- Centralizing my AI notes in one clean place that doesn't get lost among bookmarks and screenshots.
- Having a public showcase in my name, shareable — and while I'm at it, proving that a non-developer can ship and run a complete site with Claude Code.
Stated target: merchants / business owners who get it fast, without excluding beginners.
2. The idea → the framing (decisions, rejected alternatives)
The stack choice was settled early, and partly on the AI's advice once I described the need. Three non-negotiable principles:
- Simplicity / zero build. No toolchain, no npm, no compilation step to maintain. I open an .html, it works.
- Free + simple hosting. GitHub Pages: no server, deployment on push (~1 min). Rejected: Vercel/Netlify (superfluous here), a VPS (too heavy).
- No framework. Rejected: React / Next / Astro / a static site generator — overkill and maintenance debt for a non-dev.
The structuring decisions of this session, and what we rejected each time:
- Evergreen guides — 1 page = 1 big question, 3 levels ("In 30 s" → visual body → "Going further"), for one URL that holds authority per question. Rejected: separate beginner/advanced pages, which dilute authority.
- Visuals and logos coded in inline HTML/CSS/SVG — zero heavy images, zero dependencies. Rejected: chart libraries, official logo files.
- Cluster on the landing page (Understand / Tool up / Method / Decide) — topical authority. Rejected: multiplying nav sections.
- Dark mode via CSS tokens ([data-theme]) + Auto/Light/Dark toggle, warm anthracite background, to keep the visual DNA. Rejected: a cold neutral gray or pure black.
- Anti-FOUC: an inline script in the <head> (~3 lines, the only blocking JS tolerated), to avoid the theme flash on load.
- Verified facts, never model version numbers that go stale — to stay evergreen.
- Home-made favicon / logo inspired by Claude, integrated into my art direction, for overall visual consistency.
Examples of verified, locked-in facts: Karpathy → Anthropic (May 2026), Compound Engineering attributed to Klaassen & Shipper / Every, "AI is the new electricity" = Andrew Ng.
3. The "vibe coding": how it got built, step by step
Main tool: Claude Code, in the terminal and on the web/app, which writes, edits, and commits directly into the repo. My loop: visual preview in the browser → I ask for adjustments → re-render, until I like it.
- Reading the repo + framing the conventions (templates, tags, cache-busting).
- Launching /guides/ with Guide #1 (AI/LLM) and its 3 coded visuals.
- Production in batches: guides #2→#4, then #5→#11, then #12, then #13→#15 (SEO/GEO-oriented).
- Clustering the landing page into 4 families.
- SEO micro-optimizations (author entity @id, HowTo).
- Header/footer redesign (social networks, LinkedIn + email contact, SiteNavigationElement).
- Dark mode: demo on the home page → validation → rollout across 72 pages → finishing touches.
- Glossary: adding the 9 major AI players.
4. The stack + the tools
- Claude Code — the build agent (writing + code + commits).
- Vanilla HTML / CSS / JS — zero framework, a single style.css (~750 lines).
- GitHub — version control + source of truth.
- GitHub Pages — hosting + automatic deployment on every push (~1 min). A .nojekyll to serve the static files as they are.
- schema.org JSON-LD (TechArticle, FAQPage, HowTo, BreadcrumbList, SiteNavigationElement, Person) + llms.txt / llms-full.txt — the GEO layer.
No API and no scheduler for this project: everything goes through my Claude subscription — so no tokens billed by usage.
5. The headaches (what broke and how we fixed it)
- The theme flash (FOUC). On load, the page flickered light before switching to dark. → Fixed with a ~3-line inline script in the <head>, the only blocking JS I tolerate, which applies the theme before the first render.
- The stubborn iOS cache. Safari/iOS kept the old CSS/JS. → Disciplined cache-busting (?v=…) on every asset change.
- Two sessions in parallel on main. Several sessions were pushing to the same branch → collision risk. → Systematic resync (fetch + ff/rebase) before every push, and idempotent scripts.
- Never touch the vault. Hard rule: coffre.js / vault.json (AES) are untouchable. Dark mode was deliberately not applied to the vault so as not to risk breaking it. Respected.
6. Time spent (real) and tokens / cost
- 3 calendar days: May 30 → June 1, 2026.
- ~70 commits over the period (a good share of them for this session: guides, glossary, dark mode, nav/footer).
- Split into several short sessions throughout the day.
- Real seated time: most of it on Saturday (May 30), several effective hours — and even then, in parallel with another project (codename "Cobra"). The rest spread over short sessions on Sunday and Monday.
- Cost: zero per token — everything through the Claude subscription, no API. For this case, we're talking time, not cost.
7. What this illustrates
- No framework needed to ship. Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS + GitHub Pages is enough to run a 70+ page site, clean, fast, with dark mode and a serious GEO layer.
- AI moves the bottleneck. The work is no longer "knowing how to code," it's deciding and verifying. Claude Code does the typing; I make the choices.
- Honesty is a feature. Owning a pre-existing foundation, orders of magnitude rather than fake numbers, careful claims on sensitive topics (GEO = emerging field) → it makes the whole thing credible and citable.
Update · September 1, 2026
Three months later: bilingual, a hundred pages, a Brain behind it
Since this account, the site has gone bilingual (a complete English mirror, automatic translation of every new page), passed a hundred pages per language (some thirty guides, seventy journal entries), gained two RSS feeds, a static render of the AI Watch that AIs can read, a weekly consistency check — and, in September 2026, a complete second pass to stay consistent with ways of working that changed in five months. The initial decisions (zero framework, zero build, GitHub Pages) haven't moved an inch. The raw material, meanwhile, now lives in a private Brain of which this site is the curated version.
Going further
- → Case study — the AI Watch bot (the other project of the weekend, real cost ~cents/day)
- → Making-of — shipped in a weekend
- → The guide: a site + an AI bot in a weekend?


================================================================
CASE STUDY
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/etude-de-cas-veille-ia.html
Published: 2026-06-01
================================================================

Build in public: an agent that fetches AI news, has the Claude API summarize it, and publishes it to Telegram + to the site, with no server, orchestrated by GitHub Actions. 2-repo architecture, CI headaches, real cost ~a few cents/day.

Home › Guides › Case study — AI Watch bot
Case study · Build in public
AI Watch bot:from idea to production
An agent that fetches AI news, has the Claude API summarize it, and publishes it in two places (Telegram + the site's "AI Watch" page) — with no server, orchestrated by GitHub Actions.
By Hugo Lahutte · June 1, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~10 min read build in publicagent IAAPI ClaudeGitHub Actionssans serveur X/Twitter accounts ─┐ ├─► twitterapi.io ─► Claude API (FR summary) ─┬─► Telegram (daily push) RSS (feeds.txt) ────┘ └─► feed.json ─► site (archive) ⏰ triggered every morning by GitHub Actions
One collection run, two outputs. The feed.json is the data contract between the two repos.
1. The spark / the initial need
I wanted to follow AI news (labs, models, tools, research) without spending time on it or drowning in the hype. With an angle of my own: covering AI at large and above all the AI that's useful to merchants / business owners — the concrete stuff for a company.
A real case had already put me on the trail: an LLM writes me a hi-fi press review every morning from about thirty sources. The AI Watch is the generalization of that mechanic.
A twofold purpose from the start:
- a Telegram channel (t.me/VeilleIA_HL) — daily push, ephemeral;
- a public archive on the site (the "AI Watch" page) — permanent, SEO/GEO-optimized, citable by AIs.
2. The idea → the framing (decisions, rejected alternatives)
- Two separate repos (veille-ia = engine, knowledge-hub = site) — to isolate the secrets (API keys, bot token) from the public site. Rejected: putting everything in the site's repo, secrets exposed.
- Bot = data engine / Site = display, linked by a single feed.json — separation of responsibilities. Rejected: the site collecting/summarizing on its own.
- Reading feed.json at runtime (browser fetch), not at build time — a feed.json push shows up without redeploying. Rejected: regenerating the site on every update.
- Archive page ≠ Telegram — the archive is permanent, Telegram is ephemeral. Rejected: relying on the Telegram history alone.
- Renaming "Flux IA" → "Veille IA" (AI Watch) + URL /veille-ia/ (redirect from /flux-ia/) — a more accurate industry term, better SEO/GEO anchoring. Rejected: "Flux IA," "Radar IA."
- Tweet media: official X embed + automatic thumbnail+link fallback — X embeds are fragile, the user is never stuck. Rejected: the embed alone (breaks often).
- Transformative French summaries, never the tweet copied over — hard copyright rule. Rejected: copying the tweet (not allowed).
Categorization — settled: tags only
At first I'd imagined classifying each item along 2 axes ("business" vs "AI at large"). In the end, simpler: each entry carries tags (anthropic, openai, modeles, agents, produit…) and the site filters by tag, without imposing 2 rigid boxes. More flexible, more fine-grained, and it avoids forcing a news item into a single category.
3. The "vibe coding": how it got built, step by step
The project happened in two stages: a framing in chat (the decisions above, formalized in handoff MDs), then the actual build of the code with Claude Code in the veille-ia repo.
The pipeline that was built (veille/):
- twitter.py — fetches the recent tweets per account via twitterapi.io (+ advanced_search for the backfill).
- Filtering — removes the noise (retweets, replies, out of window).
- feed.py — Claude (role: "neutral, anti-hype editor-in-chief") selects the noteworthy topics and produces structured entries through an enforced JSON Schema. The factual fields (URL, date, media, author) are not entrusted to Claude: they're read back from the source tweet by its index [n].
- digest.py — writes the Telegram digest.
- telegram.py — publishes (with splitting of messages > 4096 characters).
- main.py — orchestrates the two outputs from the same collection run.
- backfill.py — generates the initial feed.json (May 2026), budget-capped.
The whole thing runs without a server: two GitHub Actions workflows (veille.yml daily at 05:00 UTC ≈ 7am Paris, and backfill.yml manual).
4. The stack + the tools
- twitterapi.io — tweet collection (Twitter having shut down its free access). Billed per use, a few cents/day. Key <TWITTERAPI_IO_KEY>.
- RSS (feeds.txt) — complementary sources outside X.
- Claude API (Anthropic) — editorial selection + neutral French summaries. Model claude-opus-4-8 (switchable to claude-sonnet-4-6 to reduce the cost). Key <ANTHROPIC_API_KEY>.
- Telegram Bot API — pushes the digest. Token <TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN>, channel t.me/VeilleIA_HL.
- GitHub Actions — the scheduler (1 run/day) that orchestrates collect → summarize → 2 outputs.
- GitHub (veille-ia) — engine + secrets. GitHub Pages (knowledge-hub) — the site.
- feed.json — the data contract between the two repos (cumulative). seen.json — the deduplication memory.
- Cross-repo bridge — at the end of the job, veille-ia commits/pushes feed.json into knowledge-hub through a dedicated PAT <KH_REPO_TOKEN>.
🔒 Never a published secret
All the tokens above are placeholders. They live in the Secrets of the private veille-ia repo; the public site contains none of them; the cross-repo PAT is dedicated, limited in scope, never reused from another purpose.
5. The headaches (what broke and how we fixed it)
Faithfully reconstructed from the code + the repo's Git history.
- The cross-repo bridge fighting with itself. First reflex: rebase before pushing feed.json. Result → add/add conflicts. → Since our feed.json is the source of truth, we overwrite the site's version: git reset --hard origin/main then copy + push, with 3 resync attempts. (commits 7cf2157 → ec80ca4)
- Telegram blocking everything. Bot not an admin of the channel (403 "bot is not a member") or a network hiccup → the whole delivery fell over, including the feed.json. → Telegram sending made non-blocking (try/except) and optional: no Telegram configured → we skip, but we still produce the feed. (commits 500a8ce, e9717d1)
- The secret name that didn't match. The code expected TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID, the secret was named TELEGRAM_CHANNEL_ID. → Alias accepted on both sides. (commit e9717d1)
- Invalid GitHub Actions workflow. A secrets.* inside a step's if: — forbidden by GitHub. → The "token missing → skip" guardrail moved into the script ([ -z "$KH_REPO_TOKEN" ]). (commit ba581b3)
- Unbalanced backfill. Without a quota, a few chatty accounts ate up the whole budget. → Per-account quota (fair collection across ~45 accounts) + strict global guardrail on the total. (commit 00afa3f)
6. Time spent (real) and tokens / cost
Time. Framing (2-repo architecture, feed.json contract, stack, guardrails) spread over several short exchanges, formalized in two handoff MDs. Setup on May 31, 2026 (accounts + secrets), according to the timestamps of my screenshots: ~3:14–3:19 PM (twitterapi.io account + 1st secret), ~6:44–6:50 PM (Telegram bot via BotFather + 3 secrets), ~11:42–11:43 PM (4th secret + "no workflow yet" screen). A span of ~8.5 hours over the evening — but those are clock gaps between screenshots, not actual working time. The real work end to end (creating the accounts, pasting the 4 secrets, hooking up the workflow) is counted in tens of minutes, not hours.
Cost (unlike the site, here you pay per use):
- twitterapi.io: €100 prepaid "to see" — even though Claude advised me to start from zero. It's a comfort ceiling, not an expense: the real consumption for ~45 accounts stays in the order of a few cents/day, so those €100 last a very long time.
- Claude API: one daily digest = a handful of cents. claude-opus-4-8 by default; claude-sonnet-4-6 to reduce it further.
- GitHub Actions: free within the limits for public repos.
- Budget guardrails: 1 run/day, RSS/tweet caps, low prepaid balance, capped backfill (no loop on advanced_search, strict ceiling of ~1500 tweets). See also How much does AI cost.
7. What this illustrates
- A useful agent fits in ~300 lines and 0 servers. Collect → summarize with the Claude API → dual publish, orchestrated by a free GitHub Actions cron. No infrastructure to manage. (What's an agent? → the guide.)
- The right architecture avoids the headaches. Separating engine and display, isolating the secrets, locking a data contract: most of the remaining bugs were integration details, not design holes.
- We keep the human (and the LLM) honest. Factual fields read back from the source; copyright respected (French summary, never a copy); a neutral, anti-hype editorial line, even when the news isn't flattering for Anthropic.
Coming up / what's next
- Document the Telegram / AI Watch project (step-by-step guide "My AI watch agent").
- Pinned welcome post on the Telegram channel.
- Guides page filterable by tag on the site side.
- LinkedIn comms: announce the project and follow it over time — two good concrete use cases, with real time and cost figures.
Update · September 1, 2026
What broke since — and the rule that came out of it
This bot's twin, the hi-fi watch bot, stopped for three weeks in June 2026: the name of the model it called was hard-coded, and that model reached its end of life. Fixed in August — the model is now picked automatically, the sources went from 30 to 64, an alert goes out if a source stops responding for three days, and the cost is capped at a few euros a month. The rule, engraved since then in my dev context file: never hard-code a model name. → HiFi Watch: fixed, expanded, made reliable
Going further
- → Case study — the Knowledge Hub site (zero token cost)
- → Making-of — shipped in a weekend
- → The AI Watch page, live

MAKING-OF
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/guides/making-of.html
Published: 2026-06-01
================================================================

Behind the scenes: from a dinner with friends to the “beautiful baby delivered in 2 days.” A complete static site and an AI Watch bot put into production in a weekend, paired with Claude Code, without being a developer.

Home › Guides › Making-of — shipped in a weekend
Behind the scenes · Build in public
Making-of:shipped in a weekend
This site — and an AI Watch bot — from a dinner with friends to the "beautiful baby delivered in 2 days." Without being a developer, paired with Claude Code.
By Hugo Lahutte · June 1, 2026·Updated September 1, 2026 · ~3 min read build in publicClaude Codecoulisses
The story, short version
Friday, May 29, 2026, dinner with friends. I'm talking again about what I tinker with using AI. Since I'd already told the same story at lunch, I tell myself: I need one single place to show all of this, instead of re-explaining it every time.
Saturday morning, I launch the site. And one thing leads to another, everything follows and goes to production almost immediately:
- a journal, a glossary, a tag system, a search;
- a clean dark mode (across 72 pages);
- an AI Watch page;
- and even a bot that fetches AI news, has the Claude API summarize it, and publishes it to Telegram + to the site.
The whole thing designed as one piece, right down to the home-made favicon / logo (inspired by Claude, integrated into my art direction) for complete visual consistency.
A beautiful baby delivered in ~2 days — without being a developer, paired with Claude Code.
The two use cases to follow
This is what I document in detail, with figures for time and cost:
- The Knowledge Hub site — a static HTML/CSS/JS site, zero framework, on GitHub Pages. Token cost: zero (Claude subscription). Here we're talking time.
- The AI Watch bot — a serverless agent (GitHub Actions): X/Twitter → Claude API → Telegram + site. Real cost: a few cents/day (€100 prepaid "to see," it lasts a very long time).
And after that
LinkedIn announcement of the project, documentation of the Telegram channel, and public follow-up of both projects over time — because the best proof that a non-dev can ship is to show the making-of, with the numbers to back it up.
Update · September 1, 2026
And since then
The "beautiful baby delivered in two days" has held up: bilingual in June, reviewed by Fable 5 the day after its release, a hundred pages per language by September, and a complete second pass in September 2026 with Fable 5.1 — method rewritten, six guides added, glossary doubled — because in five months, the ways of working had changed. The principle hasn't moved: document in public, with the numbers to back it up.

================================================================
GLOSSARY — AI TERMS, PLAINLY DEFINED
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/lexique/
================================================================

- Artificial intelligence (AI) : Software capable of tasks that used to require a human brain (understanding, deciding, creating). "Classical AI" is specialized; generative AI is versatile.
- Generative AI : An AI that produces new content (text, image, code) from a simple instruction, instead of executing a single programmed task.
- LLM (large language model) : The engine behind assistants like Claude or ChatGPT: a model trained on enormous amounts of text that predicts the most plausible continuation of what you type.
- Token : The basic unit an LLM reads and produces: a chunk of a word. The length of exchanges and their cost are measured in tokens.
- Hallucination : When an LLM confidently invents a false answer. Hence the basic rule: verify facts, numbers, and references.
- Prompt : The instruction you give the AI. A good prompt — clear, with the context and the goal — changes the result of one answer. But what weighs on every answer is the context (CLAUDE.md, Brain, skills).
- Brief (mission brief) : What you write for an AI that will work on its own, as opposed to a prompt that aims for a single answer: a goal with its success criterion, context that is provided (files, folder, connector) rather than described, the task split into steps, the format and constraints, and checkpoints (a plan before execution, a preview before sending). It only contains what is specific to the mission: the permanent lives in the CLAUDE.md, the repeatable in a skill.
- Success criterion : The sentence "we'll know it's good when…" written before acting: the counter is right, the script passes, the email fits in 120 words. The fourth of the Karpathy-style principles, and indispensable as soon as an AI acts on its own — without a criterion it doesn't know when to stop, and "done" means nothing. Best of all: a criterion that checks itself (a test, a health-check script).
- Multimodal : Capable of processing multiple types of input — text, image, audio — not just text.
- Open weights : A model you can download and self-host (e.g. Llama, Mistral), as opposed to "closed" models accessible only via a service.
- Anthropic : The American lab that creates Claude, focused on model reliability and safety.
- Claude : Anthropic's AI assistant. A family of models (in 2026: Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku — the Claude 5 family) and several products: Chat (to talk things through), Cowork (to delegate office work), Code (to act inside a project).
- Fable / Opus / Sonnet / Haiku : Claude's four sizes: Fable (the class above, the most capable), Opus (the heavyweight), Sonnet (the balanced one), Haiku (the fast one). Rule: the cheapest one that gets the job done.
- Claude Chat / Cowork / Code : Three ways to use Claude: talk things through (Chat), delegate office work with no terminal (Cowork — desktop, web, mobile), act on files and projects (Code — terminal, browser, mobile). House rule: Chat writes, Code executes.
- Terminal : The window where you type commands instead of clicking. Looks scary, but it runs on copy-paste.
- API : A programmed pipe connecting two pieces of software. It's one of the ways to connect a service to Claude, in an automated way.
- MCP (Model Context Protocol) : An open standard created by Anthropic in late 2024: a "universal plug" to connect Claude to tools (Shopify, Drive, Gmail, GitHub…) with no custom integration. In the Claude apps, it's called a connector. Since 2026, Claude doesn't just read anymore: it acts, subject to validation.
- AI agent : Claude given a goal and the means to act on its own, in a loop, until it delivers — instead of just answering. In 2026: inside a session, as subagents, as scheduled routines, or hosted on a server. Always within a frame: goal, budget, frequency, success criterion.
- GitHub : An online space where your project lives with its full history; once connected, updates deploy themselves.
- Repository (repo) : The "folder" of a project on GitHub, with all its files and history.
- Commit : A saved, timestamped version of a project on GitHub. You can always go back to it.
- Cron : A timer that runs a task automatically at regular intervals (e.g. every morning at 7 a.m.). The "infrastructure" form of recurring tasks, alongside loops (ephemeral) and routines (scheduled on Claude's side).
- RSS : A standard format for automatically pulling new articles from a site. The basic building block of any news watch.
- Bot / Telegram channel : A program that posts messages on Telegram; a public channel is followable by anyone via a simple link.
- CLAUDE.md : A file Claude reads at startup: tone, conventions, pitfalls turned into rules. It saves you from re-explaining everything in every conversation. Versioned in the repo (CLAUDE-{domain}-{project}.md convention), short, reviewed on a set schedule. Facts go in the Brain, procedures go in skills.
- Compound Engineering : A method (popularized by Kieran Klaassen and Dan Shipper, at Every) where every lesson becomes a reusable rule: your system gets better with use. In Hugo's setup, two levels: one mistake → one CLAUDE.md rule; one session → one capture in the Brain.
- Vibe coding : Programming by describing what you want in plain language and letting the AI generate the code. A term popularized by Andrej Karpathy in 2025. Commonplace by 2026: what sets you apart now is context engineering.
- SEO : The art of ranking well in search engines (Google…).
- GEO : SEO's equivalent for AI: optimizing your content to get **cited** by assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity). That's the goal of this site.
- Brain (private wiki) : The durable memory of what we know and decide: a private repo of Markdown files (entities, building blocks, projects, method, notes, sessions) that every AI reads through a connector. Rule: a stale brain is worse than an empty brain.
- OKF (Open Knowledge Format) : An open specification published by Google Cloud in June 2026: Markdown files with a YAML header (a single required field, "type"), connected by links, with an index. It formalizes Karpathy's "LLM wiki". The Brain's format.
- Frontmatter (YAML header) : The few "key: value" lines at the top of a Markdown file (type, title, description, tags, date…). It's what makes a plain text file machine-readable — the basis of OKF.
- Context (context window) : Everything the model "sees" at the moment it answers: the instruction, context files, documents, history, tool results — nothing else. Limited (up to one million tokens on Claude 5) and re-read with every answer. Context engineering is organizing what the AI knows.
- Compaction : When a conversation gets too long, the tool replaces its beginning with an automatic summary. Useful, but the summary keeps what the model considers essential — hence the handoff brief and the capture in the Brain.
- Context debt : What piles up when the files the AI reads (CLAUDE.md, Brain, reference pages) are no longer kept up to date: the AI decides confidently on false premises. The context-side counterpart of technical debt. Paid back through session capture and updating the pages affected — a stale brain is worse than an empty brain.
- Handoff brief : The validated summary you ask Claude for when a conversation runs long — where things stand, what's decided, what's left, the constraints — so you can start a fresh conversation without losing anything.
- Memory (of the assistant) : The feature that lets Claude remember your preferences and your projects' context from one conversation to the next (shared between chat and Cowork since August 2026). Implicit and tied to one tool, unlike the Brain — the memory you choose, can re-read, and share.
- Skill : A procedure packaged in a folder (a SKILL.md file, sometimes scripts) that Claude loads on demand when your request matches. Written know-how, portable from one tool to the next.
- Hook : A script that fires automatically at a specific point in Claude's work (before a command, after an edit). Deterministic: it checks, blocks, or logs, without thinking. A rule gets read; a hook gets run.
- Subagent : A Claude the main agent hands a subtask to, with its own context, in the background. To parallelize, isolate a heavy read, or specialize (reviewer, verifier). A workflow orchestrates several subagents.
- Plugin : A versioned package bundling skills, subagents, commands, hooks, and connectors, installable in one command — from a marketplace, or to share know-how with a team.
- Connector : A tool plugged into Claude (Shopify, Gmail, Drive, GitHub…) from a menu in the Claude apps. Under the hood, an MCP. Rule: the assistant never has more rights than the person talking to it.
- Loop : A prompt re-run at regular intervals by an agent, inside your Claude Code session, to watch or check something for a few hours. Ephemeral: it expires on its own.
- Routine (scheduled task) : A scheduled agent (every morning, every Monday) that runs in the cloud on Claude's side — Claude Code on the web, Cowork, or a hosted agent — without your machine. The link between the ephemeral loop and your own infrastructure (cron).
- Workflow (of agents) : A small script that orchestrates several subagents deterministically — a review per dimension, then a check of every finding, for example. Available in Claude Code since June 2026. Save it for tasks that deserve a dozen agents.
- Claude Code : Claude's agent that acts inside a project: reads and edits files, runs commands, deploys. In the terminal, the browser, the desktop app, or on mobile (cloud session). Included in every paid plan.
- Claude Cowork : Claude's assistant for office work, which carries out a job end to end with no terminal: files, spreadsheets, presentations, a built-in browser, routines, and learning a skill by recording your screen. On desktop, web, and mobile since summer 2026.
- Auto mode : In Claude Code, the mode where Claude decides routine permissions on its own, with protections against manipulation. Became the default in August 2026.
- Prompt injection : Booby-trapped instructions hidden in a web page or an email an agent reads, to push it into doing something other than its task. 2026 models resist it far better; the real protection is still limited rights.
- Human validation : The principle: the AI reads, analyzes, and proposes automatically; a person validates anything that changes a price, a stock level, a campaign, an email, or a publication. The flow: request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement.
- Idempotent : Said of an action you can run several times without producing several effects. It's what makes an automation recoverable: replaying a publication or an import duplicates nothing.
- HL OS : The system I'm building to run my companies with AI: a shared foundation (database, AI layer, identity and rights, action log) and five building blocks — Zéro, Knowledge, Content Machine, Growth, Socle IA (AI Core). One core, several contexts.
- Building block : In HL OS, a system under construction: a scope, a living specification, a development plan with success criteria ("we'll know it's right when…"), and a dated Decisions section.
- Growth : HL OS's "action-first" decision building block: it brings together sales, acquisition, SEO, web, email, and social, and proposes a handful of actions ranked by impact, confidence, effort, and risk, with their evidence. Automatic reads, validated writes. In production for Cobra since September 2026.
- Content Machine : HL OS's publishing building block: one capture, N destinations. The base unit is the attested observation; a post or an article is just a rendering of it, proposed by the machine and validated by a human. Never a publication without validation.
- Attested observation : A few media files, a voice memo, or a note, at a place, at a time, by an identified person. The Content Machine's base unit. "Witnessed" (seen in the field) and "documented" (read, owned) are kept separate, both in the database and in the rendering.
- Provenance : Who, where, when behind a piece of content. The first-hand experience signal that search engines and answering AIs reward — and the exact opposite of mass-generated content. "Provenance is the product."
- Repurposing : Turning existing material (a magazine article, an archive) into renderings suited to other destinations (social, website, newsletter). In the Content Machine, the "documented" material from Haute Fidélité magazine.
- Embargo : A date before which a piece of content can't go out. In the Content Machine, it's a lock, not an instruction: the door stays shut until the date.
- Zéro (email + tasks building block) : The HL OS building block that sorts and summarizes emails and turns an email into a task. The Brain's daily signal source, and one of the publishing triggers ("to publish").
- Socle IA (AI Core) : HL OS's shared AI layer: writing in my voice, embeddings for search, a router that picks the model by tier and logs every call, and a server-side encrypted-secrets pattern. The other building blocks call it; they don't reimplement it.
- HF-OS : Haute Fidélité's in-house ERP, built from scratch in five days with Claude Code in June 2026 (CRM, ad sales, invoicing, payment reminders). Now the technical foundation of HL OS: a single application (headless CMS + web framework + PostgreSQL).
- ERP : A company's central management software (sales, purchasing, inventory, invoicing). At Cobra: Odoo, extended almost daily with Claude Code. At Haute Fidélité: HF-OS, custom-built.
- Odoo : The open-source ERP Cobra runs on (sales, purchasing, inventory, invoicing), extended with in-house modules. The commercial truth: actual sales, margin, stock.
- Shopify : The e-commerce platform behind the Cobra and Haute Fidélité stores. It describes the web flow; Odoo carries the actuals. Plugged into Claude through a connector, and open to shopping agents since 2026.
- CDC (cahier des charges / spec) : The document that describes what we want to build: where, what, what must not change. At Cobra, every Odoo change has its numbered CDC — and since 2026, the AI re-reads the request and checks its assumptions against the real database before a single line is written.
- Build vs buy : Build it yourself or buy it (or have it built). In 2026, AI is collapsing the cost of customization: the math flips for anything specific to a business — from the ERP to the steering layer.
- Pull request (PR) : A merge request: a batch of changes proposed on GitHub, reviewed and automatically checked (CI) before it enters the production version. Claude Code's unit of work. HF-OS: 96 PRs in five days.
- CI (continuous integration) : The automatic checks that run on every change to a project (lint, tests, build) or on a schedule (GitHub Actions). In my case: auto-translating pages, regenerating the indexes, a weekly consistency check.
- Surgical deploy : Pushing to production the exact commit of one feature, never a whole branch where developments are mixed together. A hard rule born from a production release that broke everything in May 2026.
- Webhook : A signal one service sends automatically to another when something happens (an order placed, a status changed). The opposite of a cron: you don't go check, you get notified.
- Embeddings : Turning a text into a sequence of numbers that captures its meaning, to find documents that are close in meaning rather than in wording. The basis of a semantic search index — the one the Brain doesn't need yet.
- RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) : Having the model look up the relevant documents (via embeddings) before answering, instead of relying on its memory. The Brain does the same thing by navigation, with no index — for as long as that's enough.
- Vector database (pgvector) : A database that stores embeddings and finds the ones closest to a question. In HL OS: PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension, planned as an index derived from the Brain — rebuilt from the files, never the source of truth.
- PostgreSQL : The open-source database that serves as the foundation for HF-OS and the HL OS building blocks. One single database, shared.
- Headless CMS : A content management system that provides an admin and an API without dictating how things are displayed. HF-OS runs on a headless CMS (Payload) and a web framework (Next.js) in a single application.
- SSR (server-side rendering) : Producing the page as complete HTML on the server, rather than building it in the browser with JavaScript. Essential to be read by AI crawlers, which don't run JavaScript.
- JSON-LD (structured data) : A machine-readable block of data, placed in a page, that says who's speaking and about what (author, article, question/answer). The vocabulary is schema.org. On every page of this site.
- llms.txt : A text file at the root of a site that summarizes its content for AIs, page by page (plus its extended version, llms-full.txt, with the full text). An agent's entry point to this site.
- Claude · HL / Claude · Cobra : My two Claudes, deliberately kept apart: HL (personal account — steering, strategy, editorial, method, this site) and Cobra (company account — Odoo and Shopify dev, purely technical). The badges on every journal entry.
- Session capture : The end-of-session ritual: re-read, write the session entry in the Brain, propose updates to the reference pages touched, run the confidentiality filter. The second level of Compound Engineering.
- Shell (empty placeholder page) : In the Brain, a page whose title is real but whose content doesn't exist yet: it says so and asks questions instead of answering them. You never make up the content of a shell.
- Mythos (model class) : The class of Claude models above Opus, inaugurated by Fable 5 in June 2026. "Mythos" also refers to the version without certain guardrails, reserved for trusted-access programs (Project Glasswing: cyberdefense, life sciences).
- Cache (context cache) : The model reusing what it has already read in a conversation, billed at a fraction of the price. A well-structured conversation (stable context first, variable questions after) costs less than a messy one.
- Telegram topics : The sub-channels of a Telegram group. In the Content Machine, one topic per context (personal, work, magazine): posting in the right topic says where the capture comes from, with no manual tag.


================================================================
FABLE 5.1 REVISITS THE WHOLE SITE: METHOD V2, SIX GUIDES, A GLOSSARY DOUBLED
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/journal/refonte-knowledge-hub-fable-5-1.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

Five months after its creation, this site described a method that was no longer mine: versioned context files, an OKF Brain, Cowork, skills, routines, connectors that act, the Claude 5 family — none of it was there. On the day Claude Fable 5.1 was released, a full pass: the Method rewritten (v2), six new guides (Brain, context, skills, guardrails, HL OS, Content Machine), twenty-three guides updated, a glossary grown from 27 to 85 terms, the home and project pages brought up to date, three entries for the summer's projects, and the English mirror. Without inventing anything: the Brain first.

← Journal
Perso · Knowledge Hub
Fable 5.1 revisits the whole site: method v2, six guides, a glossary doubled
Claude · HL · September 1, 2026 · Perso metadocseo-gtmen-prodPerso
Context
This site was written in May and June 2026. Five months later, it was still right — and yet wrong: the method described instruction files pasted into a chat when they now live in my repos; the Brain didn't exist; Cowork was a promise; the model lineup had been renewed three times; skills, routines and connectors that act appeared nowhere; and six guides were missing to explain what I actually do today. A method site that's five months behind the method is the textbook case of the stale brain.
The day Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1, I handed it the full pass — the way I'd handed Fable 5, the day after its release in June, an audit of the same site. The mandate: reread everything, bring everything up to today's date, explain simply, keep it evergreen, invent nothing, and keep the glossary current.
What was done
- The Brain first. The session started by reading my Brain (entities, building blocks, method, notes, sessions) to find out what had changed — not the model's memory, the source of truth. Then the site's own AI Watch, which held the exact chronology of the summer (Fable 5, its suspension, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Cowork everywhere, Fable 5.1), and a few web searches to check the facts that might have moved.
- The Method rewritten (v2): two layers of context — the CLAUDE.md files (“how to work with me”) and the Brain (“what we know”) —, three doors (Chat, Cowork, Code), two agents, skills and connectors, the two-stage loop (rule + capture), the guardrails, an updated starting prompt, and a changelog since May.
- Six new guides: the Brain and the OKF format; context; skills (and hooks, subagents, plugins); “AI proposes, the human validates”; HL OS; the Content Machine.
- Twenty-three guides revisited: fourteen rewritten in depth — seven on September 1 (Claude and the Claude 5 family; Chat, Cowork or Code; cost, with September's orders of magnitude; loops, routines and scheduled tasks; MCP and the connectors that act; agents and their forms in 2026; the CLAUDE.md and what it isn't), seven the next day, the practice guides, because a dated insert wasn't enough when the way of working itself had changed (the prompt turned brief; the Karpathy-style principles when AI acts on its own; three-tier Compound Engineering; why AI changes work; the retailer; data and permissions; GEO) — the others updated with dated inserts — Fable's eventful summer, the signals of 2026, what three months of GEO taught, the follow-ups to the case studies.
- The glossary: from 27 to 85 terms, in French and in English, with links to the guides and the entries where each notion comes to life. Brain, OKF, skill, hook, subagent, routine, context, compaction, human validation, HL OS, Growth, Content Machine, provenance, idempotent, embeddings…
- The Guides page reorganized (the new ones, understand, equip, method, decide, my systems, case studies), the home page, the project pages and the About page brought up to today's date, and three journal entries for the summer's projects: the Brain, HL OS, the Content Machine.
- The English mirror of everything that moved, the sitemap, the search indexes, the llms.txt file in both languages, the consistency check — the full linking, as for any publication.
What was hard / unexpected
Deciding what stays dated and what becomes evergreen. A guide that tells the story of June 9 must not be rewritten as if it had been written on September 1: it gets an “update” insert at the top, and its story stays. A foundational guide (agents, cost, MCP), on the contrary, must be rewritten with no trace of its old version, because a reader in December shouldn't have to do the subtraction.
Publishing without betraying what's private. The Brain contains pages marked private; HL OS and the Content Machine are described there with details that don't get out (accounts, amounts, internal addresses, decisions in progress). The rule held: we publish the principles, the architecture, the firm decisions and the dated state; never a sync. Going from the Brain to the site is an editorial act.
Not inventing. On several points (what actually runs in production, release dates, prices), the temptation was to write what “should” be true. Every time: check in the Brain, in the AI Watch or on the web, or hold back. A wrong guide is worse than a missing guide — the same rule as for the Brain.
Stack
Claude Fable 5.1 in Claude Code (cloud session), the Brain read through the GitHub connector, the site's AI Watch as the chronology, a few web searches for the facts that move, a small Python page generator in the session's sandbox to keep the chrome identical, the repo's scripts (sitemap, llms-full, feeds, consistency check), subagents for the English mirror. Zero dependencies added to the site: still HTML and CSS, a single stylesheet.
What it illustrates
A method site is a public brain: it goes stale in silence while the journal grows. The pass isn't an event, it's a ritual — and the next one already has a date. Second lesson: the useful work wasn't writing, it was deciding what to say and what to leave out, guide by guide. Fable wrote; I arbitrated. As with everything else.

- The glossary
- Fable 5 reviews the site (June 2026)
- The Brain: my private wiki in OKF format

HL OS: FIVE BUILDING BLOCKS, ONE FOUNDATION
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/journal/hl-os-cinq-briques-un-socle.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

What I've been building since June has a name: HL OS. A shared foundation (a database inherited from HF-OS, an AI layer, identity and permissions, an action log) and five building blocks — Zéro, Knowledge, Content Machine, Growth, AI Core (Socle IA) — with their boundaries decided on September 1. One core, several contexts (Cobra and Haute Fidélité isolated), a single flow request → analysis → preview → validation → execution → log → measurement, and one priority on record: make audience measurement reliable before moving any budget.

← Journal
HL Consulting · HL OS
HL OS: five building blocks, one foundation — the map of the system
Claude · HL · September 1, 2026 · Perso stratagentinfraen-coursPerso
Context
Since June, I'd been building several things in parallel without naming them together: a magazine-publisher ERP built in five days (HF-OS), a mail-and-tasks building block, a shared AI layer, a content machine, a private brain, and — since late August — Growth, the action queue that replaces ten dashboards at Cobra. Each had its spec, its decisions, its plan. What was missing was the map: how it all fits together, what's shared, what must never be.
On September 1, while writing the Growth building block into the Brain, the map drew itself. What I'm building has a name: HL OS. Not a collection of scripts — an operating system, in the sense of “what everything else runs on”.
What was done
- The foundation, named: a shared database (inherited from HF-OS — a single application that serves the dashboard, the admin and the API), a shared AI layer (writing in my voices, embeddings, a router that picks the model by tier and logs every call, secrets encrypted server-side), identity and permissions (allowlist login, roles), and an action log.
- Five building blocks, each with its boundary: Zéro (mail + tasks, the source of daily signal), Knowledge (the Brain and its index — the “inbound” direction), Content Machine (one capture, N destinations — the “outbound” direction), Growth (measure, reconcile, diagnose, recommend, prepare an action) and AI Core (Socle IA) (the other building blocks call it; they don't reimplement it). Growth measures and recommends; the Content Machine makes and publishes; Knowledge keeps. Three decisions from the same day set these boundaries: Knowledge's “outbound” direction is attached to the Content Machine; Growth covers organic and paid on the measurement side but never publishes; the two share campaign identifiers so that D+3 and D+14 results feed the next batch.
- One core, several contexts: Cobra and Haute Fidélité share the intelligence, never the accounts, the secrets, the data or the operating rules. The first Growth instance runs for Cobra; the Haute Fidélité instance will reuse the core as an isolated context.
- The single flow of an action: request → analysis → preview of the change → validation → execution → log → measurement. Automatic reads and refreshes; writes to Shopify, Odoo, the ad platforms, email or social networks require validation as long as no finer-grained permission exists. The assistant never gets more rights than the person talking to it.
- The immediate priority, on record: the reliability of audience measurement. Observed coverage against real orders is too low to move a budget on that signal alone; a seven-day daily watch, read-only, compares the store, the ERP and analytics without touching the tracking.
What was hard / unexpected
Resisting the urge for a separate “decisions” folder. Each building block and each entity carries its own dated Decisions section; that's where the trade-off lives, not in a buried session. The stance holds as long as decisions stay easy to find — it's written as a switch-over criterion, not as a certainty.
Not freezing a snapshot into truth. Growth's state as of September 1 (what's connected, what's reliable, what isn't yet) is recorded as a dated block, with the explicit instruction never to copy those values as permanent. A stale brain is worse than an empty brain; a stale table of numbers, even more so.
The word “OS” is a big one for an outfit my size. I own it: the day I started calling this an OS, I stopped thinking of it as a collection of scripts, and the boundaries between building blocks became decisions rather than accidents.
Stack
A headless CMS and a web framework in a single application, PostgreSQL, hosting as a persistent process; Cobra's internal apps hub for the Growth instance; the Claude API through the AI Core router; the Odoo, Shopify, Google Analytics, Ads, Search Console, Merchant Center and Brevo connectors, plus the social networks' native APIs on the measurement side; Telegram as the Content Machine's cockpit; the Brain in OKF format as memory.
What it illustrates
The value isn't in one more tool. It's in a layer above the tools that reads everything, reconciles the facts, proposes and keeps the trail — and in the boundaries that make that layer safe: a shared core, isolated contexts, validation before any write. The hard work wasn't the code: it was deciding which source to believe (Odoo carries what was actually sold, Shopify the web flow, the ad platforms their self-reported attribution) and preventing misleading reconciliations. The AI typed the code; the trade-offs stay human. The full guide: What is HL OS.
See also
- What is HL OS: an operating system for running a group with AI
- Growth: replacing ten dashboards with an action queue
- Content Machine: the September 1 pivot
- The Brain: my private wiki in OKF format
- HF-OS: the foundation, deployed

GROWTH: REPLACING TEN DASHBOARDS WITH AN ACTION QUEUE
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/journal/growth-centre-actions.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

Loose ideas at the end of the week, a weekend with ChatGPT and Codex, then a Growth Hub connected to real data and running in production by Tuesday.

← Journal
Cobra · Growth
Growth : remplacer dix tableaux de bord par une file d'actions
ChatGPT · Codex·1er septembre 2026·Cobra datamarketingagentstraten-prodCobra En quelques jours, Growth est passé d'un tableau de bord en lecture seule à un centre de décision qui rapproche commerce, acquisition, SEO, performance web, email et social. L'objectif n'est plus de montrer davantage de chiffres : il est de dire quoi traiter maintenant, pourquoi, et avec quelles preuves.
Un point important sur la méthode : contrairement à la plupart des projets documentés jusque-là dans ce journal, Growth n'a pas été construit avec Claude. Le cadrage, l'architecture, le développement, les tests, le déploiement et cette documentation ont été réalisés presque entièrement dans ChatGPT avec Codex. Claude n'est intervenu qu'à la marge sur ce chantier.
Le problème
Les informations utiles existaient déjà, mais elles vivaient dans des outils différents : Odoo pour les ventes, la marge et le stock ; Shopify pour le flux e-commerce ; GA4 et Google Ads pour la mesure ; Search Console et Merchant Center pour la visibilité ; Brevo pour l'email ; Lighthouse pour la performance ; les plateformes sociales pour l'organique et le paid.
Chaque outil sait produire son tableau de bord. Aucun ne répond seul à une question simple : quelle action mérite réellement notre temps aujourd'hui ?
Ce qui a été construit
- un accueil limité aux actions prioritaires ;
- une barre principale pour poser une question, ouvrir une preuve, rafraîchir les données ou préparer une action ;
- un rapprochement Odoo ↔ Shopify et une lecture croisée GA4, Ads et ventes réelles ;
- un backlog SEO issu de Search Console, complété à la demande par DataForSEO ;
- des contrôles Merchant Center, Lighthouse, liens, erreurs HTTP, Brevo et réseaux sociaux ;
- un moteur commun réutilisable pour une future instance Haute Fidélité dans HL OS ;
- un garde-fou : toute écriture sensible reste soumise à validation humaine.
Données de démonstration. Tous les noms, chiffres et recommandations de cette capture sont fictifs.
Comment le système est découpé
Le produit repose sur deux dépôts de code et une plateforme de données. Cette séparation évite que l'interface Growth reconstruise ses propres chiffres ou accède directement aux données brutes.
- Le dépôt cobra-data fabrique la donnée fiable. Il collecte Odoo et Shopify en lecture seule, intègre les autres sources analytiques, nettoie, déduplique, rapproche les identifiants et construit les indicateurs métier.
- BigQuery conserve les différentes couches. cobra_raw reçoit les copies techniques, cobra_staging les fiabilise, cobra_marts publie les vues métier stables et cobra_audit garde la trace des traitements.
- Le dépôt applicatif cobra-pilotage, dans apps/growth, transforme les faits en décisions. Growth lit uniquement les marts autorisés et les indicateurs agrégés de fraîcheur. Il ne peut ni modifier BigQuery, ni consulter raw ou staging, ni écrire dans Odoo ou Shopify par défaut.
Data fabrique les faits ; BigQuery les conserve et les partage ; Growth les transforme en décisions ; l'humain donne l'autorisation.
Comment circule une action
La collecte, les contrôles, la détection des anomalies et le classement peuvent tourner automatiquement. Une action sensible suit en revanche un contrat explicite : preuve, aperçu, validation humaine, exécution autorisée, journal et mesure avant/après.
La mécanique reste la même pour Cobra ou Haute Fidélité ; les données, comptes, profils métier et droits restent séparés.
Le changement de philosophie
Le produit avait commencé comme un tableau de bord. C'était utile pour vérifier que les données remontaient, mais insuffisant pour changer la façon de travailler. La page d'accueil a donc été retournée : les indicateurs détaillés sont devenus des preuves secondaires. Le premier écran présente quelques propositions classées par impact, confiance, effort et urgence.
Le flux cible est volontairement lisible : demande → analyse → aperçu du changement → validation → exécution → journal → mesure. Growth peut lire et rafraîchir automatiquement. Il ne doit pas modifier un prix, un stock, une campagne, un email ou une publication sociale sans le droit correspondant.
Données de démonstration. Cette capture ne contient aucune donnée réelle de Cobra.
La difficulté réelle
Le code de l'interface n'était pas la partie la plus coûteuse. Le travail difficile consistait à décider quelle source croire et à empêcher les rapprochements trompeurs. Odoo reste la vérité commerciale. Shopify décrit le flux web. Les plateformes publicitaires donnent leur attribution déclarée. GA4 décrit le comportement observé. Ces chiffres peuvent être comparés, mais ils ne doivent jamais être confondus.
Le premier apprentissage important est venu de cette règle : lorsque la couverture analytics est insuffisante par rapport aux commandes réelles, Growth doit recommander de fiabiliser la mesure avant de proposer un déplacement de budget.
Temps comprimé et valeur de développement
Le cadrage a commencé pendant le week-end, la première trace projet date du 31 août et la première version a été mise en production le 1er septembre.
PrestataireChargeDélaiBudget HTFreelance senior polyvalent30–45 jours6–9 semaines25–42 k€Petite équipe spécialisée40–55 jours-homme4–6 semaines40–70 k€Agence avec pilotage et garantie50–70 jours-homme6–10 semaines60–95 k€ La valeur de remplacement du développement actuel se situe autour de 45 à 55 k€ HT, avec un point central proche de 50 k€ HT. Une industrialisation complète — supervision durable des connecteurs, boucle avant/après, droits fins et documentation d'exploitation — porterait plutôt l'ensemble vers 65 à 80 k€ HT.
Ce chiffrage estime un coût de reconstruction externe, pas la valorisation financière du logiciel ni un retour sur investissement. Repères : baromètre Malt 2026 et synthèse des TJM IT en France.
Ce que ça change
La valeur n'est pas d'avoir ajouté un nouveau tableau de bord à la collection. Elle est de pouvoir progressivement cesser d'ouvrir dix interfaces pour reconstituer une situation.
Growth rassemble les faits, propose le prochain travail et conserve les preuves accessibles à l'expert. Le même cœur pourra servir un commerçant comme Cobra ou un éditeur comme Haute Fidélité, avec des données, comptes et règles séparés.
La prochaine étape n'est donc pas d'ajouter cent graphiques. C'est de fermer la boucle : mesurer ce qui s'est réellement passé après chaque action, puis rendre la recommandation suivante meilleure que la précédente.
Voir aussi
- Le « Cobra App Store » continue de s'industrialiser
- Suivi des prix et alignement concurrentiel automatique

CONTENT MACHINE: THREE PUBLISHING PROJECTS BECOME A SINGLE SYSTEM
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/journal/content-machine-une-capture-n-destinations.html
Published: 2026-09-01
================================================================

On September 1, the attested-content machine (spec v2 from July 30), the Brain's “outbound” direction and the “to publish” trigger become a single system: the Content Machine. One capture, N destinations; the attested observation as the base unit; three inputs (Telegram capture, repurposing of the Haute Fidélité magazine, “publish this idea”); routing by context; firm decisions (Telegram stays the cockpit, pluggable and self-hosted publishing, the Atlas of Asia as the pilot for the travel journal, order: social → web → print). Deadline: the Haute Fidélité show, late September.

← Journal
HL Media · Content Machine
Content Machine: three publishing projects become a single system
Claude · HL · September 1, 2026 · Haute Fidélité marketingagentstraten-coursHaute Fidélité
Context
Three publishing projects each lived on their own: the “attested-content machine” (a v2 spec dated July 30, a foundation in place — collections, login, indexing guardrail, entity page with structured data), the “outbound” direction of my Knowledge building block (“publish this idea” from the Brain to this site), and the “to publish” trigger of the mail-and-tasks building block. Three inputs, three governances, one same problem: publishing what was lived, without losing your voice, without ever publishing alone.
On September 1, rereading the three specs side by side in the Brain, the conclusion was unavoidable: it's a single system. One capture, N destinations. The name: Content Machine.
What was done
- The pivot: the Content Machine becomes the pivot building block for publishing. Knowledge's “outbound” direction is attached to it (Knowledge keeps only the “inbound” direction: the Brain and its index); the project's old name is kept as an alias so no links break.
- The principles, reaffirmed: the base unit is the attested observation (a few media files, a voice memo or a note, at a place, at a time, by an identified person); the post, the article, the printed page are only renderings of it; witnessed and documented are kept separate, in the database and in form; the machine never decides; provenance is the product.
- Three inputs, one same log: field capture (Telegram, under ten seconds, offline, partial sends), repurposing of the magazine (PDFs and visuals of the current issues and the archives — as the publisher, I hold the rights, which lifts one reservation from the spec), and “publish this idea” from a Brain document marked publishable.
- Routing by context: a single Telegram group, one topic per context (personal, professional under my own name, magazine). Posting in a topic states the context; inference from the content is only a suggestion. Each context has its default visibility and its own rules (location metadata stripped, no indexing of minors, LinkedIn as draft only, hard embargo on the magazine side).
- The day's decisions: Telegram stays the cockpit (WhatsApp ruled out: 24-hour window, imposed templates, re-encoded media that breaks print, a third party in the loop); the social layer stays pluggable behind a single interface, with a self-hosted, replaceable publishing tool rather than services billed per account; measurement doesn't depend on the publishing tool (Growth reads the platforms' native stats); the Atlas of Asia (Atlas d'Asie) — our travel journal from this summer — is the handmade pilot of the journal the machine will have to know how to replicate; the magazine's site and the travel journals are headed for a dedicated domain, while this site and the Atlas stay where they are.
- The build order: social → web → print. We validate the engine where a bad output costs nothing. One external deadline: the Haute Fidélité show, late September.
What was hard / unexpected
Separating context from destination. As long as I was thinking “one Instagram account = one project”, nothing fit together. Context is provenance (where, when, why); destination is where it gets published; one context deploys to several destinations. That sentence collapsed three specs into one.
Giving up tools already evaluated. Two multi-account publishing services had been shortlisted in July; re-evaluated with several Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube accounts, their per-account cost became a penalty. Dropping them was easy because the social layer had been designed pluggable: the adapter changes, the machine doesn't move.
Not over-governing. The Atlas of Asia is live, with family photos; the temptation was to add the visibility locks planned for the machine. Decision, owned: validated as is — we don't complicate what works.
Stack
The HL OS foundation (headless CMS + web framework + PostgreSQL, media on object storage), a provider-independent model router with small / large / fallback tiers and logging of every call, Telegram with its topics, a self-hosted publishing adapter behind a single interface, server-side rendering and structured data for the web, character-count calibration for print.
What it illustrates
When everyone can generate content, the only thing that still sets you apart is having been there — and being able to prove it. A useful content machine in 2026 isn't a machine for producing more: it's logistics between what was observed and where it needs to land, with locks before every output and a human who decides with one button. The full guide: Content Machine: one capture, N destinations.

================================================================
AI DOESN'T CODE MY REQUEST
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/journal/cdc-odoo-ia-verifie-avant-de-coder.html
Published: 2026-08-28
================================================================

An internal chain where a request for an Odoo change is described in 8 fields, submitted with screenshots and a (auto-transcribed) video, and reviewed by AI in two passes: it asks structured questions, the server checks the facts in the real Odoo database read-only, then the AI concludes. It reclassified a dev request as ten minutes of configuration, and spotted that a proposed solution didn't solve the stated problem. ~100 s and a few cents per review.

← Journal
Cobra · Method
AI doesn't code my request — it verifies what it assumes
Claude · HL · August 28, 2026 · Cobra agentinfradocen-prodCobra An internal chain where a request for an Odoo change is described in 8 fields, submitted with its screenshots and video, and reviewed automatically — the review going to check in the real database what the request takes for granted.
The review expanded: the verdict and the points to fill, each with the exact question to ask the author.
Context
Odoo change requests arrived as a one-liner in a message: "we'd need a button to…". The same three pieces of information were always missing — where exactly to put the thing, what should happen on click, and above all what must not move. The result: two or three round trips before anything moved, and now and then a change that broke something else along the way.
What was done
A complete chain, from guide to tracking:
- A method guide: ten blocks to fill, and above all a vocabulary to name the zones of an Odoo screen — "top right" points to four different places, and that's where most requests get lost.
- A guided form: an Essential mode with 8 required fields (two minutes), a Complete mode for the ten blocks. The "guardrails" block becomes required automatically when the chosen scope indicates the change will write data — 11 required instead of 8, without the author having to think about it.
- The actual submission: drag-and-drop screenshots, video up to 400 MB. The server extracts the audio and has it transcribed; the transcript is added as an appendix to the request. Nothing left to retype.
- The automatic two-pass review (the core, detailed below).
- A tracking page: verdict, what's missing, and an editable life cycle — to review → reviewed → in progress → in pre-prod → delivered.
The method guide — what the page is for, and above all how to name an Odoo screen zone precisely.
The submission form in Essential mode: 8 fields, dictation possible, a pill summary.
Result: the review runs in ~100 seconds for about 15,000 tokens, i.e. a few cents per request; transcribing a 5-minute video costs about three. On the test requests, it returned "not codable as is" with 9 then 11 points to fill — each phrased with the exact question to ask the author.
The tracking page: clickable counters, color-coded verdict, editable status per request.
A submitted video and its auto-generated transcript, added as an appendix to the request.
What was hard / what we learned
A model must not assert things about a system it can't see. Hence two passes instead of one. The first returns JSON — missing blocks, gaps, edge cases — plus a list of checks to run in the database. The server runs them read-only: whether a model exists, whether a field exists and its type, with a whitelist of methods and a cap of twelve checks. The second pass writes knowing the facts.
The mechanism: each question from the model set against the fact observed in the real Odoo database (read-only).
The gap between the two is stark. One request cited a margin field as if it existed: it doesn't, and the review found the two standard fields actually present in the database. Another described a change to the repair module: the model repair.order doesn't exist in the installation, and the review concluded that the subject was in fact a Helpdesk ticket — so "adding a stage to a Helpdesk status bar is data configuration, not development". A dev request had just turned into ten minutes of setup.
But the best point wasn't technical. The request was justified by "fifteen calls to the supplier a week", and the review noticed the proposed solution didn't remove them: "one more manual step avoids no call: it says ‹ we've ordered ›, not ‹ when it arrives ›". That's exactly the gap between the stated need and the imagined solution that a rushed human reviewer lets through — and that you normally only discover once the feature is shipped.
A notification channel wired to production has no test mode. My trials sent real alerts to the phone, one bearing a colleague's first name as the request's author. Hugo thought a real request had just come in. Two fixes: a switch to mute notifications during a test run, and test data that's visibly fake — the author is now called "TEST — do not process". The cost of that mistake wasn't technical, it was in trust.
The day the feature ships, the doc describing it becomes false. The guide still asked to paste the transcript by hand while the server was already doing it on its own. Hugo caught it, not me. Updating the instructions has to be part of the same pass as the deploy, not a later cleanup.
Stack
Odoo 18 queried over XML-RPC read-only, Python and Flask for the submission service, ffmpeg for audio extraction, a speech-transcription model, the Claude API (Opus 5) for the two-pass review, Caddy and systemd for exposure and supervision, static HTML pages in the house style, and a notification to mobile. All on a small instance already in place.
What this illustrates
We often expect an AI to write the code. The gain was elsewhere: having it verify what the request assumes, before anyone codes. The pattern that works has three beats — the model asks structured questions, the system answers with facts verifiable read-only, the model concludes knowingly. We never ask it to guess the state of the system, and we never let it write to it.
A less technical corollary: two minutes spent describing a request well save three round trips. The tool's role isn't to replace the person asking, it's to make it easy for them to ask well. And sometimes, the best answer to a development request is that there's no development to do.
See also
- An integrator code review handled point by point
- The Cobra App Store keeps industrializing

THE BRAIN: MY PRIVATE WIKI IN OKF FORMAT, READ BY ALL MY CLAUDES
URL: https://hl-consulting.tech/knowledge-hub/en/journal/brain-okf-wiki-prive.html
Published: 2026-08-22
================================================================

A tweet about the Open Knowledge Format triggers a revision of my Knowledge building block: Markdown becomes the source of truth, a private repo in seven folders (entities, building blocks, projects, personal, method, notes, sessions) read by all my Claudes through a plain GitHub connector, and the vector database + MCP server steps pushed back behind a written switch-over criterion. A capture ritual, the shell rule, and one conviction: a stale brain is worse than an empty brain.

← Journal
HL Consulting · Cross-cutting method
The Brain: my private wiki in OKF format, read by all my Claudes
Claude · HL · August 22, 2026 · Perso docmetastraten-prodPerso
Context
A tweet, on a Friday evening in August: an open-source plugin for the Open Knowledge Format, the specification Google Cloud published in June that formalizes Karpathy's “wiki for LLMs”. Two questions behind it: can I put everything I do into a wiki, and can a single wiki serve both my Claudes — the personal account and the Cobra account — plus another assistant now and then?
The “Knowledge” building block of my system had already been specified in late July, with a PostgreSQL database and a vector index as storage, and a homemade MCP server to plug it into three clients. So the real question was: does OKF replace that plan, or slot into it?
What was done
- The brain bundle: a private git repo, seven folders — entities (the group's structures), building blocks (the systems under construction), projects (what has an end), personal (always private), method (prescriptive), notes (revisable), sessions (the raw journal) — a root index.md and a log.md for structural changes.
- The front-matter convention: OKF's standard fields (type, title, description, tags, date) plus two homemade ones — confidentialite (prive or publiable), which makes the public/private guardrail machine-readable, and auteur (me, Claude HL or Claude Cobra), without which it's impossible, six months later, to judge how reliable a page is.
- The Knowledge building block, revised: Markdown becomes the source of truth; the database and the vector index become a derived index, rebuilt from the files — and pushed back until navigation is no longer enough.
- The capture ritual: a skill that, at the end of a session, writes the sessions/ entry and proposes targeted edits to the reference pages it touched. Then, the next day, the shell rule (a shell being an empty placeholder page: it announces itself as empty and asks questions; we never invent its contents), the notes/ folder with its status (draft, held, revised, abandoned) and its mandatory “what could take this apart” section, and a small linter that checks all of it before every commit.
What was hard / unexpected
The “OKF solves multi-client sharing” trap. It doesn't: OKF is a format, not a service. It syncs nothing, searches nothing, exposes nothing. What lets one wiki serve several Claudes is the access layer — so the MCP server was still needed… until we noticed that the GitHub connector is enough as long as the bundle stays small: agents start from the index and follow the links. Hence the MCP steps being deferred, and one sentence written in place of the step: the day “find me what we said about order dedup” no longer surfaces the right document, we build the index.
No auto-trigger possible. The idea of launching the capture automatically past a certain conversation length doesn't hold: no mechanism fires on a context threshold, and hooks only run in Claude Code — not on mobile, not in Cowork. The answer came through instruction rather than infrastructure: a CLAUDE.md rule that, when the conversation gets long, offers to close with a handoff brief and to capture.
A pleasant side effect: the item “Claude project documents have no export” disappears. Those documents natively become pages in the bundle.
Stack
OKF (Markdown + YAML front matter), git, a private GitHub repo, the GitHub connector in the Claude apps, a Python linter. PostgreSQL and pgvector deferred to the moment navigation is no longer enough.
What it illustrates
A standard format doesn't replace infrastructure, but it can delay the moment it becomes necessary — and that delay is the real win. The initial plan built the server in step 2; the GitHub shortcut covers the same need with zero lines of code, and leaves a clear signal for knowing when to build. A corollary, now a note in the Brain: writing down the switch-over criterion beats building the step ahead of time. And one conviction that governs everything else: a stale brain is worse than an empty brain. A missing document triggers a search; a wrong document triggers a decision.
See also
- What a Brain is, and why it's my real asset
- Claude custom instruction system (CLAUDE.md + extensions)
- HL OS: five building blocks, one foundation
- My method, updated September 2026
